fix(tun): loopback self-route on macOS so you can ping your own IP

A point-to-point utun does not get the <own-ip> -> lo0 route that
broadcast interfaces get automatically, so packets to our own address
were routed out the TUN and dropped by the forwarding loop as 'no peer
for dst'. Add route_self_loopback(v4, v6), called from activate() after
link-up, to install host routes for our own dual-stack addresses via
lo0. No-op on Linux (kernel local route table already handles it).

feat(invite): make QR opt-in via --qr flag

The QR code consumed most of the terminal on every 'ray invite'. Default
to text-only (code + join command) and add --qr to render the scannable
code on demand, with a faint hint pointing to the flag.
style(status): move member count to network header row

feat(update): nightly + pinned-version channels, build-stamped sha, daemon-version diff

`ray update` gains three per-invocation targets (no persisted channel):
  - default: latest stable release (semver-gated, unchanged)
  - --nightly: rolling pre-release rebuilt on every commit to master;
    since nightlies share a crate version, the up-to-date decision compares
    the published checksum against the *running* binary's sha256, not semver
  - --version X: pin a specific release (downgrades allowed)
Plus --list to enumerate available releases.

build.rs stamps the git short sha into RAY_GIT_SHA; `ray version`/--version
and `ray report` now print `<crate-version> (<sha>)` so a nightly build is
identifiable. New .github/workflows/nightly.yml rolls the `nightly` tag and
rebuilds all four targets on each push to master.

Also surfaces the daemon-vs-client version diff: `ray status`/--check report a
stale daemon (e.g. an update that never restarted it) via a new IPC field.

fix(tun): assert IPv4 100.64.0.0/10 route on macOS activate

macOS route_peer_range only re-added the IPv6 200::/7 route on every
activate; the IPv4 /10 route was installed implicitly by the tun crate
at device creation and never re-asserted. macOS drops that connected
route across an up/down cycle (and some versions never install the
network route for a point-to-point utun at all), leaving a peer
reachable over IPv6 but not IPv4 -- "connected but can't ping". Add
the /10 route explicitly alongside 200::/7, idempotently, so it is
restored on every up cycle.

docs: tighten CLAUDE.md prose, note nightly/git-sha in README

Condense the verbose Modules + Key flows paragraphs (drop run-on clauses and

ci(release): generate grouped changelogs with git-cliff

Add cliff.toml and wire git-cliff into both release workflows so each release
body is built from the conventional commit messages:
  - release.yml: `--current` renders the tag's grouped changelog (Features /
    Bug Fixes / … ) plus a `prev...new` compare link
  - nightly.yml: `--unreleased` lists commits since the last stable vX.Y.Z
    (the rolling `nightly` tag is excluded via tag_pattern)
Both checkouts now fetch full history/tags so the diff range resolves.

feat(transport): version the mesh ALPN as the protocol-compat gate

Embed MESH_PROTOCOL_VERSION as a leading segment in the per-network ALPN
(rayfish/net/<version>/<prefix>). iroh negotiates the ALPN during the QUIC
handshake, so peers on different mesh versions share no common ALPN and cannot
connect — the version gate is enforced by the transport with no in-band
handshake. Bump the constant on a breaking mesh wire change to sever old peers.
The connect/files/pair ALPNs already carry their own version segment.
docs: document the ALPN-version-bump rule for connect/files/pair protocols

feat(proto): surface ALPN version mismatches to the user

The versioned ALPN is the hard compatibility gate but fails opaquely (no
connection, no reason). Two recoveries:

- ray join publishes the coordinator's mesh version in the signed network
  record (m,<v>) and compares it before dialing, bailing with a precise
  'network runs vX, you speak vY — run ray update' instead of a generic
  connect failure.
- connect_to_peer_with_alpn maps an ALPN-mismatch handshake error to an
  actionable 'peer may be on an incompatible version' hint, covering every
  dial path (join/connect/file/pair) as a heuristic fallback.

Pure helpers (mesh_version_from_record, is_alpn_mismatch) are unit-tested.

fix(firewall): make ICMP conntrack echo-type-aware to close an inbound leak

ICMP has no ports, so an echo-request and its reply collapsed to the same
conntrack Flow. A recent outbound ping primed an entry that a later inbound
echo-request matched as "return traffic", leaking inbound ICMP past a deny
default (or a removed allow-icmp rule) for up to the flow timeout.

Parse the ICMP type + echo identifier into PacketInfo, key the Flow on the
identifier, and apply the request/reply asymmetry real conntrack uses: only an
outbound echo-request opens a flow, and only an inbound echo-reply may use the
conntrack bypass. An inbound echo-request is always new inbound and faces the
rules/default. Your own ping still gets its replies under deny-inbound; a peer
can no longer ride your outbound ping to reach you.

Flow is now Copy (all fields are Copy), dropping a clone.

The unanchored regex 'v[0-9].*' matched 'ray-proto-v0.1.1' (it contains

peer_ip4, peer_online, peer_endpoint, net_role, has_net) that parse
`ray ... --json` with jq instead of scraping ANSI tables; polling
(retry_until, wait_roster); firewall data-plane probes (tcp_probe,

New `closed-net` scenario (3 hosts): live approval (requests/accept/deny),

Both registered in tests/e2e.sh and documented. Scenarios stay manual

fix(firewall): scope rules to non-joined networks; fix e2e UDP probe

The daemon rejected `ray firewall add --network <name>` when the node
wasn't currently on that network, but `network` is a match filter, not a
live reference: a rule scoped to a network you'll join later (or have
left) should be kept and simply never match. Downgrade the hard
rejection to a warning (logged + noted in the reply) so the rule is
retained.

Also fix the firewall e2e harness:
- udp_probe started its receiver by SSHing to the destination's VPN ip,
  which isn't routable from the test runner (tcp_probe SSHes to the
  public ip and uses the VPN ip only as an in-host target). Thread the
  destination's public ip through fw_allows/fw_denies and start the
  receiver there.
- move the UDP test port 5353 -> 5400 to avoid colliding with the
  daemon's own mDNS listener (UDP 5353).

feat(update): authenticate GitHub API calls with gh token

`ray update`/`--check`/`--list` hit api.github.com anonymously, capped at
60 requests/hour per IP — easy to trip while iterating. Resolve a token
from GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN, falling back to `gh auth token` when the gh
CLI is installed and logged in, and attach it as a bearer header to the
two api.github.com calls. Lifts the limit to 5000/hr; stays anonymous
(unchanged) when no token is available. Release-asset downloads on
github.com aren't rate-limited and remain unauthenticated.

fix(firewall): default suggest peer to any + propagate suggestions instantly

The `ray firewall suggest --allow/--deny` grammar required a `PEER:`
prefix, so the obvious `--allow tcp:22` parsed `tcp` as a peer hostname.
On the joiner that hostname didn't resolve, so the allow was silently
dropped while the whitelist catch-all deny was still appended — inverting
the intent from 'open SSH' into 'block everything'.

parse_suggest_token now treats a leading protocol keyword (tcp/udp/icmp/
any) as 'peer omitted', defaulting the peer to `*`. So `tcp:22`, `icmp`,
and explicit `earn01:tcp:22` / `*:tcp:22` all parse as intended.

Also broadcast a payload-free MemberSync after publishing suggestions so
connected members reconverge from the signed blob immediately instead of
waiting up to 60s for the group poller (mirrors the rename flow).

Switch the daemon's file appender from rolling::daily to the rolling
Builder with max_log_files(7), so logs older than ~a week are pruned
automatically instead of accumulating forever.

fix(dns): fix NetworkManager mode read on Linux (borrow + owned String)

Two Linux-only errors the macOS build couldn't catch (caught by the e2e

The systemd-resolved D-Bus path hardcoded the link DNS server as

.ray queries went to 127.0.0.1:53 — which no longer listens after the

Verified on a live host: dig @100.100.100.53 already resolved; only the

feat(dns): inotify resolv.conf re-assert + NetworkManager dns=none quieting

Direct-mode anti-trample, hardened for the umbrel case (NetworkManager in
default mode + a :53 resolver, which forces the /etc/resolv.conf takeover).

- run_resolv_reassert now watches /etc via inotify and repairs a trampled
  resolv.conf in ~ms instead of a 5s poll. Watches the directory (survives
  the atomic rename-replace NM/resolvconf use), with an initial assert + 30s
  tick as backstops, and a clean fallback if the watch can't arm. Threads the
  captured search domains through so a repair preserves them.
- On an NM host, DirectResolvConf::apply installs a dns=none drop-in and
  reloads NM so it stops regenerating resolv.conf entirely; revert removes it.
  Marker-guarded so we never touch an operator's own NM config.

Crash safety (dns=none makes a crash dangerous: NM silenced + resolv.conf
pointing at the now-dead resolver would blackhole DNS):
- panic hook calls emergency_restore_resolv_conf() to restore the backup and
  drop the dns=none snippet synchronously before abort().
- restore_stale_backups() also cleans a stale drop-in on next start (hard kill).

The inotify re-assert + backup/restore mirror Tailscale's direct manager; the
dns=none NM quieting is our own stronger "stop the fight" step (Tailscale
prefers NM D-Bus integration, which we already use when NM has a split-DNS
backend).

fix(config): shard per-network files + atomic writes to stop silent network loss

The single `networks.toml` was rewritten non-atomically (truncate+write) by
every load-modify-save call site with no lock. `activate()` spawns one restore
task per network concurrently, so interleaved writes/reads produced a torn read
that parsed as a valid-but-shorter config and got persisted — silently dropping
networks (observed: 3 networks down to 1 across an up/down cycle).

Shard config so a write to one network can never clobber another:
- globals in `settings.toml`, each network in `networks/<name>.toml`
- all writes go through `write_file` (temp file + atomic rename — no torn reads)
- targeted `save_network`/`load_network`/`delete_network`/`save_settings`;
  converted all 16 former `config::save` call sites
- `migrate_legacy` splits an existing `networks.toml` on first load (kept as
  `networks.toml.bak`)

Also move the config tree to `/etc/rayfish` on Linux (system-service location),
owned `root:rayfish`: dirs 0750, secret-bearing files (secret_key, networks/*,
settings.toml, invites/*) 0600 root:root, non-secret 0640 root:rayfish. The
`rayfish` group is created on install; `migrate_location` relocates a pre-/etc
`~/.config/rayfish` tree on upgrade. macOS location unchanged. Every module now
resolves paths through `config::config_dir()`.

Adds per-network round-trip, migration, unsafe-name, and a concurrency
regression test (24 concurrent saves must all survive).

fix(ci): use git-cliff --latest for release notes; drop trivial audit test

--current relied on the tag sitting at HEAD, but on a tag-push the runner
checks out a detached HEAD and the rolling nightly tag shares the commit,
so git-cliff reported "No tag exists for the current commit". --latest
picks the newest tag matching cliff.toml's tag_pattern from the timeline,
independent of HEAD.

Also drop audit::tests::test_log_path: it only asserted a hard-coded path
shape and broke CI by creating /etc/rayfish as the non-root runner.

feat(daemon): rate-limit + close control-plane flooders; coalesce reconverge

MemberSync/BlobUpdated triggers (and MeshHello/invite gossip) are cheap to
send, carry no per-message auth, and each MemberSync drove a pkarr resolve +
potential reconverge. A single member could spam them to burn CPU/network.

- src/ratelimit.rs: ControlGate, a per-connection token bucket (ratelimit
  crate) + strike counter. check() -> Allow/Drop/Close.
- Gate both control read loops (member listener, coordinator control reader);
  on sustained flood close the connection with forward::ABUSE_CODE (non-
  intentional disconnect, reconnect allowed, no quarantine).
- Coalesce MemberSync/BlobUpdated into a per-network debounced reconverge
  worker (~300ms, single-in-flight) so trigger bursts collapse into one
  pkarr resolve + reconverge and a slow reconverge never blocks the accept loop.
- TODO(abuse-hardening) left on the unbounded pending-join queue (out of scope).

feat(firewall): comma-list ports + short CLI aliases

`ray firewall add --port` now accepts a comma list (80,443 or 22,8000-9000),
expanding to one rule per item, alongside the existing single port / range / *.
parse_port_list is a pure, tested helper; the bare-number 80,443 no longer fails
as an invalid port.

Add visible_alias shortcuts across subcommands: create→new, leave→rm,
status→st/ls, version→ver, update→upgrade; firewall add→a, remove→rm/del,
show→ls/list; invite list→ls, revoke→rm; admin list→ls; connections
list→ls, approve→ok.

feat(firewall): additive suggestions + status pending summary

Suggested firewall rules are now purely additive: each allow/deny token
materializes exactly one rule and nothing is synthesized. An allow-list no
longer appends a network-scoped catch-all deny — it relies on the node's own
inbound default-deny to block the rest. Under the default-deny posture the
catch-all was redundant, and it surprised operators reviewing
`ray firewall pending` with a deny rule they never suggested.

`ray status` now ends with a `pending` summary of things awaiting the user
(firewall suggestions, join requests, file offers, connection requests), each
with the command that clears it. Counts ride StatusResponse (per-network
pending_suggestions/pending_requests, global pending_files/pending_connects)
and are exposed under `pending` in `--json`.

feat(firewall): opt-in fail-fast REJECT (TCP RST / ICMP unreachable)

Denied packets are silently dropped by default (stealthy). `ray firewall
reject on` switches to REJECT: a denied packet gets a synthetic reply so the
initiator's socket fails immediately ("connection refused") instead of
hanging to a timeout.

- src/reject.rs: build_reject() synthesizes a TCP RST (RFC 793 reset rules)
  for TCP, or ICMP/ICMPv6 destination-unreachable (UDP -> port-unreachable,
  other -> admin-prohibited) otherwise, src/dst swapped. Hand-rolled v4/v6 +
  TCP/ICMP checksums, no new deps. Returns None for loop-risk cases (incoming
  RST, incoming ICMP error, multicast/broadcast source, too-short packet).
- forward.rs: both deny directions reject when enabled. Outbound injects into
  our own TUN; inbound sends back over the peer connection (the initiator's
  conntrack admits the RST, the seeded allow-in-icmp rule admits the ICMP).
- Config toggle reject: bool (serde-default false, so existing and fresh
  firewall.toml stay on silent-drop), reject_enabled(), IPC FirewallReject,
  daemon handler, CLI `ray firewall reject on|off`, shown in `firewall show`.
- New rejects_sent metric.

feat(config): custom relay, discovery-dns, and DNS-upstream servers

Add 'ray config get/set/unset' for three global server overrides written to
settings.toml (client-side, like 'ray mdns'), applied on daemon restart:

- relay: custom iroh transport relays (multiple allowed); augment keeps n0
  defaults, --replace swaps them out
- discovery-dns: custom pkarr/discovery server for the endpoint (stacked via
  address_lookup) and the dht pkarr client (first URL, via a startup OnceLock)
- dns-upstreams: Magic DNS forwarders for non-.ray names, merged over the
  system-captured set at activate

Presets 'rayfish'/'n0' resolve to the rayfish-operated URLs / iroh defaults.
Validation rejects bad URLs/IPs and unknown keys before persist. Defaults are
unchanged when unset (byte-for-byte same endpoint bind). Verified against the
iroh 1.0.0 builder API (relay_mode + address_lookup).

feat(update): print pending release notes on ray update

Fetch each pending release's body from the GitHub releases API and print
it before swapping the binary (and in --check when behind). Stable walks
every release in (current, latest] newest-first; --nightly/--version show
the single resolved release's notes. The fetch is best-effort and bounded
to 5s so a slow or unreachable API can never freeze the update.

Also backfill CHANGELOG.md: the missing 0.1.2 section and the unreleased
entries since v0.1.2.

fix(hostname): reliably propagate ray hostname renames

A member's rename only reached the signed blob via a single MeshHello to a
coordinator, which was dropped if the member wasn't connected to one at that
moment, if the reconnect resent a hostname captured at daemon startup, or if
the live link was coordinator-dialed (no accept-side control reader). The
coordinator and every peer then kept showing the old name while the renamed
node showed the new one.

Make the rename a durable intent and drive it to completion:

- Add config.pending_hostname, the "deliver this rename" intent. Unlike
  my_hostname (which tracks the blob and is overwritten on reconverge) it
  survives a stale-blob reconverge and a daemon restart, so the diff that
  drives redelivery doesn't self-erase.
- Announce the current name fresh from config (outgoing_hostname) on every
  (re)connect instead of a value frozen at startup.
- drain_pending_rename re-sends MeshHello to every roster coordinator by
  dialing (so the coordinator's accept-side reader always reads it), on each
  reconverge, on the converged-hash early return (the stuck case), and on a
  30s backstop tick gated on a pending rename.
- apply_roster_to_dns is pending-aware: hold and show the requested name until
  the blob confirms it (rename_satisfied, collision-suffix aware), then clear.

Also:

- ray status: gather_conn_info falls back to the best available path
  (Direct > Relay > Tor) when none is iroh-selected, so a live connection
  reports its real path instead of "?".
- ray status: the network join code prints on its own line again
  (println! + indent stripping the trailing newline glued it onto the last row).
- Log files capture rayfish at debug while the console stays at info, so
  ray report bundles carry the rename-flow trace without RUST_LOG.

Adds tracing breadcrumbs across the rename lifecycle (queued, received,
unconfirmed/confirmed, drain) and unit tests for choose_path_index and
rename_satisfied.

feat(diagnostics): add ray ping and ray netcheck

ray ping <peer> sends live echo probes (new ControlMsg::Ping/Pong) over a
peer's mesh connection and reports per-probe RTT, packet loss, and whether
the path is direct or relayed. The receiver echoes the nonce over a fresh
stream (the control readers drop the request stream's send half), and the
pinging daemon correlates via a ProtocolRouter.pending_pongs nonce->oneshot
map. -c/--count, -i/--interval, and --json supported. Old peers don't reply
and show 100% loss, so no mesh protocol bump is needed.

ray netcheck reports local conditions from the iroh endpoint: bound UDP port
(fixed-forwardable vs ephemeral fallback), home relay and its latency, public
IPv4/IPv6, and UDP reachability via net_report (unstable-net-report feature).

Both commands are open reads (any local user).

fix(update): strip "(deleted)" from exe path when rewriting service unit

ray update swaps its own binary with self_replace (which unlinks the
running binary) and then rewrites the systemd unit / launchd plist using
std::env::current_exe(). On Linux that path reads back with a trailing
" (deleted)" once the old inode is gone, so the unit became
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/ray (deleted) daemon and the daemon crash-looped
with "unrecognized subcommand '(deleted)'", taking the node offline until
a manual reinstall.

Sanitize the path before substituting it into the unit so remote
self-update no longer bricks the service. Covered by a unit test.

fix(firewall): stop accepted suggestions from re-queuing and duplicating

Any change to a network's signed blob (a join, a rename, a new reusable
key) flips the blob hash and triggers a reconverge, which re-materialized
the whole suggested-firewall set and re-queued it for review, including
rules this node had already accepted. Accepting one of those repeats via
the picker appended a second identical rule.

Filter already-installed suggestions out of the pending queue (full rule
equality, so a coordinator flipping a rule's action still surfaces), and
merge picker-accepted rules by selector via firewall::dedup_by_selector
(newest wins) so a re-suggested rule replaces its predecessor instead of
stacking.

feat(firewall): add Tailscale-style mesh SSH

Embedded SSH server reachable by mesh identity, no SSH keys to manage.

- ray firewall ssh on|off: run an SSH server on this node's mesh IPs:22
  (kernel TCP, no userspace netstack); seeds/removes an allow-in-tcp:22
  passthrough rule (RuleOrigin::Ssh).
- ray firewall ssh allow|deny <net> <peer>: per-network allow list
  (peer hostname/mesh-ip/short-id, or * for any peer on the network),
  persisted as NetworkConfig.ssh_allow; live via an ArcSwap snapshot.
- ray firewall ssh show: state + per-network allow lists.
- russh server: auth_none gated on the resolved peer identity; PTY +
  interactive shell + exec via pty-process, dropping to the requested
  unix user (getpwnam). ed25519 host key persisted at config_dir/ssh_host_key.
- Lifecycle tied to the data plane (start/stop on activate/deactivate
  and the ssh on/off IPC).

Security prerequisite: ingress source-IP anti-spoofing in
forward::evaluate_inbound (DropReason::Spoof) so a peer can only source
packets from its own mesh IP, making identity-from-source-IP trustworthy.

Closes #45

fix(ssh): use russh ring backend to unbreak cross-compilation

russh's default aws-lc-rs backend pulls aws-lc-sys, whose C build fails

fix(ssh): userspace port NAT for mesh :22 (portable, no host-sshd conflict)

The kernel rejects binding <mesh-ip>:22 while a host sshd holds
0.0.0.0:22 (EADDRINUSE, even with SO_REUSEADDR/REUSEPORT) — and that is
the common case on servers, so the embedded SSH server never answered and
the host sshd did, bypassing ray's authz.

Instead of an OS-firewall redirect (nftables/pf/WFP, one impl per
platform), bind the listener on <mesh-ip>:41384 and translate mesh :22
<-> :41384 inside our own forwarding path: inbound rewrites dest
22->41384, outbound rewrites source 41384->22, TCP checksum fixed
incrementally (RFC 1624). Portable across every platform the TUN runs
on, no OS firewall, gated on the SSH server being active. The host sshd
keeps :22 on all other interfaces.

feat(apply): add user aliases and groups to the deploy spec

A ray apply spec can now define optional top-level `aliases:` (a friendly
name for a user's identity) and `groups:` (a named set of aliases and/or
hostnames), then reference them as firewall subjects or peers instead of
listing every hostname. An alias names a person and expands to all of that
person's currently-joined device hostnames; a group expands to the union of
its members.

then literal hostname; `*` is never expanded; colliding proto specs merge

feat(kick): add `ray kick` to remove a member from a closed network

Coordinators can now remove a member from a closed network by hostname,
mesh IP, or short id. The member is pruned from the roster + approved
list, the signed blob is republished, and every node disconnects from it
mesh-wide (not just the coordinator).

Mesh-wide teardown is roster-driven: reconverge_and_apply now runs
prune_departed_peers, closing and unrouting any live connection whose
peer is no longer in the just-applied signed roster (removing a peer from
the roster alone only stops routing to it; its reader keeps injecting
inbound datagrams until the connection closes). A pruning member can't
see the KICK_CODE on a connection it closes itself, so its reconnect loop
would re-dial the peer and re-form the link; prune_departed_peers records
the peer in the daemon-wide MeshCtx.pruned_peers set and the reconnect
loop consumes that one-shot entry to skip the re-dial. The kicked node
receives KICK_CODE (treated like LEAVE_CODE) so it stops reconnecting.

Refused on open networks (target would re-join) and against a coordinator
or self. Config on the kicked node is untouched, so it can re-request to
join; revoke its invite/reusable key to bar it permanently.

fix(ssh): reuse the host's OpenSSH ed25519 key for mesh SSH

The embedded mesh SSH server generated its own random host key, so once
the :22 NAT took over, a stock client saw a different fingerprint than

CHANGED.

load_host_key now discovers the host's configured host keys via sshd -T
and presents the first ed25519 key that loads unencrypted, so clients
that already trust the host keep matching their known_hosts pin. Hosts
with no usable ed25519 key fall back to the persisted generated key.

The alias is stored per-network in config (never in the signed blob), shows

fix(join): keep member network alive when coordinator offline at restore

A member (non-coordinator) whose daemon restarted while its coordinator
was unreachable aborted its network restore and never registered the
network: no ALPN handler, absent from `ray status`, inbound mesh
connections rejected with "no handler for ALPN". Restore only runs once
at boot with no retry, so the network stayed gone until the node happened
to restart again while the coordinator was online (its config was never
lost). A member was observed stuck like this for ~13 hours.

The member already holds the verified group blob (roster, keys,
firewall), which is enough to be in the network. Restore no longer treats
the coordinator connection as a hard prerequisite: on a failed dial or
handshake it registers the network from the blob and seeds the reconnect
loop with every roster member, so the node connects to any available peer
(not just the coordinator) and links the coordinator back when it
returns. The happy path (coordinator reachable) is unchanged.

Side effect: a network no longer takes ~30s to appear in `ray status`
after a member restart against a reachable coordinator.

perf(datapath): drop-newest on full datagram buffer + tune QUIC transport

On the TUN read loop, check datagram_send_buffer_space() before send_datagram:
if the peer's QUIC datagram send buffer can't take the packet without evicting
an older queued one, drop the new packet here (drop-newest) and count it under
a new DropReason::Backpressure, rather than letting QUIC drop the oldest queued
packet. For a VPN the already-accepted older packet is the more useful one. The
send path stays non-blocking (no cross-peer head-of-line blocking).

Tune the iroh transport config for the data-plane shape (one datagram stream
per peer + a few control streams): send_fairness(false) to drop pointless
round-robin scheduling, and GSO pinned on explicitly so it can't silently
regress. Congestion controller and full per-peer backpressure are left as
measured follow-ups.

On the Android target the packet interface is a VpnService fd, so the desktop

and OS-level DNS configuration never compile. Gate their now-unused imports

fix(android): start the node before bringing the tunnel up

RayfishVpnService.startTunnel established the OS VPN interface and then called
Node.up() without ever calling NodeHolder.ensureStarted(). Because the service
is START_STICKY, the system can run it with no Activity created and the UI's
ensureStarted never running, so up() returned NotStarted: the interface was up
(key icon on) while the data plane stayed down and the toggle read as stopped.
Run ensureStarted() before up() so the service is self-sufficient.

fix(android): initialize JNI context so the node starts and the tunnel comes up

On device the node never actually started: Node.start (build_headless) panicked
with "android context was not initialized". iroh-dns reads the system DNS
servers over JNI through ndk-context, which needs the app's JavaVM + Context
registered. Our .so is loaded by JNA, not System.loadLibrary, so nothing
registered it. Add a JNI entry point (RustlsInit.nativeInit, backed by the
android_jni module) that Kotlin calls once before start(): it initializes
ndk-context and rustls-platform-verifier (the latter for relay/discovery HTTPS
against Android's trust store). Wire the crate-bundled Kotlin AAR into Gradle
via cargo metadata so the verifier's Java side is on the classpath.

With the node finally starting, Node.up hit a second, latent bug: it built the
AsyncFd-backed tun reader/writer before block_on, on a plain service thread with
no reactor, panicking with "there is no reactor running". Enter the runtime for
the duration of up() before constructing them.

real VPN state (both were the reported bugs).

mobile: forward public DNS on Android and fix the tunnel IP

The Android tunnel captured all DNS to the in-daemon Magic resolver, which
answers .ray names and refused everything else, so public browsing broke
while the VPN was up. The resolver already forwards non-.ray queries to its
upstream set, but that set was empty on Android (no resolv.conf to capture
like on desktop). Add a set_dns_upstreams path from the platform: the service
reads the underlying network's DNS servers via ConnectivityManager and passes
them to the node before the tunnel captures DNS, so non-.ray lookups forward
to the phone's real resolver (that traffic egresses directly since only
100.64.0.0/10 is routed into the tunnel). Reading them needs
ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE, now declared.

Also fix the tunnel address: status() derived the node IP from the first
active network, so with no networks yet it was empty and the tunnel fell back
to a placeholder with a broken return path. Derive it from the node identity
instead (the same value every network uses), so the tunnel comes up on the
real mesh IP on first bring-up.

fix(mesh): don't let a stale disconnect evict a reconnected peer

When a peer's process is killed (common on mobile), it never closes its
endpoint. The peer restarts and re-dials with the same identity; the
coordinator registers the fresh connection before the old one's idle
timeout fires. When the stale connection finally times out, its reader
fired a DisconnectEvent and the cleanup and reconnect loops removed the
peer's route by (ip, network) unconditionally, evicting the fresh
connection. The peer still held a live link so it never redialed, and it
showed offline on the coordinator until toggled.

Tag each DisconnectEvent with the dropped connection's stable_id and only
remove the route when the stored connection is still that same one
(remove_peer_from_network_if). The synthetic cold-restore kick carries
None and still forces its reconnect dial. Roster-driven removals (kick,
prune) stay unconditional.

Mechanism: device certs gain a signed `generation`. Unpairing (primary only)
bumps the user's generation and publishes it as a one-number "floor" to pkarr
under the user's own key (`_rayfish_certgen`, self-authenticating). Every peer
rejects a cert below the signer's floor, so revocation is enforced verifier-
side and reaches networks the revoking user does not coordinate. The devices
you keep are re-issued fresh certs at the new generation, auto-pushed over the
mesh (`ControlMsg::CertRefresh`); a keeper offline during the bump refreshes on
its next reconnect. The removed device is dropped from your networks, demoted
locally (no own-device auto-admit or file auto-accept), and best-effort told to
wipe its own cert (`ControlMsg::Unpaired`).

Back-compat: `generation == 0` signs over the device key alone, exactly the
pre-epoch scheme, so certs already issued keep verifying with no reissue.

Enforcement runs through one pure `revocation::cert_decision` helper at
admission, the MeshHello handler, and reconverge/prune. The floor cache is
fail-open when unseen (floor 0) and monotonic once seen. A small, never-
published local do-not-reissue set stops a revoked device refreshing back in.

Limits (documented): the floor is republished only while the primary runs;
any unpair rotates the whole fleet, so an offline keeper is rejected by other
users' networks until it reaches the primary; only the primary can unpair.

fix(mesh): spawn the peer data reader on a peer's first connection

`PeerTable::add` decides whether to start the single per-connection data
reader (in `register_peer_conn`) from its `conn_changed` return. The check
was self-defeating: `or_insert_with` seeded a brand-new entry with the
incoming `networks`/`conn`, then computed

    first_ever   = e.networks.is_empty();          // already {net} -> false
    conn_changed = e.conn.stable_id() != stable || first_ever;  // conn==conn -> false

so a peer's first registration returned `conn_changed = false` and the
reader was never spawned. Outbound worked, inbound datagrams reached QUIC
but nothing consumed them, so every mesh connection saw 100% inbound
packet loss (and the audit `connect` event never fired). It affected every
network, not just direct connections.

Decide newness from the entry's state before the add mutates it, via the
`Entry` API so a vacant slot (new peer) is known for certain, and extract
the pure `connection_is_new(prior, incoming)` helper.

reconnect as new but a same-connection re-add as not, and an end-to-end
test that a tagged datagram sent over a real connection is untagged and
forwarded to the TUN by `spawn_peer_reader`. Verified the real-connection
tests fail on the pre-fix logic.

user taps "Unpair this device" (new Node::unpair FFI + You screen control),

network's live nullifiers at admission, the coordinator MeshHello handler, and

fix(audit): log disconnect when a peer's last network drops via remove_by_network

The audit contract is one `disconnect` event per peer that fully drops (see the
PeerTable.audit doc). `remove` and `remove_peer_from_network` honor it, but
`remove_by_network` (the `ray leave` path) removed a peer's last-network entry
without logging, so leaving a network silently skipped the disconnect audit for
any peer only reachable via that network. Log it in the same place it cleans
`by_id`, matching the other two removal paths.

refactor(daemon): extract MeshConnection owning both planes of a peer link

ConnectionManager::drive_mesh_connection into its own MeshConnection type
(src/daemon/mesh_connection.rs). One MeshConnection drives a single mesh
connection for its whole lifetime: it spawns and owns the connection's one
data reader, runs the accept_bi/ControlFrame demux loop, and is the single
place that reports the DisconnectEvent to the supervisor when the loop ends.

This removes the split ownership where the forward.rs reader reported the
drop while the demux ran elsewhere. The reader (spawn_peer_reader) is now a
pure forwarder: on connection loss or cancellation it just exits, since the
owning MeshConnection observes the same close. ForwardCtx drops its
disconnect_tx; the LEAVE_CODE/KICK_CODE intentional-close classification

fix(android): forward public DNS through DnsResolver.rawQuery

While the VPN was up, non-.ray lookups were handed to the underlying
network's IPv4 resolvers and forwarded as plaintext UDP on port 53,
ignoring any Private DNS (DoT/DoH) the device had configured. That is a
privacy downgrade: a user on encrypted DNS silently dropped to cleartext
whenever Rayfish was active (issue #81).

Run a small loopback UDP proxy (DnsProxy) that forwards each raw query
through the Android platform resolver via DnsResolver.rawQuery, pinned to
the underlying non-VPN network. rawQuery honors the system Private DNS
setting, so encrypted DNS keeps working. The Rust Magic DNS resolver
points its upstream at 127.0.0.1:<proxy-port> instead of the bare
resolver IPs.

The app is also excluded from its own tunnel (addDisallowedApplication on
its own package) so its sockets use the real underlying network and DNS
can't loop back through the TUN.

Rust: Resolver gains set_upstream_addrs for explicit ip:port upstreams
(the desktop bare-IPv4/:53 path is unchanged); the mobile FFI parses each
upstream string as either a socket address or a bare IPv4 on port 53.

DnsResolver needs API 29; on older devices DnsProxy.start returns null and
the service falls back to the previous plaintext upstream path.

fix(mesh): decide membership only from the signed record; fix unpair, status, overlay flap

Four fixes from a live-mesh debugging session where a valid member
(scw-iroh) kept dropping out and a self-unpaired device stayed listed.

- transport: never publish overlay IPs (100.64.0.0/10, 200::/7) as iroh
  transport candidates. A node advertising its own tunnel address made
  iroh try to run the tunnel over itself, so paths flapped and drove the
  reconverge churn below. Root cause of the drop-outs.

- mesh: a connection close never changes membership. Only a signed roster
  decides who is a member, so a kick-coded or flapping close is transport
  teardown, never an eviction (a member can no longer evict the
  coordinator during a flap). A real `ray kick` is now an explicit,
  network-scoped `ControlMsg::KickedFromNetwork`: the member confirms it
  against the signed record and leaves just that network only when the
  record confirms the removal. A coordinator ignores the message.

- unpair: a secondary that unpairs itself now asks its primary, in-band
  over the live link (`ControlMsg::RequestUnpair`), to write the
  authoritative nullifier across the networks it coordinates, then tears
  itself down. Before, a secondary could not revoke its own device (it
  holds no network key) so it just disconnected and lingered in the
  roster. Best-effort: if the primary link is down, the local teardown
  still happens and the primary keeps a stale entry until `ray unpair`.

- status: group devices by effective identity so a visible primary
  anchors its own group instead of being printed twice.

fix(connect): persist direct-network co-coordinator key across restart

A `ray connect` requester is made a co-coordinator of the auto-created
direct network on admission. The old path granted the network key over a
separate best-effort `AdminGrant` stream sent right after the Welcome: the
key reached the requester's live state, but its config write raced
`finalize_join`'s config rewrite and lost, so the key was never persisted.
On the next daemon restart the requester came back as a plain member and
could no longer manage the link. Verified live: after `systemctl restart`,
`ray admin <net> list` reported "not a coordinator".

Fold the key into the join handshake's `Welcome` instead (a new optional
`direct_key`, verified against the network pubkey before adoption). It is
delivered synchronously on the stream the joiner already reads, so
`persist_join_config` writes it atomically before `finalize_join` and the
requester survives a restart as a co-coordinator. This also removes the
best-effort no-retry grant stream entirely; `AdminGrant` stays for
`ray admin add`. Folds into the unreleased mesh v2 wire batch.

Also fix the e2e harness: `run.sh` invoked `ray admin list <net>` but the
CLI grammar is `ray admin <net> list`, so the coordinator check errored for
both peers regardless of state.

fix(mesh): drop overlay IPs from iroh's direct-address candidates

Use iroh's new `Builder::direct_addr_filter` to keep rayfish overlay addresses
(100.64.0.0/10, 200::/7) out of the gathered direct-address set, so a mesh IP
bound on the TUN is never advertised, published, or offered as a holepunch /
NAT-traversal candidate. Previously the overlay IP leaked into the candidate set
and peers dialed it, looping the underlay back through the tunnel (a flapping
path that fell back to relay latency).

Pins iroh (and iroh-base/-dns/-relay) to the fork branch carrying the API,
upstream PR n0-computer/iroh#4397.

fix(android): fully tear down the tunnel on disable

Disabling the VPN dropped the mesh connection but left the interface up:
the key icon stayed and the tun device lingered, and the control plane
kept the radio busy. The offline stop path closed the endpoint but never
released the tunnel fd.

Regressed in bef248f, when Android disable moved from down() (which calls
detach_tun and closes the fds) to the offline stop() path. That path only
cancels the shutdown token and closes the endpoint; the TUN writer never
observes the token (it exits on channel-close, and tun_tx keeps a sender
alive), so its dup of the VPN fd leaked and the interface stayed up.

both the interface and the endpoint go down and the device goes fully

and write halves via an Arc instead of split() into two objects, with no
lock. read_into exposes an initialised MTU-sized tail on the caller's
pool and recv's into it (tun-rs has no ReadBuf/AsyncRead, so read_buf's
uninit fill is unavailable), preserving the zero-copy split_to hand-off.
The IPv6 /128 is now assigned by the DeviceBuilder cross-platform,
replacing the netlink/ifconfig configure_ipv6 shell-out; the 200::/7

This is the groundwork for a later Linux GRO/GSO write-batching path.

feat: on-demand mesh connections with idle teardown

Connect to peers lazily on the first packet that needs them instead of
eagerly dialing every roster member at startup, and tear down connections
that have been idle past a timeout. An idle on-demand node holds zero peer
connections, so it draws no QUIC-keepalive radio (near-zero mobile battery).
The link re-forms automatically on the next packet either side sends.

On by default (`on_demand`, opt out with `ray config set on-demand off`);
`idle_timeout_secs` tunes the teardown window.

- Lazy dial: run_mesh buffers packets for an unconnected peer, dials once
  (5s-timeout-bounded, in-flight dedup), then flushes the buffer on connect
  or drops it on failure. RosterRouteMap resolves the (non-reversible) mesh
  IP back to an identity for known-but-unconnected members.
- Idle teardown: IDLE_CODE close reason + last-activity tracking (tx/rx/
  control) + a stable-id-guarded reaper, spawned only on on-demand nodes.
  handle_disconnect never reconnects an Idle close, and on-demand suppresses
  the eager Transient/Kicked reconnect (re-dial is lazy).
- Local restore: coordinator and member restore register from the verified
  blob + seed the route map without dialing.
- Status: three-state active/idle/offline (PeerState). Offline shows only
  after a real failed reach; a fresh boot reads all-idle. `ray ping` dials
  on demand and refreshes reachability.
- CLI: `ray config` covers the auto-update and on-demand on/off toggles.
- Metrics: lazy_dials / lazy_dials_failed / idle_teardowns.

Implements the connection-lifecycle half of #78 (discovery/publication
suppression deferred).

fix: make on-demand opt-in (default off)

Idle teardown only holds if every peer honors the IDLE_CODE close and declines
to reconnect. On a mixed fleet (or against any peer that re-dials after the
close) the reaper and the peer's reconnect fight, flapping the link every idle
cycle: the connection tears down, comes back relay-first, and forwarding churns.
On always-on servers that is pure downside with no battery benefit.

Default on_demand to false so a node only tears down idle links when explicitly
opted in (`ray config set on-demand on`); the mobile embedder still forces it on,
where the battery win is real and the fleet is a single device.

No data-plane change: with both peers opted in, the Idle/Transient reconnect
suppression already prevents the flap.

fix: make desktop TUN read cancel-safe (was wedging the data plane)

run_mesh races the TUN read in a select! against dial-completion, so the read
future is dropped the moment a lazy dial finishes. The desktop read_into grew the
caller's pool by READ_RESERVE bytes before its recv().await and only truncated
after, so a cancelled read left those stray bytes in the pool. Every later
split_to(n) then sliced at the wrong offset, parsing every packet as garbage and
silently killing all forwarding and Magic DNS until a restart. This is why the
mesh worked until the first on-demand dial completed, then went dead.

Read into an owned scratch buffer and append to the pool only after recv returns,
so a cancelled read leaves the pool untouched. Document the cancel-safety
requirement on the TunRead trait; the Android reader already satisfies it
(advance_mut runs only after the synchronous read).

Reverts the stopgap on_demand=off default: with the read fixed, on-demand works,
so it stays on by default.

feat(on-demand): eager-connect + per-connection idle teardown

Replace the fully-lazy on-demand model with eager-connect plus per-connection
idle close, so status is accurate from boot and older peers stay reachable.

- Eager-connect the roster at startup on all nodes (like the desktop default),
  so a peer we cannot reach shows Offline instead of optimistically Idle. On-demand
  now only governs teardown, not startup.
- Each connection times itself out: a select arm in MeshConnection::run closes the
  link with IDLE_CODE after idle_timeout of no data-plane traffic, reports Idle,
  and exits. Removed the separate idle reaper (the owning loop is the only closer,
  so it also reports, with no cross-task signalling).
- Gate idle-close on a per-peer capability: peers advertise FEATURE_IDLE_CLOSE in
  NetworkHandles (sent by both ends, unlike the one-way MeshHello). A peer that
  does not advertise it (a build predating the idle close code) is held open, never
  flapped. The feature bit is #[serde(default)] so legacy frames decode to zero.
- Idle is measured on the data plane only. last_active is stamped by outbound
  send_datagram and inbound resolve_inbound_by_id (both piggyback on lookups the
  hot path already does) and seeded on connection install. Control frames no longer
  count, so background control chatter cannot hold an idle connection open.

fix(on-demand): keep a persistently-offline peer flagged offline

The eager dial stamped reachability on its result, but the reconnect
supervisor retried through dial_peer_once without ever re-stamping, so
only the boot-time failure was recorded. After STATUS_OFFLINE_WINDOW
(300s) that stamp went stale and a still-down peer decayed back to idle.

Stamp reachability inside dial_peer_once itself (the shared choke point
for both the reconnect loop and the lazy dialer): note_fail on a failed
dial, note_ok once a live connection exists. Each reconnect retry now
refreshes last_fail every <=30s, well inside the window, so a peer stays
offline while it is down and flips to active on the next successful dial.
Drops the now-redundant stamp in the lazy dial_target path.

fix(exit-node): keep inbound connections alive under a full tunnel

Selecting an exit node cut the client's own inbound connections. A default
route into the TUN captures every packet with no more specific route, and
that includes the replies sshd generates for a session that arrived on the
public IP: routing is stateless, so the reply is just an outbound packet
whose destination happens to be the remote peer. It went into the tunnel,
came out of the gateway masqueraded to the gateway's address, and the peer
dropped an answer from a host it never contacted. A headless box locked
itself out the moment `ray exit-node use` landed, with no way back in but
the serial console.

The client now installs an nftables conntrack pair alongside its ip rules:
`prerouting` marks any connection whose first packet arrived on a non-TUN
interface, `output` restores that mark on the locally-generated replies so
they match the existing fwmark bypass rule and leave the way they came in.
It matches only on our own ctmark, so traffic the node originates (iroh's
already-marked sockets included) is untouched. Tailscale does not do this
(tailscale/tailscale#10940 is open); reaching the host over the mesh IP was
the only recourse.

The e2e asserts it directly: step 4 now runs an ordinary `ssh` command while
the tunnel is up, which is what used to hang. That also lets the client phase
drop the detached self-reverting probe it needed to survive its own SSH dying,
so the scenario is plain commands again, with a self-revert failsafe armed on
the host before any tunnel goes up.

Simplification pass over the rest of the module while here:

- `enable`/`disable` are idempotent and drive off the on-disk sysctl snapshot
  alone, so the panic-hook path is no longer a second restore implementation
  (`emergency_teardown` is gone; the hook calls `disable`). `ExitServer` drops
  its snapshot cell and the dead-code cfg_attrs that went with it.
- `Daemon::apply_exit_node` reconciles both roles in one place, replacing the
  copy of that logic in `activate` and in each of the two IPC arms.
- `evaluate_inbound` takes an `ExitContext` instead of four loose arguments,
  losing its `too_many_arguments` exemption and shrinking every call site.
- one nft runner instead of two; the mark hex is derived from `SOCKET_MARK`
  rather than duplicated as a second constant that had to agree with it.

fix(tun): re-assign the overlay IPv6 address on activate

Linux flushes an interface's global IPv6 addresses when its link goes down
(keep_addr_on_down defaults to 0) and never restores them, while IPv4
addresses survive. The overlay /128 was only assigned when the TUN device was
created, so `ray down` dropped it and `ray up` never put it back: the node kept
routing 200::/7 into the TUN while owning no address in it, and every IPv6 peer
silently got no answer until the daemon restarted. IPv4 kept working, which is
what made it look like a peer-specific failure.

Re-assign the address over netlink on every activate (idempotent, replace), and
assert it in the exit-node e2e, which cycles the data plane repeatedly.

refactor(exit-node): cut the dead nft forward chain and duplicated plumbing

The gateway's nftables `forward` chain was decoration: it had `policy accept`,
and an `accept` rule only ends the chain it sits in, so it could never override
a drop in another table (ufw, firewalld, Docker's iptables policy) and added
nothing where no such drop existed. Only the postrouting masquerade does real
work, so that is all we install now.

The rest is duplication:
- one `reload_exit_state` instead of `reload_exit_policy` + `reload_exit_client`
  reading the same config off disk twice on every activate;
- `exit_node_allow` / `exit_node_use` find their network once instead of
  scanning the list, then scanning again with an `expect`;
- the forwarding loop threads a plain `ExitClient` (default = no selection)
  instead of an `Option<&ExitClient>`, and picks the peer to dial through one
  `dial_dst` helper rather than repeating the overlay-or-exit branch;
- `ray exit-node status` no longer re-filters by network client-side, which the
  daemon already did.

Also import the exit-node types instead of spelling out `crate::exit_node::…`
at each use, and hoist the per-function `use` lines in the Linux kernel helpers.

fix(exit-node): an exit node is an internet gateway, not a way into its LAN

The gateway accepted any non-overlay destination from an allowed peer and handed
it to the kernel to forward and masquerade. That included every address the
gateway can reach but the internet cannot: its private LAN, its loopback, and
169.254.169.254, the cloud metadata service that hands out the instance's
credentials. Permitting a peer to route out through you should not also give it
the inside of your network. Transit is now limited to globally-routable
destinations; reaching a gateway's LAN is a subnet-router capability, not
something an exit-node offer implies.

Two smaller fixes alongside it:

- `ray exit-node use` validated the chosen peer against the roster by device
  identity only, while the data path matches on the user identity too. Selecting
  a paired multi-device peer was rejected as "does not advertise an exit node"
  even though routing to it would have worked. Both matchers now agree.
- The panic hook removed the gateway's forwarding/NAT but left the client's
  full-tunnel rules and conntrack table behind, outliving the TUN they point at.

refactor: collapse the repeated netlink and roster boilerplate

Three functions in `tun.rs` each opened a netlink socket, spawned the connection
driver, resolved the TUN's link index, and aborted the driver on every path out,
around one real call. That preamble is now `with_tun_link`, so `ensure_ipv6_addr`,
`route_peer_range` and `route_magic_dns` are each just the call they make.

The exit-node control plane had the same shape: every method opened the network,
took the state lock and walked the roster inline, nested three or four closures
deep. `roster` / `roster_member` do that once. As a side effect the roster is now
matched the same way everywhere (device identity, or the user identity a paired
peer is stored under), which is what the `exit-node use` fix was about.

fix(exit-node): stop the exit peer bypassing the client's firewall

Return traffic from the chosen exit node was waved straight through: accepted
before the anti-spoof check and before the firewall, with any source IP it liked.
Selecting an exit node therefore handed that peer the ability to reach every
service on the host, unfiltered, which is a trust escalation nobody asks for when
they ask for an internet gateway.

The bypass was never needed. The firewall's conntrack keys a flow symmetrically
(`local` is the source outbound and the destination inbound), so our packet to
8.8.8.8:443 and its reply hash to the same entry. The reply only fails the
ingress anti-spoof, which demands the source be the sender's mesh IP and a reply
is sourced from the host we reached. So exempt exit return traffic from that one
check (and only when the sender is our exit peer on that network, the source is
public, and the packet is addressed to us), then run the firewall as normal: the
conntrack entry our own outbound packet created is what admits the reply.

The exit node is still on-path for the flows we open and can forge within them,
as any gateway or ISP can. What it can no longer do is dial a service we never
opened a flow to.

fix(exit-node): roll back a failed enable, refuse overlay transit, keep pre-existing connections alive

Four fixes from an audit of the branch:

- `enable()` is not atomic: the forwarding sysctls go on before the NAT rules
  load. A failure there left the host forwarding without masquerade, pushing
  overlay-sourced packets out the uplink un-NAT'd while the daemon still
  accepted transit. Roll back the sysctls and drop the offers instead, and
  report it. Snapshotting the prior sysctls is now a precondition of enabling
  rather than best-effort: without that file we could never put them back.

- `is_transitable` did not actually exclude the overlay ranges its own comment
  claimed it did (`is_private()` does not cover 100.64.0.0/10). Only latent,
  since the data path routes an overlay destination to its peer long before it
  asks about transit, but the function reads as the whole answer to "may we
  forward this?" and should not depend on its caller having checked.

- The client's conntrack mark was only set on `ct state new`, so a connection
  already established when the tunnel came up kept a ctmark of 0, its replies
  went out the tunnel, and it was cut. This killed the very SSH session you run
  `ray exit-node use` from. Mark every packet arriving on a non-TUN interface.

- `ray exit-node use` off Linux reported success and then routed nothing, since
  the full-tunnel install is Linux-gated. Say that instead.

feat(exit-node): offer an exit node on macOS and FreeBSD

The gateway role was Linux-only because it was written against nftables. Both
BSDs have pf, so the same shape works there: turn on the forwarding sysctls
(`net.inet.ip.forwarding`, `net.inet6.ip6.forwarding`) and load a NAT rule that
masquerades overlay-sourced traffic to the address of whichever uplink the
default route uses, per family, re-resolved by pf so a DHCP renewal cannot
strand it on a stale address.

pf only evaluates an anchor the main ruleset references, and that ruleset is the
host's, not ours: rewriting it would trample whatever firewall is already
loaded. So we load into an anchor it already points at. macOS's stock pf.conf
carries `nat-anchor "com.apple/*"`, so a sub-anchor beneath it needs no change
to any file we don't own; on FreeBSD the operator adds the anchor themselves. In
both cases we verify the reference exists before trusting it, because a rule in
an unreferenced anchor is silently never matched, and a gateway that forwards
without masquerading is worse than one that refuses to start. pf is taken with
`pfctl -E`, whose reference count means we neither disturb a pf that is already
up nor tear one down that somebody else still wants; the token rides in the same
on-disk snapshot the sysctls do, so the panic hook can give it back.

Nothing here builds FreeBSD (it is in neither CI nor the release matrix, and
neither cargo nor cross can cross-compile it from this tree), so the two values
that differ between the BSDs are `cfg!` expressions rather than `#[cfg]` items:
that way both arms are type-checked wherever the file builds at all, instead of
being code no compiler sees until it reaches a user.

Using an exit node stays Linux-only. It rests on marking iroh's underlay sockets
so they can be policy-routed around the tunnel they carry, and neither BSD has
an equivalent we can reach through iroh yet.

feat(exit-node): socket hook groundwork for using an exit node on macOS

UDP and the relay's TCP dial) and re-runs on rebind. On Linux the hook sets
SO_MARK as before, now covering the relay connection too, which previously
leaked into the tunnel and deadlocked when the exit peer was relay-only. On
macOS it pins sockets to the default-route interface (IP_BOUND_IF), gated on a
FULL_TUNNEL flag so peers on non-default interfaces stay reachable while no
exit node is in use; flipping the flag requires an endpoint rebind, wired up in
a later commit.
