fix(android): serialize VPN bring-up and teardown, fix null-intent dispatch

Toggling the VPN off and back on quickly raced startTunnel() (main
thread) against stopTunnel() (a spawned thread): both read and wrote
the tunnel/dnsProxy fields with no synchronization, and a fast
off-then-on could leave the service reporting the VPN on with no
tunnel and no DNS proxy pointed at the right port. Route all bring-up
and teardown through a single-threaded executor so an off-then-on
always ends with the tunnel up and an on-then-off always ends in
standby or offline, with no interleaving possible. startForeground is
still called synchronously and promptly; only the blocking FFI work
moves to the executor.

Also fix onStartCommand matching action-less start intents into the
null-intent restart-recovery branch: distinguish a genuinely null
intent from one with no action set, so a caller that starts the
service without pre-writing the enabled pref still gets a tunnel
instead of a stop.

Minor: post the standby notification text before the blocking
teardown instead of after, and import java.util.concurrent types
instead of using fully-qualified names.

fix(android): run Node.up inline and stop blocking onDestroy on the executor

startTunnelBlocking spawned Node.up onto a detached thread and returned
right away, so the serializing executor could run a queued stop task
before up() had actually executed: an on-then-off double-tap could let
a late up(fd) re-attach the TUN after down() already ran, leaving the
data plane live while the notification reads standby. detachFd() also
raced tunnel?.close() from the stop path. Call Node.up inline instead,
since startTunnelBlocking already runs on the executor thread and
never the main thread.

onDestroy also blocked the main thread on submit(...).get() for the
whole executor queue plus its own teardown, risking the 20s
foreground-service ANR deadline behind a queued startTunnelBlocking.
Dropped the wait: nodeExecutor.shutdown() already lets every queued
task, including this teardown, run to completion in the background,
so the blocking wait bought nothing.

fix: keep standby node alive on lost VPN slot and races

establish() returning null means the VPN slot went to another app
(Tailscale, say), not that anything is broken; with stay-online on we
now stay in standby and keep the control plane running instead of
stopSelf()-ing the whole service. The offline ACTION_STOP path now
calls stopSelf(startId) instead of a bare stopSelf(), so a queued stop
can no longer kill a service a newer start command already landed for.
dnsProxy.stop() is wrapped so a throwable there cannot skip the rest of
teardown or crash the process, and startAutoAcceptPoller() in
enterStandby moved onto nodeExecutor so autoAcceptPoller is only
touched from one thread.

fix(android): start the file poller and stop the dns proxy on the lost-slot standby path

The establish()-null standby branch returned before startAutoAcceptPoller()
ran, so files stopped landing in Downloads on exactly the path standby was
built for. It also left dnsProxy pointed at a socket and thread with no
tunnel to serve, leaking one more of each on every retry since setEnabled
stays true. Start the poller and stop/null the proxy in that branch.

Also wrap the body of every nodeExecutor.execute submission in a top-level
try/catch so a throw from the VpnService.Builder chain (malformed address
from status(), only blank-checked) can no longer reach the default
uncaught-exception handler and kill the process.

fix(android): unify tunnel bring-up failure path and structural poller start

Route Builder throws and establish() returning null through the same
failure handler, since a malformed tunnel/mesh address (only blank-
checked, not validated) previously escaped the pfd == null path and
was swallowed by the outer executor catch: dnsProxy stayed set with
no tunnel to serve, leaking a socket and thread on every retry, with
no standby fallback and no stopSelf when stay-online was off.

Also start the auto-accept poller directly in stopTunnel's standby
branch instead of relying on some earlier path having started it, and
null the tunnel field when Node.up() throws after detachFd() so a
retry can rebuild instead of needing a full stop first.

fix(android): unify Node.up() failure with the other bring-up failure paths

Node.up() throwing used to just log and null the tunnel field, skipping the
dnsProxy stop and standby fallback that establish()==null and a Builder throw
already got. That left dnsProxy orphaned (leaking a socket and thread on every
retry) and could leave the service alive with a stale "Mesh tunnel active"
notification when stay-online was off. Extracted the shared recovery into
handleBringUpFailure() and route all three failure points through it, and only
start the auto-accept poller on paths that actually claim standby.

Also fix stopTunnel's standby branch: it started the poller without ever
bringing the control plane up, so a fresh service instance (e.g. from
HomeScreen's ACTION_STOP) could post "Online, VPN off, files still work" while
the node was never started and no file would ever arrive. Now calls
NodeHolder.ensureStarted before downNode, same as enterStandby does.

fix(android): ensure control plane before standby in handleBringUpFailure

handleBringUpFailure could post the standby notification and start the
auto-accept poller without the control plane actually running, on the
path where ensureStarted failed inside startTunnelBlocking but
establish() still succeeded. Bring the control plane up (idempotent)
before declaring standby, mirroring stopTunnel's standby branch.

Also thread startId from onStartCommand through startTunnel and
startTunnelBlocking into handleBringUpFailure, so its offline branch
uses stopSelf(startId) instead of a bare stopSelf(), consistent with
the ACTION_STOP path.

feat(android): add the stay-online toggle to the You screen

Wires NodeHolder's stay-online pref (added in tasks 1-2, previously
dead) to a ToggleCard on You and drives RayfishVpnService directly:
turning it on while the VPN is off starts the service into standby,
turning it off while in standby takes the node fully offline. A flip
while the VPN tunnel is up only changes what the next teardown does.

fix(android): keep-files-working toggle must not start a VPN tunnel

Turning on "keep files working when the VPN is off" started the
service with a plain intent, which lands in startTunnel() and runs the
full Builder/establish() chain: exactly the VPN slot grab (and consent
dialog) the toggle exists to avoid, since the whole point is to let
another VPN app (Tailscale) hold that slot while Rayfish keeps its
control plane up for file transfer.

Add a dedicated ACTION_STANDBY that routes straight to enterStandby(),
bringing up only the control plane, and have YouScreen use it instead
of the action-less intent when the VPN is currently off.

fix(android): gate stay-online toggle on real VPN state, not stale intent

NodeHolder.isEnabled is persisted intent, not observed state, and goes
stale-true exactly when another VPN app steals the slot: the flagship
case this feature exists for. Reboot with the toggle left on, enable
Tailscale, then open Rayfish left isEnabled true with no tunnel, no
node, and no service, so YouScreen's guard silently dropped the standby
request.

- YouScreen: gate on status?.running instead of NodeHolder.isEnabled,
  and fix a stale comment about RayfishApp never calling ensureStarted
  (followLink does).
- RayfishVpnService: ACTION_STANDBY is now a no-op when a tunnel is
  already up, so a pref flip can never tear one down.
- RayfishApp launch restore: clear the stale isEnabled intent when
  VpnService.prepare() shows another app holds the slot (same reasoning
  onRevoke already uses), and start standby directly when stay-online
  is on but the VPN is not being restored, so a killed process actually
  comes back online instead of requiring a toggle bounce.

fix: stop the standby toggle from acting on a stale status cache

status is a 2s poll cache and can be null or lagging right after an
Activity recreation, so the You-screen "keep files working" toggle could
read stale data in both directions: kill a VPN the user just turned on in
Home, or silently no-op when it should bring standby up.

Send ACTION_STANDBY unconditionally on the ON branch (it already no-ops
when a tunnel is up). Add ACTION_EXIT_STANDBY for the OFF branch instead
of bare ACTION_STOP: it tears the node fully offline and stops the
service only when there is no live tunnel, leaving a running VPN alone.
Both decisions now come from the service's own tunnel field, which never
lags.

fix: decide standby/exit-standby on nodeExecutor, not the main thread

ACTION_STANDBY and ACTION_EXIT_STANDBY read the tunnel field on the
main thread inside onStartCommand, but it is only written on
nodeExecutor by startTunnelBlocking and stopTunnel. For the seconds
those calls take to run, the main-thread read is stale, so a
just-started tunnel could be torn down by ACTION_EXIT_STANDBY, and
ACTION_STANDBY could silently no-op while a teardown it thought was
already done was still in flight, leaving the notification wrong.

Move both guards inside nodeExecutor.execute, where they run
serialized against the bring-up/teardown and see the settled value.
ACTION_STANDBY still posts the foreground notification promptly (it
arrives via startForegroundService) and corrects it if a tunnel turns
out to already be up. ACTION_EXIT_STANDBY now returns START_STICKY
instead of START_NOT_STICKY, since stopSelf(startId) already cancels
the sticky restart on the path that actually stops.

Also fix a comment in YouScreen.kt that claimed the tunnel field never
lags; it lags until the service re-checks it on nodeExecutor.

fix(android): seed standby notification from current tunnel state

When ACTION_STANDBY arrives, use tunnel == null as the initial notification text (a best guess to meet the foreground-service deadline) rather than unconditionally assuming standby. The executor task still decides for real and corrects the notification if needed.

Also correct the YouScreen comment: ACTION_STANDBY routes to enterStandbyBlocking on nodeExecutor and re-posts the notification if a tunnel is up, not a pure no-op.
feat(files): track in-flight transfers in a registry

fix(transfers): clamp note_progress to size and test re-send of a finished hash

note_progress assigned transferred unclamped while provider_progress already
clamped to size, so a receive-side bug reporting more than the offer's size
could push a TransferInfo past 100%. Clamp it the same way.

Also add a regression test pinning down that re-registering a send for a hash
that already finished does not disturb the earlier Done entry.
feat(files): report byte progress while downloading an accepted file

fix(files): don't mark a transfer Done before the file hits disk

accept_file finished the transfer registry as soon as the blob fetch
completed, before get_bytes, create_dir_all, fs::write, or chown ran.
A write failure (full disk, bad permissions) after that point still
returned an error to the caller, but the registry, and the Android
completion notification it drives, already said the file was saved.

Move finish(true) to right before the successful return, and add a
FinishGuard (Arc<TransferRegistry> + id) that marks the transfer
failed on drop unless explicitly disarmed by success(). This also
covers a cancelled accept_file (e.g. daemon shutdown mid-fetch)
leaving an entry stuck in Transferring forever.

Also fix the peer label in the registry to use fmt_short(), matching
list_files and every other tracing call in this file; it was using a
raw 8-char prefix instead of the usual 10-char short id.

feat(files): learn when a peer actually pulls a sent file

send_file returns once the offer is delivered, not when bytes move: the
peer pulls the blob out of our store whenever it accepts. Wire the
iroh-blobs provider events (NotifyLog on get requests) into the transfer
registry so a sender can tell Offered from Transferring from a real Done,
and register the outgoing transfer at offer time so those events have a
hash to match against.

fix(files): register a send before the offer can be pulled, match provider events by peer

send_file registered the transfer only after the offer round-trip finished,
but an auto-accepting peer can fetch the whole blob and close its connection
before that. Every provider event then arrived before the entry existed, so
the send stuck at Offered forever and the ghost entry never expired (list_at
only evicts finished entries). Register right after add_slice, before
dialing, and finish(false) the entry on each send-path failure instead.

Provider events also matched on blob hash alone, so the same file offered to
two peers registered two entries under one hash, and whichever peer pulled
first completed the oldest entry, regardless of who it actually was. Add
`connected: ConnectMode::Notify` to the event mask, track connection id to
peer id in the bootstrap pump, and match provider events on (hash, peer) so a
pull by one peer can never complete another peer's entry. An event for a
connection whose peer never resolved is drained (so the provider never
stalls) and dropped rather than falling back to hash-only matching.

Also make register_send's display label the peer's fmt_short(), matching
register_receive, and let a Started event revive an entry that previously
finished Failed, so a retried pull that succeeds doesn't leave the sender
stuck showing a failure for a file that did arrive.

fix(transfers): bound revive-on-Started and drain unhandled provider notify variants

Transfer registry: only revive a Failed send on a fresh Started if it failed
recently (within TERMINAL_TTL) and the failure happened during a pull, not on
the offer path. Terminal entries are evicted lazily inside list_at, so a
Failed entry past its TTL that never gets swept could otherwise be revived
forever, and an offer that never reached the peer (dial/open_bi/send_msg
failure) has no pull to retry. send_file's three offer-failure sites now call
a new fail_offer(id) instead of finish(id, false) so the entry is tagged
not-revivable.

Provider event pump: GetManyRequestReceivedNotify, PushRequestReceivedNotify,
and ObserveRequestReceivedNotify fell into the catch-all arm and dropped their
update channel. In iroh-blobs 0.103, EventSender::request() gates all four
request kinds on the same get mask field, so NotifyLog enables notifications
for get_many/push/observe too, even though Rayfish only issues single-blob
Gets today. Dropping their rx early makes the provider's transfer_progress
hit SendError::ReceiverClosed and abort the request. Drain and discard those
three like the Get arm does, without touching the registry.

Also reworded a comment overstating what NotifyLog guarantees: it does not
mean a slow pump can never stall the provider (client_connected and
notify_streaming do await on the channel), only that our pump body never
awaits anything but recv and that progress uses try_send.
feat(mobile): expose in-flight transfers over the FFI
feat(android): show progress and completion notifications for transfers
docs(changelog): note accurate Android transfer notifications

fix(android): stop stuck transfer notifications and unbounded auto-accept threads

Serialize TransferNotifier.poll so the two concurrent drivers (SendService,
the VPN background poller) can no longer race a result notification against
a stale progress bar, cancel ongoing notifications once their transfer
leaves the registry or on process start (they otherwise never clear:
notify() survives process death but the in-memory transfer registry does
not), scope SendService's wait loop to its own batch instead of every
outgoing transfer ever offered, poll transfers from HomeScreen's loop so
own-device auto-accepts notify with the app open and the VPN off, and move
FileAutoAccept onto a small bounded executor with capped retries instead of
one unbounded raw thread per offer.

Also: one shared notification channel definition, ensureChannel done once
per process instead of per post, wider notification id space, and a unique
id per send-failure notification.

fix(android): stop result notifications self-cancelling and other review round-2 bugs

- postResult now drops the transfer id from postedProgress before posting, so
  pruneVanished can no longer mistake a posted result for a vanished progress
  bar and cancel it out ~60s later when the terminal entry ages out of the
  registry.
- The cold-share stale-notification sweep now skips FLAG_FOREGROUND_SERVICE
  notifications and restricts to our own id range, so it can no longer target
  SendService's live foreground notification on a cold share.
- HomeScreen filters own-device file offers out of the displayed list while
  auto-accept is enabled, since FileAutoAccept.run only starts the download
  and returns before it finishes.
- SendService now bounds a send batch from both sides (max id before the
  offer loop, snapshot after it) so a concurrent second batch's transfers
  can no longer pin the first batch's wait loop to the full timeout, and
  skips waiting entirely if either snapshot fails instead of falling back to
  an unscoped count.
- TransferNotifier.channelEnsured is volatile and only set true after the
  channel is actually created, closing a race where another thread could
  notify() before the channel exists.

fix: serialize concurrent send batches and fix stale transfer state

Serialize SendService's offer-scoping region (before-snapshot through
offer loop through after-snapshot) behind a companion lock so two
concurrent shares can no longer stamp each other's transfer ids into
their batch, which made one batch wait the full 3 minutes for a file
another batch's peer never accepted. The wait loop itself stays
unlocked so batches still wait in parallel.

Expose FileAutoAccept's permanently-given-up ids so HomeScreen can
exempt them from the own-device filter: a file auto-accept gives up on
after 3 attempts was previously invisible with no way to save it.

Add TransferNotifier.reset(), called from NodeHolder.stopNode, to
clear the terminal/postedProgress sets when the node goes fully
offline. The core's transfer ids restart at 1 on the next start, so
without this a later transfer reusing an id could be muted by a stale
entry from before the stop.

Also drop a transfer's id from `terminal` if it comes back in a
non-terminal state, so a failed send the core revives after a peer
retry gets progress and a result again instead of leaving a stale
"Could not send" notification for a file that arrived.

fix(android): reset file-offer ids on stop, shrink send batch lock

Own-device file offer ids restart at 1 whenever the daemon is stopped
and started again, same as transfer ids. FileAutoAccept kept its
handled/attempts/gaveUp sets for the life of the process, so a reused
id after a disable/enable cycle would never be auto-accepted again and
would stay hidden from manual save. Add FileAutoAccept.reset(), called
from NodeHolder.stopNode next to the existing TransferNotifier.reset().

Also shrink SendService's batchLock to the region that actually needs
to be atomic with respect to transfer id allocation: the before/after
id snapshots and the sendFile loop. Staging each file (a plain byte
copy) now happens before the lock is taken, so it can no longer block
an unrelated share behind a slow copy.

fix(android): close cross-task seams in standby/transfer notifications

Fixes found in the final whole-branch review:

- TransferNotifier no longer marks an OFFERED transfer's "waiting" notification
  ongoing, and skips re-notifying when nothing changed, so an unaccepted send
  no longer leaves a permanent, unswipeable notification.
- The waiting notification now says plainly that a result only arrives if
  Rayfish stays running, instead of implying one is always coming; SendService's
  KDoc no longer falsely claims ensureStarted alone keeps a poller running.
- RayfishVpnService's nodeExecutor is now a single process-wide executor
  instead of a per-instance one, so a fast VPN off-then-on can no longer run
  two instances' bring-up/teardown unserialized against each other.
- A bring-up failure with stay-online off now stops the node instead of
  leaving the control plane connected with the VPN toggle off.
- NodeHolder start/stop/down now share one monitor (dropped the separate
  coroutine Mutex), so a start can no longer land after a concurrent stop and
  resurrect a node the user just disabled.
- The "Saved to Downloads" result notification is only shown, and only taps
  through to Downloads, when the file actually got there; otherwise it says
  "Saved" and opens the app, since MediaStore placement can silently fail
  (and always does below API 29).
- Removed the unused NodeHolder.isStarted and cleaned up review-round
  annotations left behind in TransferNotifier's comments.

docs(mesh): fix stale comment on TransferRegistry placement

The comment claimed the provider event pump attaching to BlobsProtocol was
"upcoming"; it has been wired up a few lines below for a while now.

fix(android): defer transfer result until the Downloads save actually lands

acceptFileOffer returns (and the core marks the transfer DONE) before
moveToDownloads has copied a single byte, so a poller could fire mid-copy,
consume no outcome, and post a permanently wrong "Saved" with a Downloads
tap target that isn't there yet - and leave an orphaned outcome for a later
same-named receive to wrongly claim. Mark the save pending before the
blocking accept starts (keyed by peer+filename+size, the closest thing to a
unique join key available across the FFI boundary) and have the poller defer
posting, without marking the transfer terminal, while a save is still
pending. Bounded to 45s so a copy that never finishes cannot mute a result
forever.

Also: write the progress dedupe map only after notify() succeeds, so a
throwing notify() cannot permanently mute a transfer; only show the "only
notified if Rayfish stays running" caveat when no poller is actually alive,
and use BigTextStyle so the shade doesn't truncate it; and in
handleBringUpFailure's offline-teardown branch, stop the now-pointless
auto-accept poller and document (rather than silently accept) that this path
can drop an in-flight receive when stay-online is off.

fix(android): fix pending-timeout window and a record() race in DownloadsOutcome

markPending was only stamped before acceptFileOffer, so the 45s window
covered the whole blocking download instead of the copy it is meant to
bound: a large own-device transfer could expire the entry before
moveToDownloads even started, letting the poller post "Saved" with the
wrong tap target while the copy was still running. Both call sites now
re-stamp markPending right after acceptFileOffer returns, restarting the
clock at the point moveToDownloads actually begins.

record() also cleared pending before writing the outcome, leaving a
window where a concurrent poll would see the key as neither pending nor
recorded and fall back to the wrong guess. Write the outcome first, then
clear pending.

fix(android): make standby the default, not opt-in

Disabling Rayfish (in the app, or another VPN app taking the single
VpnService slot) now drops the tunnel and releases the VPN slot but
keeps the control plane up by default, so files keep sending and
receiving and the device stays visible in the mesh. That is the whole
point of standby, and it should not require an opt-in toggle to get it.

The old "stay_online" toggle inverts into "go_offline_when_disabled",
a new key left at its own default (off) rather than a flip of the old
one in place: an existing user who had already turned stay-online on
has stay_online = true stored, and reusing that key with a flipped
default would silently hand them the opposite of what they asked for.
The old key is left unread and unmigrated.

Updated every standby-vs-offline read (the null-intent sticky restart,
ACTION_STOP, handleBringUpFailure, onRevoke, and the launch restore in
RayfishApp) to the new key and polarity, and re-pointed the You toggle
so it still drives ACTION_STANDBY/ACTION_EXIT_STANDBY correctly with
the meaning flipped.

docs(android): update comments to reflect go-fully-offline pref change

The go_offline_when_disabled pref inverted the standby behavior: disabling
Rayfish now keeps the control plane running by default (standby), with an
opt-in to go fully offline. Update stale references to the old "stay-online"
pref that no longer describes current behavior.

- RayfishVpnService: clarify teardown description and rewrap ACTION_STANDBY comment
- SendService: describe current node states rather than old pref
- RayfishApp: reference new pref name in description
- HomeScreen: note that full-offline case is now uncommon
feat(android): add one-tap Disable action to the VPN notification

fix(android): request POST_NOTIFICATIONS at launch on Android 13+

Without the runtime grant the permission defaults to denied, which
suppresses even the foreground-service notification, so the VPN/standby
status and file-transfer progress never appeared on Android 13+.

fix(android): use a shield status-bar icon for the VPN notification

The foreground notification used stat_sys_download_done, so it showed as
a download glyph in the status bar. Replace it with a monochrome shield.

Merge pull request #100 from rayfish/feat/android-standby-transfer-notifications

feat(android): stay online with the VPN off, and honest transfer notifications

feat(exit-node): use an exit node on macOS

The client full tunnel now works on macOS. Loop prevention is the socket
hook from the previous commit: while a full tunnel is up, iroh's sockets
are pinned to the physical default-route interface (IP_BOUND_IF), so the
transport ignores the routing table. The tunnel itself is the wg-quick
split default (0.0.0.0/1 + 128.0.0.0/1, ::/1 + 8000::/1) on the utun,
which wins by longest prefix without touching the system default route.

apply_exit_client orders the two so iroh traffic can never be routed into
the tunnel it carries: pin and rebind (Endpoint::network_change) before
the routes go in, routes out before the pin is released. Teardown on
deactivate goes through the same reconcile; a crashed daemon needs no
cleanup because the kernel drops the routes with the utun and the pin
dies with the process.

Still LOCAL ONLY, do not push: the Cargo patches point iroh and netwatch
at the sibling checkouts, whose hook commits exist nowhere remote yet.

Merge remote-tracking branch 'origin/master' into feat/exit-node

# Conflicts:
#	CHANGELOG.md

build: point the iroh and netwatch patches at the pushed fork branches

The previous two commits built against local sibling checkouts, which only
exist on the dev machine, so CI could not resolve the dependencies. The
configure_socket hook commits now live on the rayfish forks (iroh
rayfish-integration, net-tools feat/configure-socket, the latter synced
with n0-computer main), and the patches point there again.

fix(exit-node): don't fail socket binds without CAP_NET_ADMIN

SO_MARK is privileged, and the socket hook fails the bind on error, so an
unprivileged process (the test suite in CI, embedders) could not bind an
iroh endpoint at all. Skip EPERM specifically: a process that cannot set
the mark cannot install the policy routing that consumes it either, so
there is no tunnel its transport could leak into.

fix(exit-node): close the audit findings on the data path and control plane

- Return traffic: the exemption from the anti-spoof drop is now scoped to
  the exit peer's identity, not the datagram's network tag. The gateway
  tags replies with whatever shared network its generic route picks, so
  requiring the exit network blackholed every flow whenever the client
  and gateway shared more than one network. Also require a transitable
  (globally-routable) source, symmetric with the outbound check, so the
  exit peer cannot inject LAN/loopback-sourced packets; and evaluate the
  exemption lazily, only when the anti-spoof check fails.
- FreeBSD gateway: pfctl -E/-X are Apple extensions, so enable/disable
  branch per OS. FreeBSD uses plain -e/-d guarded by a pf-running check
  and an enabled-by-us marker, so an operator's own pf is never touched.
- reload_exit_state no longer mistakes a config read failure for an empty
  config (which cleared a live gateway's policy and tore down a live
  tunnel), keeps the existing tunnel when the roster cannot resolve the
  selected peer, and reports both as warnings. A pending selection is
  re-applied when reconverge lands the roster, so a daemon restart stops
  leaking traffic for the DHT-staleness window.
- The Member.exit_node advertisement now reconciles with what the gateway
  actually offers (sync_exit_offers after every apply and reconverge):
  ray down withdraws it, ray up re-advertises, a failed enable withdraws
  instead of luring clients into a blackhole, and a coordinator roster
  rebuild that wiped the flag heals on the next pass.
- ExitNodeAllow/Use IPC replies carry the reconcile warning instead of
  reporting success while nothing was installed.
- ip rule del names the full rule spec, never the bare pref, so a foreign
  rule at pref 100-102 is never deleted.
- The subprocess-heavy kernel reconcile runs on the blocking pool.
- Adopt the fork's SocketConfigurator hook (LoopPrevention) and refresh
  the fork pins; fix the ray-proto status test literal; dedup the roster
  clone and identity matching; changelog + comment cleanups.

test: fix a red IPC roundtrip test and the reliability e2e

Two test-only fixes found while running the full e2e suite; neither is a
data-path change.

ray-proto: test_status_response_roundtrip used bare rmp_serde::to_vec
(positional array encoding), but the real IPC codec (write_message) uses
to_vec_named. NetworkStatus now has two skip_serializing_if fields
(ephemeral_ttl_secs, my_exit_node) ahead of exit_offering, and array
encoding drops the omitted options and shifts the bool into the u64 slot,
so the test failed to deserialize. The wire path is map-encoded and was
always fine; switch the test to to_vec_named to match production.

reliability e2e:
- The probe labels glued a Unicode arrow to $from ("$from→$to") under
  set -u; in a non-UTF-8 locale bash folds the arrow's first byte into
  the variable name, hits an unbound variable, and aborts before any
  iperf runs. Use a plain "->".
- iperf3's control (TCP 5201) and data (UDP 5201) are dropped by the
  secure-by-default mesh firewall (inbound TCP/UDP deny, ICMP allow), so
  the icmp/flood probes passed but every iperf-udp probe read as a total
  measurement failure. Open the port on each host before probing; this is
  a loss test of the data path, not of the firewall. All 24 probes now
  pass at <=0.5pp over the direct baseline.

feat(exit-node): stay wire-compatible with v2 peers and nack unknown control frames

Revert the mesh protocol bump to 3: exit nodes are additive on the wire
(map-encoded frames, serde(default) fields), and the old build's demux
already skips frames it cannot decode, so a v0.2.0 peer stays connected
and simply cannot offer or discover exit nodes until it updates.

Keeping old peers connected turns version mismatches silent, so restore
the signal: a receiver that cannot decode a control frame probes the
variant name out of the raw msgpack (to_vec_named keys the message by
name) and answers with ControlMsg::NotSupported, which the sender logs.
Advisory only; nothing gates on it. Nacks are bounded per connection
(each kind once, at most 8 kinds, never in reply to a NotSupported) so
two mismatched builds cannot ping-pong.

fix(cli): resolve ray send paths against the client cwd

The SendFile IPC carried the path string verbatim and the daemon did the
read, so a relative path resolved against the daemon's cwd (/ under the
service manager) and failed with ENOENT. Absolutize in the CLI before the
path crosses the IPC boundary, and fail fast client-side when the file
does not exist.

feat(files): pass the ray send file as an fd over IPC

The SendFile IPC carried a path and the daemon, running as root, did the
read. That broke ray send from TCC-protected folders on macOS (root does
not bypass TCC, and the daemon has no Full Disk Access grant) and let an
operator-authorized user make the daemon read any root-readable file.

The CLI now opens the file with the caller's own privileges and attaches
the descriptor to a new SendFileFd request as SCM_RIGHTS ancillary data.

fix(exit-node): close the second audit's data-path and lifecycle findings

Three findings from auditing the branch against master:

- Transit to the gateway host itself is refused. is_transitable() admits
  any globally routable destination, which includes the gateway's own
  public IP: a packet transited there is local-delivered by the kernel,
  reaching the gateway's services without ever passing its rayfish
  inbound firewall. The exit server now learns the host's own addresses
  on every reconcile (ip -o addr / ifconfig -a) and drops transit to
  them.

- A partial Linux client install no longer stays live. install_client_routing
  bailed midway (no nft binary, ipv6.disable=1) leaving the v4 policy
  rules routing into a half-built tunnel whose conntrack-mark table never
  loaded, cutting inbound connections while the CLI only warned. The nft
  table now loads before any rule goes live, and the caller rolls the
  whole install back on failure, mirroring the macOS branch.

- Exit reconciles are serialized behind a tokio mutex. apply_exit_node
  runs from the IPC dispatcher, activate(), and the reconverge reapply
  listener on independent tasks, and the kernel enable underneath is
  check-then-write: two interleaved runs could snapshot each other's
  intermediate sysctl state, after which teardown "restores" forwarding
  to on (or leaks a pf enable token on macOS). deactivate()'s teardown
  takes the same lock.

fix(exit-node): deliver offers over the retained connection and persist the selection

The exit-node offer never reached the coordinator's roster, so no gateway ever
showed as available. Three stacked causes:

- `ExitNodeOffer` was handled only by the member accept handler, so a plain
  coordinator (the one node that records the offer on the signed roster) dropped
  it on its catch-all. Move it to a role-independent `handle_common` dispatch
  both roles run.
- `publish_exit_offer` dialed a fresh connection, wrote the frame, and dropped
  the connection before the datagram flushed, so the sender logged success while
  the coordinator never received it. Send over the peer's retained,
  ConnectionManager-owned connection instead (how the coordinator's own
  broadcasts already deliver reliably).
- A missed delivery never retried: reconverge is trigger-driven and its paths
  never re-synced offers. Re-sync on every reconverge and group poll, and wake
  the backstop while an offer is still out of sync.

Also stop wiping the local exit policy on reconnect: `persist_join_config`
rewrote the network config with empty `exit_allow` / `exit_node_use` on every
member restart, silently withdrawing the offer and dropping the client's
selection. Preserve both like the SSH allow-list already is.

Adds an over-the-wire test (member -> real QUIC connection -> coordinator records
the offer on its roster) and a config-preservation test, both verified to fail
without their fix.

feat(forward): signal path MTU for oversize datagrams instead of dropping

A packet routed to a peer whose tagged size exceeds the connection's current
max datagram size (common on a relayed exit-node path, whose datagram budget can
sit below the 1280 TUN MTU) was dropped with a bare SendFailure, so the sender's
TCP never learned to shrink and the flow blackholed (curl through an exit node
would hang).

Emit an ICMP "packet too big" (IPv4 fragmentation-needed / ICMPv6 packet-too-big,
carrying the real per-path budget) back into our own TUN before dropping, so the
local kernel lowers the path MTU for the flow and resends a packet that fits.
Not gated on reject mode: this is required PMTU signaling, not an opt-in reject.

Reuses the hand-built ICMP machinery in reject.rs; adds a PacketTooBig drop
reason and builder tests for both families.

fix(exit-node): admit return traffic by mesh IP and keep the exit peer warm

Two client-side bugs kept traffic from flowing through a selected exit node,
both confirmed by a packet capture on the gateway (outbound + NAT + replies all
worked; the client was dropping the replies and letting the link die).

- Return traffic was rejected by the ingress anti-spoof check: the exemption
  matched the exit peer by resolved *user identity*, which mismatches for a
  gateway whose device/user keys differ, so every reply was dropped as spoofed.
  Match by the sender's verified mesh IPv4 instead (resolved from our own roster,
  unforgeable, and the same whatever family the reply is). Adds a regression test
  that admits a reply when the identity differs but the IP matches.

- The selected exit peer's connection was idle-reaped like any on-demand link.
  Internet-bound traffic can't lazily re-dial it (the destination is not a roster
  member), so a reaped exit link blackholed until the next reconverge, which is
  why the tunnel only worked right after a manual `ray ping`. Never idle-close the
  peer the client currently routes through.

feat(exit-node): `ray exit-node off`, and stop claiming `ray up` when already up

- Add `ray exit-node off` / `disable`, and make the network optional: with no
  network it clears the one active exit selection (only one is ever in use, since
  there is a single default route). `ray exit-node none <net>` still works.

- `ray exit-node use`/`allow` hard-coded "(activate with `ray up`)" into the
  reply even when the data plane was already up and the change applied
  immediately. Move that hint into the reconcile path so it appears only when the
  daemon is actually on standby.

fix(exit-node): route DNS through the tunnel and warm the exit peer before pinning

Two macOS client bugs kept a cold `ray exit-node use` from actually carrying
traffic, even though the gateway forwarded fine (proven by a capture on scw-iroh).

- Cold selection blackholed: with no live connection to the exit peer, the daemon
  pinned its transport socket and installed the full-tunnel routes first, then
  dialed the exit peer over the routes it had just become, so the dial was
  captured by the tunnel it was meant to carry and never connected (a manual
  `ray ping` first was the only workaround). Warm the exit peer over the
  still-unpinned socket before pinning + routing, so the live link stays off the
  tunnel (idempotent; no-op when already connected).

- DNS didn't traverse the tunnel: macOS split-DNS sent only `.ray` to Magic DNS
  and left everything else to the system resolvers, whose port-53 queries macOS
  scopes to the physical link, so they never went out the exit and name
  resolution stalled. While a full tunnel is up, add an empty catch-all match
  domain so *all* DNS routes through Magic DNS, capture the system's real
  upstreams (`scutil --dns`) so the resolver can forward them out through the
  tunnel, and flip back to `.ray`-only split DNS when the exit is cleared.

fix(exit-node): keep iroh's relay traffic off the full tunnel (macOS)

The confirmed reason a cold `ray exit-node use` blackholed: the connection to the
exit peer is relay-routed until iroh hole-punches a direct path, and the
loop-prevention socket pin only covers direct QUIC. So the relay connection
(HTTPS to the relay server) was captured by the full tunnel it was meant to
carry and died, taking the exit link with it. A manual `ray ping` first worked
only because it forced a direct path, which the pin does protect.

Before installing the tunnel routes, resolve the configured relay servers (custom
override + n0 default) while DNS is still split, and install `/32` host routes for
them via the physical gateway so relay traffic bypasses the TUN. Removed on
teardown. Together with the warm-before-pin and DNS-catch-all changes, a cold
selection now carries traffic without any manual warm-up.

feat(exit-node): block `use` until the exit peer is on a direct path (macOS)

A fresh connection to the exit peer starts on the relay (100s of ms), and iroh
takes a few seconds to hole-punch a direct path, so the first flows after
`ray exit-node use` stalled and needed a manual `sleep`. Wait for the direct path
during the warm-up (before pinning sockets), polling `conn.paths()` up to ~6s, so
the command returns only once traffic will actually be fast. Falls through to the
relay if no direct path forms, rather than hanging.

refactor(exit-node): wait for the direct path via paths_stream, not a poll loop

Replace the hand-rolled `while Instant::now() < deadline` RTT poll with an
event-driven wait: `conn.paths_stream()` (wakes only on a real path change) in a
`select!` against a 200ms interval whose sole job is to nudge the hole-punch with
a ping, all under a single `tokio::time::timeout`. iroh only upgrades off the
relay once there's traffic, so the nudge stays; the direct-path detection is now
the stream telling us a path opened rather than us polling RTT.

fix(logs): only color console logs when stdout is a terminal

Under systemd stdout is a pipe to journald, so the ANSI escapes from the
console fmt layer ended up verbatim in syslog. Gate with_ansi on
stdout being a tty; the rolling file layer already had ANSI off.

Fixes #109

fix(exit-node): warm the exit path after the pin rebind, not before

`set_full_tunnel(true)` calls `endpoint.network_change()` to apply the
macOS interface pin, and that rebinds iroh's UDP socket. A rebind is a new
local socket, so it throws away every hole-punched path: the direct path
`warm_exit_peer` waited for was destroyed moments later, and
`ray exit-node use` returned onto a relay-only connection (slow first
flows, then a stall until traffic re-punched it).

Pin and rebind first, then warm over the socket that will actually carry
the traffic. The rebind knocks every other peer to the relay as well, and
iroh only re-punches once traffic flows, which is why `ping umbrel` went
dead after selecting an exit node: nudge all peer connections in the
background (on teardown too) so the rest of the mesh comes back without
waiting for the user to generate traffic.

fix(exit-node): reuse the live connection instead of dialing a second one

`warm_exit_peer` dialed the exit peer unconditionally. When a connection
to that peer already existed, the dial opened a *second* QUIC connection,
and since each side keeps one reader per peer the two ends settled on
different connections: every exit packet went out on ours while the
gateway read its own. The gateway's own counters proved it, `rx=0 tx=0`
for the whole window while the client reported `tx=697 rx=0`.

Gate the dial on there being no live connection, the same way the
on-demand data path and `ray ping` already do.

Also require the direct path to be the *selected* one before returning:
a freshly dialed connection lists unvalidated candidate addresses, so
"an IP path exists" fired 0.4ms after connect and meant nothing.

fix(exit-node): never pin iroh's sockets to the tunnel itself (macOS)

The socket pin resolved its target with a live `route get <family> default`,
run after the tunnel's split defaults were already installed. On a host with
no IPv6 default route of its own (common), `::` then matches the tunnel's
`::/1` and the lookup answers with the TUN, so iroh's IPv6 socket was pinned
to the tunnel it was carrying. Measured on a live client:

    route -n get -inet  default  ->  interface: en12
    route -n get -inet6 default  ->  interface: utun7

That is the transport strapped inside its own tunnel: the relay flapped
between home relays, the direct path to the exit peer closed after ~20s,
and every reply the exit node had already sent arrived in one burst the
moment `ray exit-node off` tore the routes back out.

Snapshot the physical default interface per family before the tunnel routes
go in and pin to that, falling back to the other family's physical NIC when
a family has no default of its own (leaving such a socket exactly as usable
as it was pre-tunnel rather than looping). Refuse a tunnel interface as a
pin target outright, so a stale or missing snapshot degrades to unpinned
instead of self-tunnelled.

fix(exit-node): wait for a working tunnel, not a plausible-looking path

`ray exit-node use` returned before the tunnel was usable, so the first
`curl` hung for ~20s. Two causes, both of them ordering:

The readiness wait ran before the default routes were installed, and
installing them makes netwatch fire its own network change a few seconds
later. That rebind drops every hole-punched path, including the one just
waited for, so the command returned on a path that was about to die and
traffic only resumed once iroh recovered on the relay.

And the thing waited for was path state, which has been wrong every single
time: the transport pinned into its own tunnel, the split connection, and
relay traffic captured by the tunnel all presented as a healthy-looking
path carrying nothing.

Move the wait to after the routes are in, and key it on a control ping that
comes back. A returned pong is proof the exit peer is reachable through the
finished tunnel, which is the property the command is claiming when it
returns. On timeout it proceeds with a warning rather than failing, since
the tunnel is installed and may still come good.

fix(exit-node): route the exit peer's own addresses around the tunnel

The direct path to the exit peer was the one piece of iroh's own traffic
still routed into the tunnel it was carrying. The gateway's counters show
it plainly: `rx=0 tx=0` for the entire 15s the direct path was selected,
then a burst the instant the client gave up and failed over to the relay.
The relay worked the whole time for one reason, it has a host route around
the tunnel and the direct path did not.

The socket pin was supposed to cover this, but it only applies when iroh
rebinds, and `Endpoint::network_change` does not force a rebind: it asks
the network monitor to re-evaluate, which rebinds only on a change it
judges *major*. Adding routes is not one. So the live socket kept using
the routing table, which by then pointed at the TUN.

Exclude the exit peer's direct addresses with host routes, the same
mechanism already proven to work for the relays, refreshed each round of
the readiness wait since hole-punching keeps discovering new candidates.
The pin stays as a second line of defence for sockets that do get rebound.

# Conflicts:
#	CHANGELOG.md

fix(exit-node): keep the macOS-only DNS re-assert out of the Linux build

`reassert_os_config` has one caller, in the macOS arm of `apply_exit_client`:
macOS is the only platform whose exit-node client rewrites DNS match domains.
On Linux it is dead code, so `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` (what CI runs)
failed there while every check passed on a macOS host.

fix(exit-node): keep connections that predate the tunnel on the physical uplink

Pointing the default route into the TUN captured the traffic of connections
that were already open, including the SSH session a headless host is
administered over. Their replies went into the tunnel, were swallowed, and the
session stalled on retransmits for 2-4 minutes until an inbound packet happened
to arrive. Measured on a fresh host: `ray exit-node use` completed in 94ms
while the SSH session carrying it took 245s to answer.

The conntrack table cannot cover these. Loading it is what loads conntrack, so
a connection that predates it is untracked at that moment, and the first packet
conntrack sees is our own outgoing reply, which registers the entry with its
direction inverted: neither its ctmark nor its `ct direction` identifies it as
inbound. (This is also why the bug only appeared on hosts where nothing had
used conntrack yet, and never on one where a previous run had left entries
behind.)

Sockets bound before the tunnel keep their source address, so route on that
instead: an `ip rule` per physical address, ahead of the mark and tunnel rules,
sending anything sourced from this host's own uplink addresses to the main
table. Traffic bound for the tunnel is sourced from the overlay address and
does not match, so the tunnel still carries what it should.

test(e2e): time `exit-node use` and trace remote commands

The tunnel comes up underneath the SSH session running `exit-node use`, so when
that session stalled the command returned minutes later, after the failsafe had
reverted the host. Every assertion after it then measured a torn-down tunnel and
blamed the wrong thing: five checks failed claiming the routing was never
installed, when it had been installed and removed again.

Time the command and fail on its own terms. `E2E_TRACE=<file>` logs a timestamp
and exit code around every remote command, which is what made the stall visible
in the first place; unset, it costs nothing.

chore(exit-node): time the reconcile phases at debug

The reconcile runs inside the IPC request, so anything slow in it is time the
user spends watching `ray exit-node use` do nothing. A per-phase breakdown is
what ruled the daemon out when the command appeared to hang for four minutes.

changelog
chore: Release
chore: Release

fix(android): derive app version from the crate version

versionName/versionCode were hardcoded to 0.1.4/2 in build.gradle.kts, so
every release APK reported 0.1.4 in the manifest, the app UI and the Sentry
release tag. Read the version from Cargo.toml instead and derive versionCode
from the same semver.

Closes #114

test(dns): cover the forward-to-upstream path end to end

The resolver tests covered .ray names answered locally, TCP dropped and
magic-IP filtering, but nothing exercised a non-.ray name going out to a
captured upstream and the answer coming back into the TUN. That is the
path a host depends on for all non-mesh DNS once Magic DNS takes over
resolv.conf, and it was the suspect while investigating #111.

Adds a fake upstream server and asserts the forwarded answer is injected
as a well-formed reply packet.

fix(firewall): reject IPv4 headers shorter than five words

An IPv4 packet whose IHL nibble claimed fewer than 5 words (20 bytes) was
still parsed: the check only compared the packet length against the derived
header length, which a short IHL always satisfies. The L4 offset then pointed
back inside the IP header, so extract_ports read the "ports" out of the
version/TOS/total-length fields and extract_tcp_flags read a byte of the
source address.

The result is a firewall verdict for ports the packet does not carry, in
either direction: an allow rule can be made to match, or a deny rule dodged.
Every OS drops ihl < 5 on receive, so such a packet never reaches a listener
regardless of the verdict, but the guarantee that a port match reflects the
packet's real port should not rest on the kernel.

feat(invite): checksum invite codes so a mangled one fails cleanly

An invite code was bs58(network_pubkey || coordinator || secret) with no
integrity check. base58 carries none of its own, so dropping a character
divides the encoded number by 58 and can still land on a payload of the right
length: the code decoded into a well-formed invite for a network that does not
exist, and the user saw the failure much later as a confusing join error
rather than "invalid invite code".

Codes now carry four bytes of blake3 over the payload. This is error
detection, not a security control: the payload is public and anyone can
recompute the checksum.

The decoder still accepts the older unchecksummed form, so codes already
handed out keep working and a coordinator on an older build can still mint one
this build redeems. The break is one-directional: a code minted here is four
characters longer, so a peer on an older build cannot redeem it.

Because the two forms are distinguished only by length, a truncation that
happens to shrink the payload by exactly those four bytes lands on the legacy
shape and skips the check. No checksum width avoids that; it closes when
legacy support is dropped. The tests document the boundary.

test: property tests for the data path, membership, and encodings

The pure logic in this crate was well covered by example tests, but only by
examples: hand-picked inputs on happy paths. These are the properties that
must hold across the whole input space, which is where the parser and the
address derivation actually live.

tests/common: a packet generator producing structurally honest IPv4/IPv6
packets (correct length fields, real TCP data offset, seq/ack) plus checksum
helpers, shared by the firewall and reject suites.

firewall (12): the parser never panics on arbitrary bytes, recovers exactly
the fields encoded into a packet, rejects unknown versions and short IHLs, and
never invents a field from bytes past a truncation. Evaluation: default-deny
inbound, disabled allows everything, an all-deny config can never produce an
allow, first-match-wins stated as prepend-iff-matches, and conntrack admits
the return packet of an opened flow and nothing else.

membership (17): derived v4 stays in 100.64/10 at any collision index and
avoids the reserved hosts, v6 stays in 200::/7, assign_ip never collides and
is stable for existing members, and resolve_ip_tiebreak is permutation
invariant, idempotent, and preserves the member set. Canonical blob bytes
ignore insertion order. Hostname collision resolution always yields a free,
valid name; an invite-bound name is exact or rejected.

encoding (23): round-trips for invite codes, pairing tickets, and control
frames; never-panic for every decoder; and the port-spec grammar (ordered
ranges, inverted rejected, bare number refused, wildcards, port-less protos).

reject (11): every synthesized reply parses back through the crate's own
parser, fits the MTU, has length fields agreeing with its bytes, and verifies
its checksums against the right pseudo-header. RFC 793 sequencing for both the
ACK and non-ACK branches, the right ICMP type and code per family, the three
suppression rules, the MTU landing in the field the kernel reads, and the loop
guard: a reply is never itself rejectable. Verified these can fail by mutating
reject.rs three ways (checksum, RST sequence, address swap) and confirming
each was caught.

Also covers two mesh helpers that had no tests: sender_is_coordinator, the
authority gate for coordinator-only control messages, and normalize_ssh_users,
where a bare `*` means any user including root and must collapse the list.

chore: add `just fmt-changed` to format only touched files

`cargo fmt` formats the whole crate, and `cargo fmt -- path.rs` does not
narrow it: cargo passes every target to rustfmt and appends the paths, so
unrelated files get rewritten and land in the diff mid-change. Calling rustfmt
directly on the modified and untracked .rs files is the only way to scope it.

perf(forward): cache the TUN sender per peer reader

Peer readers resolved the swappable TUN writer with `load_full()` on every
inbound datagram, paying two atomic refcount ops per packet on the hottest
path. An `arc_swap::cache::Cache` per reader revalidates against the cell and
reuses the `Arc` it already holds, cloning only when `attach_tun` actually
stores a new sender, so a re-attach still redirects live readers.

New `writer_resolve` bench group measures both: 11.0 ns -> 1.0 ns per packet.

Closes #82

feat(config): honor RAYFISH_CONFIG_DIR on every platform

The override was gated to Android and cfg(test), so a desktop node could not
be pointed at a config tree outside the platform default. Un-gate it, treat an
empty value as unset (an exported-but-empty var must not resolve the tree to
the cwd), and skip the Linux pre-/etc migration when the var is set: an
explicit location is a deliberate choice, not an upgrade in progress.

Closes #93

fix(dns): never forward to an unverified DNS upstream

The direct /etc/resolv.conf backend captured whatever nameservers the file
listed, overwrote it with the magic resolver IP, and forwarded every
non-.ray query to those addresses without checking that any of them
answer. On a host whose resolv.conf is rendered by another manager the
captured entry can name a server that no longer replies, and the result
was a box with no DNS at all: nothing resolved, and `ray join` failed
with "Service 'pkarr' failed" because the daemon could not look up the
discovery server either (#111).

Probe each captured nameserver before trusting it and keep only the ones
that answer. List the first survivor in resolv.conf after our own magic
IP, so the host keeps resolving if our resolver dies or the daemon goes
away. When nothing answers, refuse the takeover outright rather than
install a black hole the re-assert watcher would defend against manual
repair; an operator who set `dns_upstreams` still gets the takeover,
since the merge gives the forwarder somewhere to send queries.

Forwarding failures now return SERVFAIL instead of dropping the packet,
so a client fails fast instead of retrying until its own timeout, and
parse_resolv_nameservers splits on whitespace so a tab-separated entry no
longer reads as "this host has no DNS servers".

Verified on a Linux host against the reproduced failure: the takeover is
refused and system DNS is left intact with a dead upstream, still works
with a reachable one, and an upstream that dies after startup now returns
SERVFAIL rather than hanging.

fix(dht): keep the cause when a record lookup fails

`ray join` rendered every discovery failure as

    failed to resolve network record: failed to resolve network record:
    Service 'pkarr' failed

The stutter came from wrapping the same context twice, once in
resolve_network_packet and once at the call site. The missing cause came
from formatting iroh's lookup error with `{e}`: its top-level Display is
the bare "Service 'pkarr' failed" and the reason lives in its source
chain, which `{e:#}` renders and `{e}` throws away.

Wrap once, with the discovery server's URL, and render the chain. The
same `{e:#}` fix applies to the publish and contact paths, which lost
their cause the same way. Also cap a resolve at 15s: the relay is plain
HTTPS and iroh's client sets no total timeout, so a blackholed relay
could hang the command with nothing on screen.

The reporter in #111 saw only "Service 'pkarr' failed" for what was
really a DNS outage; the same failure now reads "... dns error: Resolve
failed, IPv4: Request timed out", which points at the actual problem.

fix(android): stop a late DNS answer from killing the app on teardown

DnsProxy.stop() shut its callback executor down while queries could still
be in flight. Those had already registered an fd listener with the platform
resolver, so when an answer landed the platform posted it to the terminated
executor. Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() uses AbortPolicy, so that post
threw RejectedExecutionException on the main looper, inside DnsResolver's own
frames with none of ours on the stack: the try/catch around rawQuery only
covers the dispatch, not the later callback. The throw reached the default
uncaught-exception handler and killed the process.

Build the executor by hand with DiscardPolicy so a late answer is dropped
instead of thrown, and track each query's CancellationSignal (previously a
throwaway nothing could cancel) so stop() tears the outstanding lookups down
rather than leaving them to complete against a closed socket. `running` moves
under the same lock as the in-flight set, so a query cannot be registered
after the cancellation sweep has passed.
