the --name field that was easy to mistake for the device hostname.

feat(gui): Share services toggle per network card

A freshly joined server is unreachable beyond ping because the firewall
denies unsolicited inbound. Each network card now has a toggle that adds
or removes the matching inbound allow-all-TCP rule (peer any, network
scoped), with confirmation both ways and state read from firewall show.

feat(gui): searchable command templates

Fold the console template dropdown into the command input as a datalist,
so typing filters the suggestions natively.

fix(build): import IpAddr on macOS without the desktop feature

The import in mesh/runtime.rs was gated on the desktop feature, but the
macOS exit-node helpers below it use IpAddr under a target_os gate, so
`cargo check -p ray-mobile` failed on a macOS host.

fix(android): let the share picker reach idle peers

Mobile runs the core on demand, so every mesh link self-closes after the
idle timeout. The share picker filtered on a live connection, so a couple
of minutes after the last packet a perfectly reachable peer vanished and
the user got "No peers online".

The FFI was collapsing the daemon's three-state PeerState into
connection.is_some(), throwing away the distinction between idle and
unreachable. Expose the three states instead, list every roster peer
sorted connected/idle/offline, and have SendService dial the picked peer
once before offering (Daemon::wake_peer) so the user learns whether it is
really there. A failed wake is not a send failure: the offer still queues
in the outbox, which is what the core always did.

feat(android): show the transfer percentage next to the progress bar

The bar alone says something is moving but not how far along it is, and
on a large file it can look frozen. Skipped when the bar is
indeterminate anyway (waiting on an accept, or an empty file).

perf(files): stream transfers instead of buffering whole files

Both ends streamed to disk in the middle but buffered the whole file at
the edges: send_file read the file into a Vec before hashing, and
accept_file called get_bytes (which iroh-blobs documents as "will run
out of memory when called for very large blobs") before writing it out.
Peak memory was one full file per concurrent transfer, which is what the
Android system killed the app for on large videos.

add_path on the path send, add_stream on the fd send, export on the
receive. Nothing holds more than a chunk now, and add_path reflinks
rather than copies where the filesystem supports it.

feat(android): cancel a queued send from the app

`ray files cancel` existed on desktop but was never wired through the
mobile FFI, so a send aimed at the wrong person, or at a device that
never comes back, could not be called off from the phone at all.

Exposes list_queued_sends + cancel_send and lists queued sends under
Notifications with a Cancel action. Outbox-only, matching the CLI: once
the offer is delivered the entry is gone from the outbox and the file is
the recipient's to accept or decline.

fix(android): stop a failed send from stranding its notification

Two ways the share notification could get stuck on screen with nothing
left to clear it.

updateOngoingNotification posted to the foreground service's own id
through NotificationManager.notify, so the id had two writers that
disagreed about the FOREGROUND_SERVICE/NO_CLEAR flags and
stopForeground(STOP_FOREGROUND_REMOVE) could leave the last one behind.
Route updates through startForeground instead, keeping one owner.

The send thread also called stopForegroundCompat/stopSelf as its last
statements, so anything thrown earlier (TransferNotifier.poll in the
wait loop was unguarded) killed the thread with the service still
foreground. Body moved into runBatch, cleanup into a finally.

Also promotes the provider pump's dropped-event log to warn and logs
each completed pull: a drop there means the sender can never mark the
transfer finished or reclaim the blob, which is not debug-level noise.

fix(android): retire a send notification that can never resolve

A sender only learns its transfer finished from the receiver pulling the
bytes. Blobs are content-addressed, so a receiver that already holds the
hash (the same file sent twice) pulls nothing, emits no provider events,
and the entry stays OFFERED for the life of the process. "Waiting for X
to accept" then sat on screen forever for a file that had arrived fine.

SendService now cancels the notifications for offers still merely OFFERED
when it stops watching them, and marks them terminal so the background
poller does not repost. pruneVanished could not do this: it only clears
ids that leave the registry, and a stuck OFFERED entry never does.

Bounds the wrong notification to WAIT_TIMEOUT_MS instead of forever. It
does not make it correct: with only local information the sender cannot
tell "recipient already had it" from "recipient hasn't tapped accept".
That needs a receipt from the receiver.

fix(dns): use resolved only when it is in the resolution path

Many cloud images leave systemd-resolved enabled while /etc/resolv.conf
still lists the provider's nameservers ("resolv.conf mode: foreign") and
nsswitch has no `resolve` module. glibc then never asks resolved, so
registering .ray on the TUN link succeeded and resolved nothing:
`resolvectl query host.ray` answered while `getent hosts host.ray` and
every ping/ssh by name failed.

All three resolved-backed backends were reachable in that state (D-Bus,
resolvectl, and the resolvconf symlink that redirects into resolved), so
the one backend that would have worked was never tried. Detection now
requires positive evidence that lookups reach resolved (a stub listener
in resolv.conf, or `resolve` in nsswitch's hosts line) before any of
them is chosen, and falls through to the direct takeover otherwise.

Also stop a backup-less revert from deleting /etc/resolv.conf outright,
which took the host's entire DNS down over what should have been the
undo of one line. It now edits our own entries out in place and leaves a
file it did not write untouched.

fix(ssh): warn when the host firewall blocks the mesh SSH port

The embedded server cannot bind <mesh-ip>:22 next to a system sshd, so
it listens on 30022 and the forwarding path rewrites the port. The
kernel therefore sees inbound mesh SSH as a connection to 30022, which a
"22/tcp" rule in ufw or firewalld does not cover. Under a default-DROP
INPUT policy the SYN dies in the host firewall with no clue anywhere:
the listener is up, the mesh firewall permits the flow, ICMP still
works, and ssh just hangs until it times out.

Detect that case and print the exact command to open the port, on
`ray up` and on `ray firewall ssh on`. Read-only: rayfish never edits a
ruleset another tool owns. Detection is conservative, a warning needs
positive evidence of a default-deny inbound policy plus the absence of
anything that could let the port through, and anything unparseable or
unreadable stays quiet rather than pointing at the wrong culprit.

fix(peers): attach a live connection to networks its handshake missed

One connection carries every network two peers share, and it is
registered per network as each MeshHello for that network is processed.
A hello is only registered if the network's roster already names the
sender, so one that arrives while the roster is still converging (a
restart, a fresh join, a blob that lands after the link) was dropped and
never retried.

The connection then carried a network the peer table did not list, which
is not cosmetic: the set is the in-band reachability wall, so
resolve_inbound_by_id dropped that network's inbound datagrams, and
`ray status` showed the peer Idle on it while plainly Active on another.
Only a fresh dial rebuilt the entry.

Reconverge now repairs it, as the mirror of the existing prune pass: it
runs exactly when a verified roster arrives, which is the information
that was missing when the hello landed. Re-announces the handle table
afterwards, since a peer cannot decode datagrams tagged with a handle it
was never told about.

fix(ssh): tell a refused mesh SSH client why it was refused

Mesh SSH offers only the `none` method, since identity is proven by the
mesh link itself. A peer that was not authorized, or asked for a user it
may not have, was rejected with nothing on the wire, so the client fell
through to whatever the system sshd offers and prompted for a password.
The reason sat in this node's log, where the person connecting cannot
see it, and every authorization problem presented as a password prompt
or a network fault.

Send a banner naming the peer, what it may log in as, and the
`ray firewall ssh allow` command that fixes it. Nothing is shown to a
peer that may already log in as any user.

Also warn when no system sshd host key can be reused (a container with
no /etc/ssh, a host with no sshd, an encrypted key). We then serve a key
of our own, and a client that knows this host from a LAN or public-IP
session sees a host-key change for the mesh name and reports a possible
MITM. Log the fingerprint so the swap can be confirmed rather than
guessed at.
docs(changelog): record the DNS, mesh SSH and peer-table fixes

fix(build): keep the host-firewall warning out of the Android build

`crate::ssh` is desktop-only, so referencing its `SSH_LISTEN_PORT`
re-export from the mesh-SSH IPC handler broke `cargo build -p ray-mobile`
and with it the Android job. Take the constant from `crate::forward`,
which is compiled on every platform for exactly this reason, and gate
the warning itself on the desktop feature: without the embedded SSH
server there is no NAT'd port for a host firewall to block.

Also collapse the nested `if`s in the resolved-path detection and use
`contains` over `iter().any()`, both `-D warnings` clippy failures that
only fire on Linux, where the cfg'd code is compiled.

fix(boot): recover when the daemon starts before the network is ready

A hard reboot can start the daemon before DNS answers, and two startup
steps treated that transient state as permanent.

Restoring a saved member network needs a pkarr lookup, so it needs DNS.
The one-shot restore logged a warning and gave up: the network never
registered, `ray status` showed it inactive while peers still saw the
node online, and only a manual `ray restart` fixed it. Retry with
backoff until the join lands, the network leaves the config, or the
daemon shuts down.

OS-DNS detection refuses to take over resolv.conf when the host has no
working upstream, which is exactly the boot state, and that refusal was
also final. Keep retrying in the background until Magic DNS is
configurable.

Also repair a leftover rayfish resolv.conf before building the endpoint
rather than during activate. iroh's resolver snapshots the file once at
construction, so a stale one pointed every lookup at our own Magic DNS
before it had upstreams: the daemon resolved through itself and failed.

feat(service): support OpenRC and SysV init, not just systemd

Every service command shelled out to `systemctl`, so `ray up` on a
systemd-less host (MX Linux, Devuan, Alpine, Gentoo) died with
"systemctl not found" and left the user to figure out that `ray daemon`
works on its own.

Add `init_system::InitSystem`: it detects the running init from the
`/run` markers, owns the per-init template (systemd unit, OpenRC
service, LSB SysV script), and drives install/enable/start/stop/restart.
All call sites route through it, including the daemon's own detached
auto-update restart. When no init is recognised the error now points at
`sudo ray daemon`. SysV has no supervisor, so `ray up` says so instead
of silently dropping crash recovery.

Closes #119

fix(android): confirm the copy on the QR code sheet

The QR sheet is a ModalBottomSheet, so it draws in its own window on top
of the Scaffold that hosts the snackbar. Routing its "Copied" message
through onToast put the confirmation behind the sheet: tapping "Copy
code" gave no response at all and read as a dead button.

Confirm in the button instead. copyToClipboard now reports whether the
write landed, so a clipboard refused by the platform says "Copy failed"
and logs, rather than silently looking the same as success.

Closes #118

docs(claude): document the mobile client

CLAUDE.md had no mention of ray-mobile or the Android app at all. Add a
Mobile section (UniFFI Node over the headless daemon, generated
bindings, control/data plane split), the two "where things live" rows,
and the `just apk` build line.
fmt

fix(android): stop a failed tunnel start from leaving a VPN connected

Kotlin calls up(pfd.detachFd()), so Node::up owns the VpnService fd from
its first line, but three fallible steps returned early without closing
it: the NotStarted check, the writer's dup, and the reader's
set_nonblocking. That fd is the only handle on the VPN interface, and the
framework only tears the VPN down once the interface disappears
(Vpn.java's interfaceRemoved observer), so a stranded fd left Android
showing a connected VPN while the app had fallen back to standby and
reported the tunnel off. The only way out was disconnecting from system
Settings, which then left the app unable to start the tunnel again.

Take the fd as an OwnedFd before anything fallible runs, and give
AndroidTunReader an OwnedFd constructor so the reader's own failure paths
close it too. The unsafe block now sits at the one point where ownership
actually transfers.

Also split the two failures startTunnelBlocking was conflating.
ensureStarted failing is fatal to bring-up (Node.up returns NotStarted
without it), so it must not fall through to establish() and ask Android
for an interface that can never carry traffic; it now goes to
handleBringUpFailure. A failing status() read stays soft: the node is up,
so the CGNAT fallback address is still legitimate.

Refs #116

fix(android): survive Android refusing a background foreground start

After the system killed the process, the START_STICKY restart recreated
the service with the app in the background and called startForeground to
go back into standby. A background foreground-service start needs an
exemption; specialUse (our type) has none, and a VpnService only gets one
while a tunnel is established, which is exactly what standby does not
have. The refusal threw ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException on the
main thread and killed the app instead of restoring anything.

startForegroundNotification now reports the refusal instead of throwing.
The three call sites that are genuine foreground starts (startTunnel,
enterStandby, ACTION_STANDBY) stop the service rather than run a node the
OS is about to kill; standby comes back the next time the app is opened
or the VPN enabled, both of which start us from the foreground. The rest
only retitle a notification the service already posted, so they are not
subject to the check and ignore the result.

Caught as Throwable: the exception class only exists on API 31+, and the
same call can also throw SecurityException and
InvalidForegroundServiceTypeException.

fix(android): identify the build a Sentry report came from

Sentry defaulted dist to versionCode, so every build of a version looked
identical in the dashboard. Combined with the versionName that was
hardcoded to 0.1.4 until it was derived from the crate version, this made
reports untraceable: two ANR causes fixed on 2026-07-14 kept arriving
until 2026-07-31 from testers on stale APKs, indistinguishable from a
regression without reading line numbers against git history.

Set dist to the commit the APK was built from, suffixed -dirty for a
build off an uncommitted tree, falling back to "unknown" where git is not
available rather than failing the build.

Also drop the per-send fingerprint on Send diagnostics. It was meant to
give each report its own issue and never did (488 reports in one group),
and splitting was the wrong goal anyway: hundreds of one-event issues
would bury real crashes in the same queue. The install_id and transport
tags plus the returned event id are how a single report gets found.

feat(android): report how the previous process died

A background ANR arrived with an idle main thread and no app frame
anywhere, so there was nothing to attribute it to. That is normal for a
trace captured when the process is reaped rather than when it stalled,
and it left the issue unfixable rather than merely unfixed.

Android keeps the missing piece: ApplicationExitInfo.getDescription names
the component that timed out, and getTraceInputStream holds the dump taken
when the system decided the app was unresponsive. Neither is surfaced by
the SDK's own ANR reporting. Read both at process start, on a background
thread, and report anything not seen before.

This also covers the exits that produce no report at all today. A
low-memory kill leaves no crash and no ANR, so a VPN app meant to stay
resident just vanishes from the mesh with nothing to say why.

An ANR now lands twice, once from the SDK's integration and once from
here. The two records answer different questions, ANRs are rare enough
that the noise is negligible, and enriching the SDK's event instead would
mean matching records by timestamp inside beforeSend, which is fragile
across SDK versions.

The watermark is armed on first run rather than starting at zero: Android
holds up to 16 records predating this code, and reporting them would put a
burst of months-old exits in the dashboard from every install at once.

Gated by the existing crash-reporting opt-out: with it off, nothing is
read and nothing is sent.

refactor(android): hold the prefs file once and cache the hot flags

The two flags onStartCommand and onRevoke read on the main thread are now
cached in memory, and the prefs lookup lives in one place instead of being
repeated per accessor.

Deliberately not sold as an ANR fix, because it is not one: Application
.onCreate already reads this same file to decide crash reporting before
anything can crash, and getBoolean blocks on the load latch, so the one
synchronous load is paid on the main thread at every process start before
any service runs. By the time onStartCommand reads these, the framework's
cache is warm. What this buys is that the service paths no longer depend
on that ordering holding.

Safe to cache: this process is the only writer (MODE_PRIVATE, single
process) and every write goes through a setter that updates the cache in
the same call. A read that beats the background warm-up falls through to
disk and is correct, just slower.
refactor(config): add the settings key registry

refactor(config): route every global setting through the registry

Folds config_set/config_get's relay, discovery-dns, dns-upstreams,
auto-update, and on-demand arms plus the standalone ssh, download-dir,
download-user, and hostname-default globals into the settings registry
introduced for mdns. config_set is now a thin delegate to
settings::apply_global; config_get delegates to settings::render_global
instead of duplicating the render logic.

fix(config): drop side-effecting keys from the global settings registry

ssh, download-dir, and download-user each need daemon-side work beyond a
field write (firewall_ssh_set also seeds/removes a passthrough rule and
starts/stops the live SSH listener; download-dir's CLI setter validates
an absolute path) that the bare registry write bypassed. hostname-default
never had a CLI setter, so registering it added new user-facing surface.
Drop all four; ssh/download-dir/download-user return in the task that
migrates their side-effecting handlers, hostname-default is dropped for
good.

refactor(config): register the firewall toggles as settings keys

firewall.enabled, firewall.reject, and firewall.default-in join the
registry as pure field accessors over FirewallConfig; the caller still
owns the ArcSwap hot-swap and persistence, wired in the task that
migrates the daemon handlers. firewall.default-out stays unregistered:
no existing setter touches it, so adding it now would be new
user-facing surface rather than a migration.
refactor(config): register the per-network toggles as settings keys
feat(ipc): add network-scoped config set/get

refactor(ipc): collapse the settings variants into the config registry

Fourteen IPC variants existed only to carry one value each to a handler that
loaded config, wrote a field and saved: SetMdns, Set/GetDownloadDir/User,
DownloadSettings, FirewallSetEnabled/Reject/Default, FirewallSshSet,
Firewall/FilesAutoAccept, Set/GetEphemeral and EphemeralStatus. They are gone;
every one of those commands now names a key in the settings registry and rides
ConfigSet/ConfigUnset/ConfigGet or NetConfigSet/NetConfigGet.

No command's spelling, flags or help text changes. `ray --help` (plus the help
for firewall, firewall ssh, files, config, ephemeral and mdns) diffs empty
against the previous build.

The keys with live side effects keep them. The daemon's ConfigSet handler
dispatches on the key's scope: firewall keys go through the same read-modify-
hot-swap-persist path as before, so `ray firewall off` still takes effect
instantly rather than at the next restart, and `ssh` is served by the handler
that also seeds or removes the tcp:22 passthrough and starts or stops the
listener. Per-network keys re-materialize suggested rules and drain queued file
offers as they did. Those keys also keep their exact confirmation messages,
since the generic one ends "restart the daemon", which would be false for them.

`ssh`, `download-dir` and `download-user` are registered here, with their
handlers, rather than in the earlier registry commits: registering them sooner
would have made them reachable through the plain config path with the side
effects skipped. `download-dir`'s absolute-path check moved from the one CLI arm
into the registry so it binds every caller; `download-user` still resolves a
username to a uid in the CLI and the registry takes a numeric uid only.

e2e: `./tests/e2e.sh ssh run` passes end to end on a real 2-host fleet,
including the tcp:22 open/close checks around `ray firewall ssh on|off`.
`./tests/e2e.sh firewall run` passes every firewall check on a real 3-host
fleet; its one failure is in section 6 and is pre-existing and unrelated
(tests/lib/common.sh:315 still calls `ray send <file> <peer>`, the argument
order that flipped in an earlier release).

fix(ipc): restore the confirmation and error text the settings collapse moved

Collapsing the settings variants was allowed to delete handlers; it was not
allowed to change what the user reads. Five confirmation lines regressed to the
generic "Set {key}." wording and three error messages picked up the settings
registry's phrasing instead of their own. All restored byte-for-byte:

  ray mdns on|off                  mDNS discovery enabled|disabled. Restart …
  ray files download-dir <path>    download-dir set. Restart …
  ray files download-dir --clear   download-dir cleared. Restart …
  ray files download-user …        download-user set|cleared. Restart …
  ray firewall reject x            expected `on` or `off`, got 'x'
  ray firewall auto-accept net x   expected `on` or `off`, got 'x'
  ray files auto-accept net x      expected `on` or `off`, got 'x'

The global branch of config_apply now renders through a per-key match, like the
firewall and network branches already did. The three renderers are free
functions (global_set_message, net_set_message, firewall_set_message) so tests
can pin every string without standing up a daemon, which is what was missing
when they regressed. Two of those tests also sweep each scope asserting no
live-effect key claims a restart is needed, which guards the ArcSwap hot-swap
from behind.

The on/off pre-check in the CLI gets its own error string rather than reusing
settings::parse_bool, so the exit-code fix survives: those arms print a daemon
error and still return Ok, so validating client-side is what makes a typo exit
1 rather than 0. `ray files download-dir <relative>` likewise keeps its client
side bail, so the message surfaces with its original prefix; the registry keeps
its own check so validation still binds every caller.

The "Restart the daemon" clause on download-dir/download-user is untrue
(resolve_download_target reads the config on every accept) and is restored
untouched anyway. Correcting it is a user-visible improvement and belongs in
its own change, not smuggled into a refactor.

Also: ConfigSet's doc no longer points at the deleted SetMdns, carrying over
its config-dir routing rationale; ray-proto's firewall module doc no longer
claims the deleted FirewallDefault carries these enums typed.

Behaviour note carried over from the previous commit, now stated in full: both
`ray firewall auto-accept` and `ray files auto-accept` lost a live-map guard
and now succeed on a network that is saved but not currently active, where they
used to report "network not found". The other per-network setting
(`ray ephemeral`) has always behaved that way.
docs: document the settings registry and fix the stale ssh login note

fix: settings collapse review cleanup

Four minor fixes from the final settings-collapse branch review:

- firewall_default now delegates to firewall_config_set instead of
  duplicating its confirmation message, so the wording exists in one
  place (pinned by firewall_keys_keep_the_exact_wording_their_handlers_printed).
- Document that ConfigSet.replace only applies to list-valued global
  keys (relay, discovery-dns, dns-upstreams) and is ignored elsewhere;
  no behaviour change.
- Drop an em-dash from a doc comment in ray-proto/src/firewall.rs.
- Add a test pinning that net_config_apply gates on a network's
  presence on disk rather than in the live network map, since that's
  a deliberate behaviour change from the deleted NetworkRegistry::contains
  check.

refactor(ipc): make settings keys typed instead of stringly-typed

The settings registry had two lists that could drift: the KEYS table that
lookup/keys_for read, and the match arms in apply_*/render_*. Six
`_ => bail!("unknown config key")` fallbacks meant a KEYS row with no
matching arm compiled fine and failed at runtime, and an arm with no row
was invisible to `ray config get`.

Keys are now one enum per store, in ray-proto since they travel on the
wire: GlobalKey (settings.toml), FirewallKey (firewall.toml), NetworkKey
(networks/<name>.toml), plus NodeKey = global | firewall for the messages
that need no network argument. ConfigSet/ConfigUnset/ConfigGet carry a
NodeKey and NetConfigSet/NetConfigGet a NetworkKey, so a global key
written into a network file is unrepresentable rather than rejected at
runtime, and require_network_key goes away.

The per-store split is what buys exhaustiveness. A single flat key enum
would leave every handler needing a catch-all arm to reject the other
scopes, which is the runtime check this replaces. All six fallbacks are
gone and the three render_* functions are now infallible.

Keys serialize as their plain name, the same bytes the `key: String`
fields sent, so the wire format is unchanged. An unregistered key now
fails to decode instead of reaching a handler; `ray config` is the only
command taking a key as free text, so it parses client-side and prints
the same message the daemon used to, with the same exit code. A decode
failure drops that one IPC connection and cannot crash the daemon.

Verified `ray config set bogus x` and `ray config set net.ephemeral-ttl
7200` print byte-identical errors and still exit 1.

fix(ipc): answer an undecodable request instead of hanging up

Two loose ends from the typed-key change.

A request the daemon cannot decode (a settings key this build does not
know, a variant from a newer `ray`) dropped the connection with only a
debug log, so the client could report nothing better than "connection
closed". It now gets the decode error back. Best-effort: the other
common cause of a decode failure is a client that already went away.

`ray config get <key>` parsed the key after connecting, so with the
daemon stopped a typo reported "daemon is not running" instead of naming
the bad key. Parse first, matching `set` and `unset`.

fix(ipc): bound the decode-error reply and keep it out of the log's blind spot

The error reply added in the previous commit quotes the request back: an
unknown key is reported as `unknown config key: <what the client sent>`,
and a frame carries up to MAX_FRAME_LEN (1 MiB) of it. The IPC socket is
0666 by design (authority is the per-request SO_PEERCRED check, which
runs after the decode), so any local user could send a megabyte key and
never read the reply, parking a daemon task and an fd on a write that
cannot complete. Repeat to exhaust the fd table.

The reply is now truncated to 512 bytes, which fits the longest real one
(the unknown-key error names every valid key, ~300 bytes) and any socket
buffer, so the write always completes. Truncation lands on a char
boundary.

Returning Ok(()) also meant the accept loop's debug log no longer fired
for an undecodable request, so malformed frames became invisible to
`ray report`. Log before replying.

Also from review: spell out the global keys that take the plain
load/mutate/save path in config_apply instead of catching them with `_`.
A new key silently falling through is the ssh bug the typed keys are
meant to prevent. Drop the now-dead Scope enum (the key types answer
"which store" themselves), a stale doc comment, and two tests that
asserted a const fn returns its own literal.

fix(ipc): log the real decode reason and finish the exhaustive matches

The debug line logged `%e`, and Display on an anyhow error prints only the
outermost context, so every undecodable request logged the literal string
"decode IPC message" with no key name and no reason. Truncate once and log
that, which also puts the bound in front of both sinks rather than relying
on Display to keep the client's bytes out of the rolling log.

`global_set_message` still ended in a catch-all while its two siblings had
theirs removed, so a new global key would silently inherit the generic
wording and its "Restart the daemon" claim.

The multi-byte truncation test used a 2-byte char, which left the cap on a
char boundary, so the backtrack never ran and the test passed against the
panicking slice it exists to guard.

fix(config): list every settings key instead of a hand-kept five

A bare `ray config get` and the `ray config` clap help both carried a
literal list of five keys, so the seven added by the settings collapse were
reachable but undiscoverable: the only way to learn a key name was to type a
wrong one and read the error. Both are now driven off the key enums, and the
listing covers the firewall store too.

Also lowercase the action in `ray firewall default`, which rejected `ALLOW`
while `ray config set firewall.default-in ALLOW` accepted it, and fix two doc
comments on `firewall_config_set` that described a routing through
`edit_firewall` the body does not do.

fix(mesh): keep retrying a network restore that was queued for approval

A restore that came back Pending returned instead of retrying, so the
network stayed in config but was never registered: peers on it were
unreachable and their packets dropped as an unknown network, with no way
back except a manual `ray restart`. Both `TryJoin::Pending` and
`dial_reconnect` document that the caller retries until `ray accept` lets
us in, so retry.

The same arm swallowed every other non-Joined outcome with no log at all,
which is why a node stuck this way left nothing to diagnose. Handle the
variants separately, log each retry, and log the loop's remaining quiet
exit. `ray status` now says what the `inactive` marker means instead of
leaving it as a one-word footnote.

feat(mesh): keep every saved network live instead of restoring once at boot

A network that failed to connect at startup stayed in config and was never
retried: peers on it were unreachable and their packets dropped as an
unknown network, while the node looked healthy otherwise (still connected
to peers, still answering `ray ping`). The only way out was noticing the
faint `inactive` marker in `ray status` and restarting the daemon.

Add a restore supervisor that re-checks every minute that each saved
network is live and restarts the ones that aren't, and nudge it from the
control demux when a peer sends a frame for a network we have saved but
not registered: their traffic proves the network is reachable, so there is
no reason to sit out the tick. Coordinator networks are covered too; they
previously got one attempt at boot and no retry at all.

The sweep's decision is a pure function over (saved config, live map,
in-flight set) so it is testable without a daemon, and startup shares the
same in-flight guard as the sweep so the two cannot start duplicate
restores. Nudges do no work beyond waking the task and the supervisor
holds a floor between peer-triggered sweeps, so their rate stays ours
rather than the peer's.

fix(ssh): say when an allow rule is stored but the server is off

`ray firewall ssh allow` saved the rule and reported success even with
`ssh_enabled` false, so mesh :22 still fell through to the host sshd and
the password prompt read as a broken rule. Point at `ray firewall ssh on`
from both `allow` and `ssh show`.

feat(mdns): list LAN neighbours and connect to one directly

mDNS discovery already ran in the background, but its results only fed
iroh's address lookup: the daemon logged each sighting and dropped it, so
there was no way to see who was on the LAN.

Keep the sightings in a LanPeers map on Transport, fed by the existing
browse loop, and expose them two ways: `ray mdns scan` lists them with
addresses, age, and any network already shared with the peer, and
`ray status` reports the count of neighbours not yet connected.

`ray connect` now resolves its argument against that map before falling
back to the pkarr contact lookup, so a LAN pair links up with no DHT and
no internet. The trade-off is that a LAN neighbour can send a connect
request without knowing the contact id, so `ray contact rotate` no longer
stops local requests; approval stays recipient-only either way.

`ray mdns` becomes a subcommand (on/off/scan); `ray mdns on|off` parses
as before.

feat(status): list nearby LAN peers instead of counting them

`ray status` showed only a count of LAN neighbours in its mDNS field,
which told you something was out there without telling you what. Print
them instead, as a "nearby" block with id, addresses, and age, limited to
five rows before deferring to `ray mdns scan` so a busy LAN can't push
the network list off screen. Peers already on one of our networks stay
out of it: they belong to the network blocks above.

The status reply carries the peer list in place of the count, and both
the block and `ray mdns scan` are built from one `lan_peer_infos` helper
so the two views can't disagree.

fix(join): box the TryJoin reply to keep clippy green

Adding the LAN peer list to StatusResponse grew IpcMessage past the
point where clippy's large_enum_variant fires on TryJoin, whose Pending
variant carries nothing. CI runs clippy with -D warnings, so the build
broke.

Box the reply, and match the two Joined cases inside the arm since box
patterns aren't stable.

fix(ssh): serve the sftp subsystem so scp works

OpenSSH 9.0+ scp speaks SFTP, and the mesh SSH server never answered the
subsystem request, so scp and sftp hung instead of failing.

fix(dns): only answer names under .ray

A network name was registered with the OS as its own domain, so a network
called `dev` captured every `*.dev` lookup and answered NXDOMAIN. Drop the
bare network match/routing domains and the suffix-less `<host>.<network>`
resolution path: peers resolve as `<host>`, `<host>.ray` or
`<host>.<network>.ray`, everything else goes upstream.

fix(ssh): key session state by channel, not by connection

Only the first session on a multiplexed connection ran; every later
channel hung with no output and no exit status.

fix(dns): drop the stale argument in the macOS DNS writer

The macOS build broke when write_dns_config lost its network_names
parameter and this caller kept passing it.

fix(dns): fall back to the system resolver for names the mesh doesn't hold

Magic DNS answered every name it claimed, so a claim it could not resolve
became an NXDOMAIN instead of a real lookup. Claim a name only when the
roster actually holds it and decline the rest: handle_query returns None
for a miss and the resolver forwards it upstream, so `zed.dev` reaches the
real site while a network named `dev` is joined.

That makes `<host>.<network>` safe to resolve again (a hit answers, a miss
goes upstream), keeps NODATA for a peer that has no record of the asked
type, and drops REFUSED entirely. A `.ray` name still fails with NXDOMAIN
when no upstream answers, rather than a SERVFAIL the client retries.

fix(dns): answer `.ray` misses locally instead of forwarding them upstream

A `.ray` name the roster did not hold was declined and forwarded to the
system resolver. `.ray` is not a delegated TLD, so that query could only
come back NXDOMAIN from the public root, carrying its 86400 negative TTL
in place of our own 60s SOA.

The window that matters is startup: DNS is configured before every
network has reconverged its roster, so a lookup in that gap is a genuine
miss. Forwarding it let the OS cache the name as missing for a day, long
after the peer was back, and `srv.devbox.ray` stayed unresolvable while
the daemon answered it correctly on the magic IP.

Inside `.ray` the zone is ours whether or not the roster holds the name,
so a miss now returns NXDOMAIN here. The bare `<host>.<network>` branch
still falls back, so `zed.dev` keeps reaching the real site.

feat(ssh): support port forwarding over mesh SSH

The embedded server had no direct-tcpip handler, so russh refused every
forwarded connection with "administratively prohibited" while sessions on
the same connection kept working. Handle it: ssh -L, ssh -D and ProxyJump
now work through a mesh host.

The connect runs off the session task, since that task is shared by every
channel on the connection and a black-holed target would otherwise stall
the peer's shells too.

feat(ssh): complete the mesh SSH feature surface

Everything a stock client asks for now has an answer:

- reverse forwarding (ssh -R), TCP and unix socket, bound to loopback like
  sshd's default GatewayPorts no
- unix-socket local forwarding (ssh -L port:/path.sock)
- agent forwarding (ssh -A): a per-channel socket, owned by the login
  account, that speaks to the client's agent
- locale environment variables (SendEnv/SetEnv), filtered to LANG, LC_*,
  TZ, TERM and COLORTERM so a peer can't set LD_PRELOAD on our shell
- signal requests, and exit-signal instead of an invented status code
- X11, refused explicitly: russh's default answered nothing, so `ssh -X`
  waited on a reply that never came

Socket forwarding is checked against the login account's own permission on
the socket (or the directory it is created in) first: the daemon is root,
and on a unix socket the filesystem is the access control.

Also hang up the session when its channel or connection goes away, instead
of leaving the login shell running on the host forever.

feat(ssh): hand interactive sessions to login(1)

An interactive session now goes through the host's login(1), so the parts of
a login we were skipping come from the system: the PAM account check (a
locked or expired account is refused, where before it got a shell), the PAM
session with its logind session, XDG_RUNTIME_DIR and resource limits, the
utmp/wtmp records behind who and last, /etc/nologin, and the motd.

Root is excluded: login refuses a root session on a tty outside
/etc/securetty, and refuses it by hanging with no output rather than
failing. Non-interactive commands keep the direct path too (sshd records no
login for those either). RAYFISH_SSH_NO_LOGIN=1 turns the handoff off.

Sessions also get SSH_CONNECTION, SSH_CLIENT and SSH_TTY, which anything
asking "am I over ssh" reads.

Found while testing this: the daemon kept no terminal fd of its own, so the
master end hit EIO the moment a child closed and reopened its terminal
(login does, between the PAM session and the shell) and the session went
silent with the shell still running. Hold one for the child's lifetime.

feat(completions): tab completion that knows your networks and peers

A generated script can only offer what was true when it was written, which
for `ray leave` or `ray ping` is nothing: those arguments are free-form
strings whose values live in the daemon. Move completion into the binary
(clap_complete's dynamic engine), so the installed file is a stub that asks
`ray` on every tab and the answers come from the same `Status` read the rest
of the CLI uses.

Two rules, because this runs on a keystroke: a tab never starts the daemon,
and never blocks the shell. `ipc::connect` has no timeout of its own, so
every round trip runs under a 300ms budget, and every failure (no socket, no
daemon, no reply in time) is the same answer: no candidates.

Installed rather than set up. `sudo ray up` already runs as root and already
writes system files, so it writes the stubs into the directories bash, zsh
and fish search by default: nothing to source, no rc file to edit. `ray
update` funnels back through the same function, so they stay current, and
`ray uninstall` takes them away again. install.sh does it too, for the
binary-only install that never reaches the service. `ray completions
--install` remains for doing it by hand, falling back to per-user XDG paths
when not root.

zsh needs one shim: installing onto fpath means the file is autoloaded *by*
the first tab, where the `compdef` in it would only bind from the next one,
so it calls what it just registered rather than letting that tab come back
empty.

Fixed-choice arguments get their words too (in/out, allow/deny, on/off,
protocols, settings keys), as suggestions rather than a PossibleValuesParser:
the on/off arguments also accept true/yes/1, and narrowing them here would
start rejecting spellings that work today. `ray config <TAB>` reads its keys
from config::CONFIG_KEY_NAMES, now the one list `config_get` iterates too.

fix(mobile): let a disabled node come back, and rebind when the phone moves

Stopping the node released the blob store only as a side effect of the
router's accept task noticing the closed endpoint, after
shutdown_and_close had already returned. A start that overlapped the old
store then blocked: two FsStores over one directory do not error, redb
waits for the lock, so Node::start never returned and every later call
queued behind it on NodeHolder's monitor. shutdown_and_close now shuts
the protocol router down before closing the endpoint, which is what
drives BlobsProtocol::shutdown -> Store::shutdown -> drop(db).

Around that: start and stop are both bounded by timeouts so a wedged
store cannot hang the app, a failed build closes the endpoint it had
already created, a racing start's loser is shut down instead of dropped,
and a start failure is reported to Sentry with the core log attached.

Only onAvailable/onLost were forwarded to the core, so a Wi-Fi roam, a
DHCP renew or an address change on the same network never triggered a
rebind and the phone sat on dead sockets. onLinkPropertiesChanged and
onCapabilitiesChanged now do too, debounced, and turning Rayfish on
forces a rebind so the off/on gesture can actually recover it.

test(e2e): run the functional scenarios on local docker containers

Add a second provisioning backend so the suite runs without Scaleway.
E2E_BACKEND=docker starts one systemd container per host on a local
bridge, each with sshd on 0.0.0.0:22, and writes the same .servers the
cloud backend does. Nothing above the provisioner changes: the scenarios
still deploy with rsync + systemctl and drive the hosts over root SSH.

All nine functional scenarios pass this way. exit-node, reliability and
bench stay Scaleway-only: they need hosts with distinct public IPs and a
WAN baseline, which one bridge cannot give them.

The zone column now marks which backend wrote a fleet, and each backend
refuses the other's .servers instead of driving it (or, on teardown,
deleting the only record of billed instances).

Also fix send_recv, which passed `ray send` its arguments in the wrong
order and failed every transfer check on both backends.

feat(net): ipv6-only data plane so rayfish can share a host with another VPN

Tailscale routes all of 100.64.0.0/10 into its own interface, so a host
running both loses one overlay's IPv4 half. The IPv6 ranges are disjoint,
so ipv6-only keeps the TUN's own IPv4 as a /32 (no connected route for the
/10) and carries traffic over 200::/7 alone.

The /32 stays because the magic-DNS reply is synthesized back into the TUN
addressed to whatever source the kernel picked for the query; with no IPv4
on the device that source comes from another interface and the reply is
dropped as a martian.

check_cgnat_conflict is skipped in the mode, and now reads addresses over
netlink on Linux: it used to parse ifconfig and treat a missing binary as
'no conflict', so on a server without net-tools the clash went unnoticed.

feat(dns): answer AAAA only when the data plane is ipv6-only

An A record for a peer resolves to 100.64.0.0/10, which on an ipv6-only
host is routed by the other VPN, so the packet arrives and the reply
leaves through the wrong interface. Withhold the address instead.

NODATA rather than NXDOMAIN: the name exists and its AAAA still works,
and NXDOMAIN would fail both in most stub resolvers. Reverse lookups in
the CGNAT range are declined for the same reason, so the VPN that owns
the range gets to answer them.

feat(mesh): carry an ipv6-only claim on the signed roster

A node whose data plane is ipv6-only still has a mesh IPv4 on the roster,
so peers hand it out in DNS answers and apps send packets that arrive but
are answered out the wrong interface. Members now claim the mode
(ControlMsg::Ipv6Only), coordinators record it on the signed blob, and the
hostname table holds Option<Ipv4Addr> so the responder withholds the A
record for such a peer.

Additive and map-encoded, so no MESH_PROTOCOL_VERSION bump. The delivery
and record mechanics are shared with the exit-node offer rather than
copied: deliver_self_flag / record_self_flag.

fix(dns): stop leaking a tailnet address and stop fighting over resolv.conf

Two things a host running rayfish next to another VPN gets wrong:

iroh gathered the tailnet IPv6 as a direct-address candidate and published
it in a public pkarr record. It names a network no rayfish peer can route
to, and it tells anyone reading the record that the tailnet exists.

The direct-resolv.conf backend took the file over unconditionally and then
re-asserted it on every write. Against a VPN doing the same thing, the two
rewrite each other and the host's DNS flaps. Refuse instead, and say so:
a CGNAT-range nameserver that is not ours can only be another overlay.

docs: ipv6-only mode in the changelog, readme and CLAUDE.md

Also covers config_set/config_get round-trip and settings persistence for
the on/off keys, which had no test: a key can be accepted by set and still
be invisible to get and tab completion if it is missing from
CONFIG_KEY_NAMES.

fix(dns): reach magic dns over IPv6 when the data plane is ipv6-only

Keeping the v4 magic IP in that mode does not work, which I had wrong.
Tailscale installs

  -A ts-input -s 100.64.0.0/10 ! -i tailscale0 -j DROP

and our reply is synthesized with the magic IP as its source and injected
into our own TUN, so netfilter drops it and .ray resolution times out with
nothing in the logs. Measured on a host running both: one query, two
dropped packets on that rule's counter.

The host route was never the only thing in the way. 200::/7 is ours alone
and unfiltered, so ipv6-only mode points the OS at 200::53 instead: no new
route needed (the peer range already covers it), an IPv6/UDP reply path in
dns/packet.rs, and the AF_INET6 arm through resolved, resolvectl,
resolvconf and resolv.conf. NetworkManager's IP4Config nameservers are
u32-typed and cannot carry it, so that backend steps aside in this mode.

Dual-stack hosts are untouched: still 100.100.100.53, same bytes on the
wire.

fix(compat): audit the feature surface against a coexisting VPN

Three things the ipv6-only work left inconsistent, found by walking every
feature that touches an IP or a host resource Tailscale also claims:

- the magic-DNS /32 was still installed in ipv6-only mode, planting a dead
  route inside the range that mode exists to hand over
- the host-firewall check read iptables while mesh SSH listened on IPv6, so
  a default-DROP ip6tables policy reported Clear and ssh hung silently
- the exit-node NAT matched any 100.64.0.0/10 source, so a host routing for
  both VPNs masqueraded the other's forwarded traffic

docs: correct why the ipv6-only TUN keeps a v4 /32

The comment on AppConfig::ipv6_only still carried the pre-MAGIC_DNS_V6
rationale, claiming the /32 is there so Magic DNS keeps working. It is
not: Magic DNS moves to 200::53 in this mode. The address stays because
it is the node's internal handle (peer table, roster, ray status).

The same wording was already fixed in tun.rs; this copy was missed.

feat(android): IPv6-only mode as a toggle in You

The mode existed in the core but nothing on Android could reach it. The
daemon read it from settings.toml, which on a phone lives in an
app-private directory the user cannot edit, and the tunnel was built

Embedders now pass it to build_headless as an argument, next to

toggle rebuilds the node (ACTION_RESTART_NODE) and brings the VPN back
if it was on. The tunnel follows the mode: no 100.64.0.0/10 route, Magic
DNS on 200::53, the mesh IPv4 still bound as a /32 handle.

The case on Android is not a second VPN (only one runs at a time) but a
carrier handing the phone a 100.64.x.x address of its own, which the
unconditional /10 route would swallow whole.

feat(android): add a quick settings tile for toggling the tunnel

Toggles the tunnel from the shade without opening the app. The tile is an
entry point, not a second state machine: on does what the Home toggle does,
off sends the same ACTION_STOP the notification's Disable action sends, so
it inherits the standby-versus-fully-offline behavior already in the service.
TunnelControl holds the start/stop both entry points share.

and reads RayfishVpnService.tunnelUp fresh, where an active tile would keep
showing the last pushed state after a process kill and requestListeningState
could not fix it (it does nothing for non-active tiles anyway).

Turning it on needs VPN consent, which only an Activity can raise, so the
tile hands off to an invisible VpnConsentActivity when prepare() asks for it.
With consent already held the tile starts the service directly and the shade
stays put.

build: add a just local-dev recipe

Installs this checkout as the local daemon (build, install into
/usr/local/bin, restart onto it). The restart is the point: with the
service already running, `ray up` is only an IPC call, so it neither
re-execs the new binary nor applies a start-time setting.

fix(transport): bind an IPv6 underlay socket

The endpoint builder pre-configures both an IPv4 and an IPv6 socket, but
clearing the preset's IP transports to pin the listen port dropped both,
and only the v4 one was re-added. So the node had no v6 underlay: no
direct v6 path, no v6 candidate published, and a peer on an IPv6-only
network reachable through a relay only.

Bind both families on the same port. The v6 bind is best-effort, like
the preset's, so a host with IPv6 disabled still starts.

feat(ipv6-only): switch to the mode when another VPN holds the CGNAT range

The mode could only be reached by hand, and on the machines that need it
the daemon died before anyone could reach it: `ray up --ipv6-only` hands
the flag over IPC after startup, and `ray config set` needs a live
daemon, but the CGNAT preflight killed the daemon at startup. So a fresh
install alongside Tailscale had no way in at all.

The setting becomes three-valued: on, off, and absent = auto (the
default). On auto the startup scan decides, so the node starts in
IPv6-only rather than refusing; off keeps the refusal for anyone who
wants it. An auto decision is never written back, so the mode ends when
the other VPN does, and `ray status` marks it (auto) so it is not
mistaken for a setting.

Android gets the same three states, as Auto/On/Off under You, over a
getifaddrs scan that skips our own mesh IPv4 (the VpnService interface
can already be up when the node is rebuilt, and counting our own address
would latch the mode on for good). Node.start takes the tri-state and
Status reports what auto resolved to, so the tunnel and the card both
follow the node instead of the stored preference.

refactor: delete the code the dead_code allows were hiding

Most of the `#[allow(dead_code)]` attributes were stale: the code they
covered had since found callers, and removing the attribute warned about
nothing. What was left was actually dead and is gone.

The largest piece is `NetworkHandle.disconnect_tx`, a per-network clone
of the sender kept for a coordinator-promotion path that now re-registers
through the daemon-wide channel in `MeshCtx`. It was threaded through
`join_mesh_shared` and `run_join_handshake`, which already had a
`let _ = disconnect_tx` to admit as much, and out of
`spawn_coordinator_background_tasks`, which no longer returns it.

Two attributes stay, both saying something a cfg cannot. `tests/common`
is compiled by every test binary and each uses a different subset, so
"never used" there is not evidence of dead code. `find_cgnat_conflict`
runs only on Android but is tested everywhere, which `cfg(any(android,
test))` now says directly.

refactor(ipv6-only): one Auto/On/Off enum instead of two booleans

Status carried `ipv6_only` and `ipv6_only_auto`, a pair whose fourth
combination (off, but automatically) never existed, and the setting was
an `Option<bool>` whose `None` meant auto. Both are `Ipv6Only` now, in
ray-proto: three values for the three states there have ever been.

One type covers the setting and the mode it resolves to, because they
are the same three values read from different ends. As a setting `Auto`
means decide at startup; as a reported mode it means on, chosen by the
scan rather than the operator. What the data path asks is `enabled()`.

settings.toml says `ipv6_only = "on"` from now on, and the deserializer
still takes the bare boolean older installs wrote, so an upgrade keeps
its mode instead of failing to parse and refusing to start. `ray status
--json` reports the string in place of the two flags. Android follows:
the UniFFI enum the app already had for the setting is now what `Status`
reports as well, with conversions the compiler checks against the core's.

Carries rustfmt over the previous commit's removals, and gates
`ssh_token` on `feature = "desktop"`, where its only readers live,
rather than leaving the dead-code allow that sweep had removed.

fix(macos): scope the DNS resolver to the utun so it is asked for AAAA

`.ray` names did not resolve on an IPv6-only Mac: `ssh host.net.ray`
failed while `dig @200::53 host.net.ray AAAA` answered. mDNSResponder was
only ever asking us for A records, which is the one family that mode has
no answer for.

`scutil --dns` shows why. Our resolver had no interface, so mDNSResponder
judged it against the primary one, and a Mac with no native IPv6 concludes
AAAA is pointless: `flags: Supplemental, Request A records`. Tailscale's
entry sits on `if_index : 22 (utun5)` and gets both families. So pass the
tun name down (both call sites already had it and threw it away) and put
`InterfaceName` in the DNS dictionary, in this mode only: with the v4
magic address an unscoped resolver already gets the family it needs.

`ray status` peer rows carried the mesh IPv4 in the same mode, an address
nothing on the host can send to, while the network header had already
moved to IPv6. They now agree. The rows get wider, which beats a column
you cannot paste into `ssh`.

Also restores `run_cmd_quiet`, deleted as dead code from a Linux build
while macOS service management calls it, and gives the Linux-only
resolv.conf helpers `cfg(any(target_os = "linux", test))` rather than the
dead-code allows they had. Both are why CI now builds macOS on every PR:
it was released-only, so a break cost a failed tag instead of a red check.

fix(hostfw): gate fix_command to Linux, where its only callers are

The macOS job's first run caught it: `cfg(any(target_os = "linux", test))`
looked right, but this module's tests are `cfg(all(test, target_os =
"linux"))` themselves, so on macOS the `test` arm compiled the method with
no caller in the build at all.

ci(nightly): give each target its own cache key

rust-cache's key has the runner's os and arch in it but not the target
triple, so every leg of the matrix shared `v0-rust-release-Linux-x64-…`
and friends. Whichever of a runner's two targets saved first served both,
and its sibling restored a target dir holding nothing for its own triple,
then rebuilt every dependency. In the last run the gnu, x86_64-musl and
aarch64-darwin legs compiled 2 crates each while their three siblings were
still building.

release.yml already keys per target; this is the same line, which also
lets the two workflows share one cache per target instead of each keeping
its own.

fix(macos): publish the service's IPv6 so the resolver is asked for AAAA

Naming the interface inside the DNS dictionary was not enough: configd
takes the key (`scutil show State:/Network/Service/rayfish/DNS` lists
`InterfaceName : utun4`) and then ignores it, leaving the resolver with no
`if_index` and `flags: Supplemental, Request A records`. mDNSResponder
learns a service's interface from the service's own IPv4/IPv6 entity, not
from its DNS entity, and judged against the host's primary interface a Mac
with no native IPv6 concludes AAAA is pointless. So `.ray` names, whose
only answer in this mode is AAAA, resolve to nothing while `dig` against
the same resolver answers fine.

Write `State:/Network/Service/rayfish/IPv6` alongside it, carrying the
utun, our mesh address and a /128, which is the shape another VPN's
scoped resolver has. IPv6-only mode only, and removed on revert
regardless, since the mode can change between the two.

The address comes from `DnsService`, which now holds it (it is derived
from our identity and never rotates) and passes it to whichever backend
detection picks; only macOS reads it.

fix(macos): make configd ask our resolver for AAAA

In IPv6-only mode `.ray` names resolved to nothing while `dig @200::53`
answered fine. `scutil --dns` showed our supplemental resolver unscoped
and A-only, so the system never sent us the one query we can answer.

configd sets a resolver's A/AAAA flags from its own service in exactly
one branch, guarded by an internal `__SCOPED_QUERY__` marker we cannot
write; miss it and it strips our InterfaceName and merges in the default
resolver's flags instead, which on a Mac with no native IPv6 is A-only.
configd sets that marker itself for a State:-only service when the DNS
dictionary names its own service id back, hence ConfirmedServiceID.

That only carries the flags across. The AAAA bit itself comes from
service_is_routable(), which asks one thing of the service: does it have
a default route of that family. Address, prefix and interface are not
enough, so add Router. Nothing in that path looks at the address range,
so 200::/7 was never the problem despite being neither global unicast
nor ULA.

Rank the service Never so the default route stays in configd's model and
out of the kernel: it cannot win the primary election, claims no ::/0,
and stays out of the flags merged into every other resolver. Verified on
macOS 26.4 next to Tailscale: the resolver now reports both families on
if_index utun4, dscacheutil returns the mesh IPv6, and the routing table
is unchanged before and after.

fix(macos): write the service rank before anything routable

Two problems with the previous commit's write path, both in
write_service_config.

The rank was set after the IPv6 entity and both were hard errors, so a
failure on the rank left the service published with a Router and no
rank, which is the one combination that lets configd elect us the
primary IPv6 service and put a real ::/0 on the utun. The rank goes
first now: a failure stops us before we publish anything routable.

It also failed outright when the service key already existed from
another writer. The daemon's store uses session keys, which configd
reclaims when the session ends, but a key set by anyone else is not
session-owned and a session store cannot overwrite it. Since the rank
write came first in the same function's error path, the DNS key was
never written at all and the resolver disappeared entirely rather than
merely losing AAAA. Remove before set, so a stray key cannot wedge the
daemon permanently.

perf(ssh): set TCP_NODELAY on sockets carrying SSH

Mesh SSH left Nagle on. SSH is a request/response protocol of small
writes, so every exchange waited on the Nagle/delayed-ACK standoff: one
side holds a small write back hoping to coalesce, the other holds the
ack back hoping to piggyback it on a reply, and a timer breaks the tie.

Measured against devbox over a 34 ms link, opening a session channel on
an already-established connection cost 117 ms, roughly 3.4 round trips
where 1-2 is the floor. The same measurement over OpenSSH on a slower
transport was 84 ms. Ansible opens one channel per task and paid the
difference on every one of them, which is how this surfaced.

It is not the datapath: a TCP connect to a normal forwarded listener on
the same host measured 34 ms, exactly one RTT.

russh has a `nodelay` config flag but only applies it in its own accept
loop, and we accept ourselves and hand the stream to `run_stream`, so
the flag would have done nothing. Set it on the socket instead, on all
three that carry SSH: the session, forwarded connections out, and
reverse-forward connections in. The unix-socket forwards are untouched,
Nagle being a TCP thing, and the iroh datapath is QUIC over UDP.

Also on the local GUI server, which serves the same shape of traffic.
