fix(dns): resolve the daemon's own names without the host's resolver

iroh's default reads /etc/resolv.conf at bind, so a host whose nameserver
stopped answering took the relay and pkarr down with it (#111), and a
restart that found our own magic IP still listed waited on the tunnel it
was bringing up.

fix(mesh): don't route over a network the peer no longer shares

The outbound tag was the lexically smallest network in our roster, which
a peer that left silently stays in for good when we hold the network, so
the receiver dropped every datagram while its .ray names kept resolving.

feat(cli): add `ray logs` to read the daemon log without root

The rolling files under /var/log/rayfish are root-owned, so looking at
them meant `sudo cat` plus knowing which file, or `ray report`, which
bundles a week of them into a tarball meant for sharing. `ray logs`
reads them through the daemon over IPC, in the open read tier alongside
`status` and `report`, with `--since <dur>` and `-f`/`--follow`.

The reply is the protocol's first multi-frame response: a run of
LogChunks ended by an Ok sentinel, or not ended at all under --follow.
A day of rayfish=debug output is many times the 1 MiB frame cap, and a
follow has no last frame by definition, so the handler takes the stream
instead of returning an IpcMessage, dispatched ahead of handle_request.

--since compares timestamps as strings rather than parsing them: the
appender writes a fixed-width zero-padded RFC3339, so lexical order is
chronological and the same string's first ten bytes pick the files.
The follow poll stops at the last newline, since the daemon is writing
into that file and forwarding half a line would garble it and repeat it
on the next tick, and it watches socket readability for the hangup,
because waiting for a write to fail would leak the task through every
idle stretch.

The CLI pages a one-shot read through $PAGER on a terminal and writes
straight through when piped or following.

test: wait for the gc sweep instead of a fixed budget

`a_tag_for_an_absent_blob_does_not_break_gc` went red on CI while passing
on macOS and locally. The store's gc runs on a 100ms timer and the tests
gave it a flat 600ms sleep, so the assertion was a deadline: on a loaded
two-core runner the sweep did not land inside it, and the test reported
"gc did not run" for a gc that was only late. Locally the sweep collects
at ~105ms, which is why the budget never looked tight here.

Poll for the effect instead. Both tests now wait for an untagged canary
blob to disappear, which is the one sound signal that a sweep completed,
with a 30s ceiling so a real breakage still fails loudly rather than
hanging. Checked by running them against a store with gc disabled: both
fail with "gc never collected the untagged canary".

Drops ~1.8s of sleeping from the suite as a side effect.

perf(mobile): stop re-resolving the signed record every minute

Android polls every 15 minutes now, which is only safe because
coordinators dial members that idle-closed their links instead of only
reaching the ones already connected.

fix(metrics): bind the exporter to loopback, skip it on Android

The counters map every peer's mesh IP to its RTT and traffic volumes and
were served on 0.0.0.0. Android also ran the 60s collector for an
endpoint nothing there can scrape.

feat(exit-node): support exit nodes in IPv6-only mode

`ray exit-node use` was refused outright on an IPv6-only data plane, which
is the mode a host runs in when it shares the box with Tailscale, and so
the case where an exit node is most useful. The stated reason (the full
tunnel routing over mesh IPv4) was not what the code did: the Linux tunnel
is policy routing on both families, and the exit peer's mesh IPv4 is only
a peer-table key, which exists in either mode.

Tunnel IPv6 and leave the host's IPv4 egress alone. That follows the
premise of the mode rather than working around it: mesh IPv4 carries no
traffic there, so claiming the host's IPv4 default would source transit
from a /32 this mode deliberately leaves unrouted, and take IPv4 from the
VPN the mode exists to share a host with. Install is per-family; teardown
still sweeps both, so a daemon restarted into the other mode cleans up.

Three things fall out of it:

- The gateway needs an IPv6 uplink. The offer carries `exit_node_v6` (an
  additive field, no ALPN bump, defaulting to "cannot" so an older peer
  errs toward being declined), status marks those gateways, and selecting
  one without it is refused with the reason instead of black-holing.
- Non-.ray DNS is forwarded to an IPv6 resolver for the tunnel's lifetime.
  Every upstream the OS capture yields is IPv4, so lookups would otherwise
  leave around the exit the traffic goes through. `dns-upstreams` accepts
  IPv6 addresses to name one; otherwise a public pair is used.
- A co-resident VPN's routes are mirrored into the tunnel table before our
  default goes in. Our catch-all rule sits above its rules and its
  prefixes live in a private table, not main, so `suppress_prefixlength 0`
  never rescued them: turning the tunnel on black-holed it. This was a
  latent bug in dual-stack mode too, and the fix covers both.

macOS: widen the underlay host-route exclusion to IPv6, since with the
tunnel on IPv6 those are exactly the paths it would otherwise swallow.

test(e2e): cover the IPv6-only exit-node client

Step 9 puts srv-b in the mode it runs in when it shares a host with
Tailscale and uses the same exit node. It asserts the tunnel takes IPv6
and only IPv6: the v6 default lands in table 29793, no v4 rule is
installed, `curl -6` reports srv-a and `curl -4` still reports srv-b's
own uplink. That last one is a deliberate non-property rather than an
oversight, so it is checked instead of assumed.

It also stands in for the co-resident VPN by putting a route in table 52
behind a rule at priority 5250 before the tunnel goes up, and asserting
it was mirrored into the tunnel table. Without the mirror our catch-all
at priority 102 wins and that VPN goes dark on `exit-node use`.

Whether srv-a can serve such a client depends on it having IPv6 egress,
which not every instance has, so both branches are asserted: with a v6
uplink the tunnel must carry traffic; without one the selection must be
refused by name rather than installed and left to black-hole.

fix(exit-node): keep the missing-gateway warning per family

Widening the tunnel exclusion to IPv6 dropped the warning a host with no
default route used to get. An address in a family with no route is one
this host cannot reach at all, so it is worth saying rather than
skipping in silence. Also clear the tunnel DNS override on standby, so
`ray down` does not leave the forwarder pointed at a resolver picked for
a tunnel that no longer exists.

fix(ipc): fill the new exit-node status fields in ray-proto's own test

`ExitNodeStatusView` gained `available_v6` and `ipv6_only`, and the
round-trip test inside ray-proto still built the old literal. A bare
`cargo check` only builds the root crate, so this compiled locally and
broke CI on both the check and macOS clippy jobs, which pass
`--workspace --all-targets`.

Assert the new fields rather than just filling them: `available_v6` is a
subset of `available`, not a replacement, since an IPv6-only client needs
both lists to say "this gateway exists but cannot carry your only
family". Add a decode test for a reply that predates the fields, so the
`serde(default)` that lets a CLI run ahead of its daemon is pinned.

Note the workspace flags in CLAUDE.md, which is what sent me to the
narrower command in the first place.

fix(dns): stop taking resolv.conf from a VPN that started second

The direct backend refuses /etc/resolv.conf when another overlay's resolver
is already in it, but that verdict was made once, at apply(). Hold the file
first and the re-assert watcher fought the VPN that arrived second: it only
asked "is this ours", so it rewrote their file within milliseconds, every
time, and the host's DNS was whichever write landed last. The same war the
refusal exists to prevent, from the other side.

The check now runs on every pass and the watcher stands down instead of
rewriting. Standing down is not a revert: our backup is the host from before
either VPN, so restoring it would break theirs. Drop it, keep the NM dns=none
drop-in, and hand back to the retry loop, which reclaims DNS once that VPN
leaves.

Two smaller holes on the same path. foreign_mesh_resolver matched
"nameserver " with a literal space while parse_resolv_nameservers right above
it splits on whitespace, precisely because generators emit tabs; it goes
through that parser now. And with resolvconf in the path both VPNs register,
but the system stops at the first resolver that answers, so second place
never sees a .ray query while we reported success. Say which resolver is
ahead of us instead.

fix(mesh): authenticate the sender of a control frame

A control frame is routed to a per-network handler by the network public
key in its envelope. That key is a discovery key by design: it rides in
every invite code and it is the pkarr address the network publishes
under. Nothing checked that the peer sending the frame was in the network
it named, so the handlers meant for members were reachable by anyone who
had ever seen an invite. On top of that, three handler arms did not check
the sender's authority either, each one a place where the surrounding
arms do.

Adds the control-plane counterpart of `resolve_inbound_by_id`: the demux
refuses a frame unless this network's roster accounts for the sender,
with an explicit exemption list for the messages by which a peer that is
legitimately not on the roster yet reaches us (`JoinRequest`,
`MeshHello`, and `SignedRecord`, which verifies against the network key
regardless of who carried it). Per-arm authority checks stay on top of
that rather than instead of it.

The individual holes it also closes directly:

- A device cert was recorded without verifying its signature whenever the
  sender claimed no identity beyond its own transport key. The binding it
  writes is what the inbound firewall, mesh SSH authorization, own-device
  file auto-accept and leave-pruning all resolve through, so an unsigned
  cert naming a victim earned that victim's firewall rules and SSH access
  on the receiving node. Verification now happens on one path for every
  case, and the blob's nullifier set is applied there too, since `ray
  unpair` cannot invalidate a signature.
- `MemberApproved` was honored from any sender. An entry in the approved
  list is not inert: the sender's next `MeshHello` seats it as a member
  at the IP that message chose, publishes its `.ray` name and routes to
  it. Coordinator-only now, like `InviteShare` and `KickedFromNetwork`.
- `LeaveNetwork` from a peer that was never on the roster still cost a
  re-sign, a pkarr publish and a `MemberSync` to every member, each of
  which answers with a DHT resolve and a blob fetch.
- The `ray connect` co-coordinator grant keyed on the network being a
  direct link rather than on the peer it was minted for, so a later `ray
  accept` on that network gave away the network secret key. Recorded as
  `direct_peer` and pinned to it; links minted before the field existed
  fall back to the old rule only while still unformed.
- The pairing secret was consumed before being compared, so a wrong guess
  from anyone closed the user's pairing window. It now survives a
  mismatch, which is what makes the comparison's timing matter, so it is
  constant-time.
- Incoming `ray connect` requests were unbounded, keyed by an endpoint id
  the requester mints. Capped like pending joins already were.

Verified with the docker e2e suite: closed-net (admission, invite and
reusable-key joins, co-coordinator admission with the coordinator
offline, rename, leave, kick), device-cert (pairing, the device-to-user
resolution this changes), connect, and unpair all pass.

fix(dns): finish the stand-down path's cleanup obligations

Review of the previous commit found two holes in it.

Standing down drops the configurator, and DirectResolvConf::revert is the
only thing that removes the NetworkManager dns=none drop-in, so a stood-down
node left NM muted through ray down and uninstall: the other VPN owns
resolv.conf, and if it leaves too, nothing regenerates the file. Keeping the
drop-in while stood down is still right, so revert clears it directly. It is
marker-guarded and idempotent, a no-op on every backend that never wrote one.

The watcher can also return a verdict it decided just before revert cancelled
it, since the select arm has already committed by then. Acting on it minted a
fresh, uncancelled retry token, which then reconfigured DNS for a data plane
that was down. Check the token before standing down and again before arming
the retry.

Also from the review: the merged search list is capped at the six domains the
resolver actually reads, keeping `ray` at the cost of the last entry that fits
rather than letting a truncation drop the one entry bare mesh names need; the
resolvconf rank check skips a loopback stub, which is a forwarder we
registered with and not a competitor, and runs on every register so it can see
the other VPN arrive after us; and backup_file refuses to capture a file we
wrote, which the reclaim path can now hand it.

fix(exit-node): address review of the IPv6-only exit-node support

Re-check the IPv6 gateway gate on every apply, not only at selection.
`gateway_refusal` ran in `exit_node_use` alone, so a selection made while
dual-stack survived into IPv6-only mode and installed a tunnel that carried
nothing. Under `ipv6_only = auto` that needs no user action at all: the mode
turns itself on the first time something else claims 100.64.0.0/10. Split the
refusal in two, since the halves have different lifetimes: "does not advertise
an exit node" flickers and must not drop a live tunnel, while "cannot carry
IPv6" is a standing property, so only that one is re-checked, and it falls back
to direct egress rather than keeping a dead tunnel.

Stop overstating what the DNS override does. It moves the daemon's own
forwarder; whether an app's query reaches that forwarder is the OS backend's
call. On the Linux split-DNS backends only `~ray` routes to us, so other lookups
leave over the IPv4 this mode does not tunnel. macOS re-asserts a catch-all
match domain and has no such gap. Narrow the claim in README, CHANGELOG and
CLAUDE.md, and warn at install naming the backend. Giving Linux the same flip is
left as follow-up.

Also:
- install tears down the family it stopped claiming, so a daemon killed while
  dual-stack cannot leave v4 rules behind after restarting IPv6-only
- key the DNS override on the tunnel actually going in, not on the selection: a
  rolled-back install pointed the forwarder at public IPv6 resolvers it had no
  route to
- filter the magic IPs in `set_tunnel_upstreams` as the capture path does, now
  that dns-upstreams accepts any IpAddr, and treat filtering-to-empty as no
  override
- keep the captured upstreams when an all-IPv6 `--replace` narrows to nothing,
  which otherwise left the endpoint back on iroh's resolv.conf reader (#111)
- re-probe the IPv6 uplink on the reconverge that publishes it, so a gateway
  that gains IPv6 stops advertising otherwise before the next `ray up`
- skip IPv4 underlay exclusions on macOS when no v4 tunnel exists to route around
- fix stale text in the dns-upstreams help and the forward.rs comment

fix(mesh): refuse a replayed record, expire the pairing window

Review follow-ups on the sender-authentication work.

Two of them block, and both are cases where a check the code claimed to
make did not exist:

- `SignedRecord` is the one state-changing message deliberately exempt
  from the roster wall, on the grounds that it verifies against the
  network key whoever carries it. That is true of authorship and says
  nothing about age: an old record for the network stays validly signed
  forever, and the only guard was hash *inequality*, which reads a
  rollback as a change. Replaying a copy the DHT served publicly
  re-seated kicked members, restored devices the blob had nullified,
  reverted the suggested firewall, and steered the follow-up blob fetch
  at attacker-named seeds. Records now have to be authored after the last
  one applied. The timestamp sits inside the signed bytes, so it cannot
  be edited to clear the floor, and ordering on it is what pkarr relays
  do among themselves. The same floor is applied on the DHT poll path, so
  a stale resolve cannot undo a fresh mesh record, and it is seeded on
  reconnect from the record the roster came out of rather than starting
  open. `control.rs` claimed this check already existed; now it does.

- Not consuming the pairing secret on a mismatch fixed a stranger being
  able to close the user's pairing window, but a wrong guess was also the
  only thing besides a successful pair that ever cleared it. An
  interrupted `ray pair` therefore left a standing "sign a DeviceCert for
  whoever presents these 32 bytes" on a public ALPN until the daemon
  restarted, which is worse than the bug it replaced. Sessions now expire
  after five minutes, and `ray pair` says so.

Also from the review:

- The nullifier check was per-network while the binding it guards is
  daemon-wide, so a device revoked on one network could re-earn its
  user's firewall and SSH rights with a hello on another. Asked across
  every network now, which is what the CHANGELOG already claimed.
- `stranger_may_send` is a full match with no wildcard, so a new
  `ControlMsg` fails to compile until someone decides which side of the
  wall it is on. That is the property its test described and the
  `matches!` did not have.
- A third stranger-fed queue (incoming file offers) was unbounded; capped
  like the other two, and the CHANGELOG no longer says "two".
- Pairing certifies the key that dialed rather than the key the request
  names. The client only ever sends its own, so this costs nothing.
- `knows_sender` gets the tests it was missing: seated member, approved
  but unseated, device resolved to a roster user identity, and stranger.
- Doc and CHANGELOG corrections where the prose outran the code.

Verified: cargo check/clippy/test clean (686 unit tests), and the docker
e2e suite re-run in full on closed-net, device-cert, unpair and connect.

feat(cli): group nested help pages and collapse four commands (#127)

* feat(cli): group nested help pages and collapse four commands

`ray -h` has been grouped for a while; nothing below it was. `ray firewall
--help` listed 13 actions flat, and several descriptions ran to a full
paragraph printed on one unwrapped line, because the doc comment had no
blank line splitting the summary from the detail. The root escaped that
only because a test forced 80 columns there.

help.rs now keys its grouping on a command path instead of the root:
`PAGES` maps `&[]` and `&["firewall"]` to their groups, applied through
`mut_subcommand` so depth is not special-cased, and the template grows an
`Arguments:` block when the page has positionals. Only firewall is
grouped; below about eight actions a heading per two entries is noise,
and what those pages needed was the one-line `about`, now enforced at
every depth by walking the clap model. `wrap_help` makes the detail
paragraphs wrap instead of printing one long line.

Four commands move next to the thing they act on: `connections` into

feat(dns): share resolv.conf with another VPN instead of standing down

Where rayfish manages /etc/resolv.conf directly and another mesh VPN wants
the same file, it stood down and `.ray` names stopped resolving through the
system stub. Standing down was the right call against the alternative it had
(replace their file and have them replace it back), but not against merging:
our resolver goes in first, theirs stays as the next nameserver, the search
domains are merged, and everything outside `.ray` is forwarded to them. Both
meshes resolve no matter which daemon wrote the file last, which is what
makes losing the race harmless rather than something to win.

First place is not a preference. glibc stops at the first server that answers
and their NXDOMAIN is an answer, so a second `nameserver` line never sees a
`.ray` query.

The race is damped rather than won: MERGE_COOLDOWN puts a 60s floor on how
often we write over them, and inside it the watcher sleeps and re-reads, so
what it merges with is their newest file. A change to the file's nameservers
now re-runs detection (Recapture) instead of being patched in place, because
the upstreams we forward to were captured and probed from that file. Reclaim
is the case that bites: when the VPN we merged with leaves, re-asserting our
old render would name its resolver from a forwarder still aimed at it and
take the host's DNS down (#111).

An additive write needs a subtractive undo, so revert, the panic hook and the
post-crash restore all strip our own lines when another overlay's resolver is
in the file, instead of restoring a backup that predates the merge and would
undo their DNS along with ours.

fix(dns): import strip_our_resolv_entries for every test target

The test module imported it only under `cfg(target_os = "linux")`, so the
merge-revert test that uses it did not compile on macOS. The function itself
builds wherever tests do, so the import belongs with the unconditional ones
and the test now runs on both platforms.

fix(dns): stop feeding a resolver that forwards back at us

Merging /etc/resolv.conf means forwarding everything outside `.ray` to the
other VPN's resolver, and that resolver can be pointed straight back at us:
Tailscale builds its upstreams from the live file and drops only its own two
service IPs from what it finds (GetBaseConfig in net/dns/direct.go, added for
tailscale/tailscale#7816, the same loop with resolved on the other end), so a
daemon starting on a host we already configured adopts our magic IP. Neither
side's filter catches the other's.

A name is now counted per forward to an overlay resolver and stops being sent
there past LOOP_LIMIT in LOOP_WINDOW. The count is per name, so one looping
lookup cannot take the rest of the host's DNS with it, and the threshold sits
well above what a busy host asks for legitimately (glibc does not cache, so
every getaddrinfo is a query) while a loop passes it in a millisecond because
each hop multiplies.

What the host sees when it trips: we skip that upstream, and with nothing else
captured the query SERVFAILs, which sends the stub to the next nameserver in
the file. That is their resolver, which has real upstreams of its own. So the
loop costs a round trip rather than the lookup.

docs: cut CLAUDE.md back to the register it asks for

The file tells you to keep it principle-level, and the invariants added over
the last few changes had drifted to 150-250 words each against the 35-65 of
the original ones, mostly by retelling the incident behind each rule.

Every rule and every code pointer stays; what goes is the second telling. Down
to 2919 words from 3315, below where it was before this branch added two.

feat(dns): route the other VPN's domains to the other VPN's resolver

Sharing /etc/resolv.conf puts us first for every name on the host, theirs
included, so the only way their names resolved was to forward everything to
them. That is a detour for names neither mesh owns and it is the leg that
loops when their resolver is pointed back at us, which it is whenever they
started on a host we had already configured.

The direct backend now hands the resolver a Delegation per search domain it
captured from their file, since a domain in that file is theirs by
construction: we only read it because their resolver was in it. Names under
one go to their resolver, everything else to the host's own servers. Matching
is on label boundaries, so a delegation for tailnet.ts.net does not hand
nottailnet.ts.net to somebody else's resolver.

For that to have anywhere to send general traffic, the host's real servers now
survive a merge that hides them: when the shared file names nothing but the
other mesh's resolver, the non-overlay upstreams we captured before they
arrived are kept instead of being replaced by theirs. When they had the file
first we never saw the host's servers, and forwarding everything to them is
both right and loop-free, because they hold the real upstreams.

LOOP_LIMIT stays as the backstop for the one case this cannot narrow: a shared
file that named no search domains at all, leaving no way to tell which names
are theirs.

feat(dns): decline off-mesh names on a shared resolv.conf instead of relaying

Sharing the file puts us first for every name on the host, and until now the
only answer to that was to forward everything we do not own to the resolver we
share with. glibc already does that job: REFUSED marks a server failed and it
moves to the next `nameserver` line at once, which is the other VPN's. So the
forwarder was a userspace hop in front of every name on the box, it flattened
whatever that resolver does natively into one plain UDP query, and it was the
only reason two resolvers pointed at each other could loop at all.

The render now carries every captured server rather than the first, because on
such a host those lines stop being a safety net and become the path everything
outside `.ray` actually takes. Capped at glibc's MAXNS, since a fourth line is
read by nobody.

`.ray` stays ours to answer, misses included: passing those on would hand a
mesh name to the other resolver for the same failure a round trip later.
Declining is off unless the backend reports both halves of the precondition,
somebody to share with and a live server rendered behind us, because on an
ordinary host ours is the only line in the file.

This deletes the delegation table and the upstream retention added to make
forwarding safe; the loop counter stays as insurance for paths that still
forward.

Also fixes the case that has no trigger. Neither daemon overwrites a file the
other holds (their Close checks ownedByTailscale, our restore_file checks for
their resolver), so one that leaves while we hold the file leaves its address
in it, no longer answering, with nothing for the watcher to read. On a host
that declines off-mesh names that address is the rest of the machine's DNS.
The re-assert tick now probes it, and SharedResolverGone stands all the way
down rather than rebuilding: the servers it replaced are unrecoverable, so the
only way back is to un-quiet NetworkManager, let the host regenerate the file,
and take it over again on the retry.

fix(dns): don't share resolv.conf from an address the other VPN filters

Going first in the file is only worth something if we can be reached there.
A v4 magic address sits inside 100.64.0.0/10, which is the range the VPN we
would be sharing with owns and filters (`! -i tailscale0 -j DROP`), so our
reply never reaches the stub. We would be an unanswering first nameserver and
every lookup on the host would eat the resolver timeout before falling through
to them, which is worse than not taking the file at all.

That is exactly what the IPv6-only mode exists to avoid, and it is chosen
automatically when another VPN holds the range. But `ipv6-only = off` is a
standing refusal a user can set, and nothing checked it before merging, so
that host got the slow path. It now keeps its DNS and goes without Magic DNS,
which is the same trade master made for every host.

fix(exit-node): make the IPv6 claim three-valued and rescue the peer VPN's own traffic

Four fixes from an audit of the IPv6-only exit-node work.

`Member.exit_node_v6` was a bool, so "no coordinator ever told us" and "the
gateway says it has no IPv6" were the same value. Only a coordinator that knows
the field can write it, and one on 0.3.0 deserializes Member into a struct
without it and republishes without it, so a claim that passes through one comes
back as a denial. `exit_offer_out_of_sync` then compared a pair it could never
satisfy, and since that gates the reconverge worker's 30s backstop tick, a
v6-capable gateway on an older coordinator did a pkarr resolve and a re-delivery
to every coordinator every 30 seconds, indefinitely, while IPv6-only clients
refused a gateway that works.

It is now ExitFamilies {Unknown, V4, Dual} on both the roster and the wire
message. Unknown is the serde default, skipped on the way out, so a roster with
no claim encodes as it did before the field existed and the blob hash is
unchanged. Unknown compares equal in the sync check and is allowed at selection
with a warning in the reply, since refusing would rule out every gateway on a
network whose coordinator predates the feature. `enabled` stays a plain bool:
it shipped, and re-encoding a deployed field fails the old decoder on the whole
message.

mirror_foreign_routes only ever rescued the PREF_TUNNEL path. PREF_SRC and
PREF_BYPASS sit above it and both look up main, which is the one table a
policy-routing VPN keeps nothing in, so traffic sourced from that VPN's address
missed and took the physical default: an SSH session that arrived over Tailscale
died the moment `exit-node use` ran. PREF_FOREIGN (98) now sends the mirrored
destinations to our table, one rule per prefix actually copied, reclaimed by
reading back what is installed.

A refused selection cleared exit_selection_pending, and reconverge only nudges
exit_reapply while that is set, so a client that refused a gateway stayed on
direct egress even after the gateway gained IPv6 and republished. It stays
pending now.

operator_upstreams counted raw config strings while resolve_upstreams narrows to
IPv4, so an all-IPv6 dns-upstreams waived the refusal to take over resolv.conf
and then contributed nothing: the host took the file, installed the re-assert
watcher, and lost every name outside .ray. Both now go through
config::has_usable_upstream.

feat(proto)!: array-encode the network wire, mesh protocol 3

Msgpack named encoding writes struct fields as a keyed map, which costs a field
name per field on every frame. Switching the network protocols to the positional
array form takes about a third off the largest thing on the wire: a 50-member
GroupBlob goes from 6041 to 4061 bytes. The per-packet path is unaffected, since
data datagrams never touched this codec.

Positional arrays cannot tolerate a hole, so every `skip_serializing_if` on a
wire type is gone (25 of them): omitting a field shifted every later field a slot
and decoded as the wrong one. `#[serde(default)]` stays and now carries the whole
compatibility story, which is narrower than before: a shorter array from an older
build defaults its trailing fields, so fields are append-only and the tolerance
runs one way only. Reordering two same-typed fields decodes clean and silently
swapped; there is a test for that, because a diff that moves a line does not look
like a protocol change.

Not backward compatible, so all four ALPNs are bumped in the same change:
mesh 2->3, pair/connect/files 1->2. Peers on different versions share no ALPN, so
a mesh upgrades together.

Two callers keep named encoding on purpose, and are documented as such:
`identity::store_device_cert` writes to disk, where no ALPN gate exists and a
re-encode would strand every paired device's identity binding; and IPC, which has
no version negotiation and is read by a CLI whose binary is swapped before the
daemon restarts. Neither crosses a network, so neither saves a byte.

fix(proto): repair the unknown-variant probe under array encoding

FrameProbe declared only `msg`, which was right while the wire was
map-encoded and wrong the moment it became an array: it read the frame's
first slot, which is `net`, so every frame carrying a variant this build
does not know failed to decode outright instead of being nacked with
NotSupported.

The tests missed it because they built their fixtures with to_vec_named,
a shape no peer emits any more. They now encode the way a peer actually
would, and the probe tests cover both `net` states, since a scoped frame
is where a misread first slot returns the network key as a variant name.

Same for the remaining legacy-peer fixtures: an "old" message is a
shorter array now, not a map with keys missing, so they truncate the
struct instead. The GroupBlob one was not even a truncation, and the
reverse-direction half of the ExitNodeOffer test is gone: mesh 3 shares
no ALPN with a build that could have read it.

fix: repair what round 1 of review found

Six findings from three independent reviewers, each verified against the
code before acting on it and each with a test that fails without the fix.

A coordinator's firewall `deny` installed as an `allow` on every member.
HostSuggestions kept skip_serializing_if on both of its fields, and it
rides the signed blob, which is now an array: skipping an empty `allows`
left no hole, so `denies` slid into slot 0. Both fields are
BTreeMap<String, String>, so it decoded clean and inverted. This is the
hazard ipc.rs already documented, on the one path where the type crosses
a network. It was introduced by the compact switch and never released.

Withdrawing an exit offer never converged. Withdrawal publishes Unknown,
record_exit_offer maps that back onto the claim it already holds, so the
roster kept a Dual that offer_disagrees then compared against forever: a
pkarr resolve and a re-delivery to every coordinator, every 30s, for the
life of the daemon. The families only mean anything while the offer
stands.

The standing IPv6 gate never ran against a live tunnel. The nudge was
keyed on exit_selection_pending, which reload_exit_state clears the
moment the tunnel installs, so the one case the re-check exists for was
the one case it never saw. A gateway that lost its IPv6 uplink kept the
client's whole tunnel pointed into a black hole until the next `ray up`.

Re-applying a tunnel leaked. The catch-all came down first and went back
up last, with one `ip` process per mirrored prefix in between. The
mirroring made that window ~10x longer, and the nudge fix above makes it
fire more often. It now stays standing across the rebuild.

Multipath foreign routes were dropped, because the route line carries no
`dev` of its own. A dropped foreign route is not a no-op: the prefix
falls to our catch-all and that VPN's destinations go nowhere.

macOS pinned the IPv4 underlay in IPv6-only mode, carving it out of
whichever co-resident VPN owns IPv4 there, which is the setup the mode
exists to share with. tunnel_relevant already applies this filter one
layer up.

Also: CLAUDE.md claimed the blob is ALPN-gated. It is not, it rides the
shared blobs ALPN, and only the join path checks the mesh version, so
its field order is the thing that has to be right. And the e2e cleanup
missed prefs 98 and 99, where a leftover rule reads back as a match for
an assertion about state the run never created.

feat(exit-node): make the family claim answer for the return path

An IPv6-only gateway has an IPv6 uplink, so the uplink probe alone
called it Dual. It is not: that mode assigns mesh IPv4 as a /32 with no
100.64.0.0/10 route, so a dual-stack client's tunnelled IPv4 gets
masqueraded out fine and the un-NATted reply finds no way back into the
gateway's TUN. One-way, silent from both ends, and the field that exists
to turn exactly that into a sentence was making a positive claim that
was false.

The claim is now derived from both facts, giving V6 where the uplink
alone said Dual, and the refusal is symmetric: an IPv6-only client
refuses a gateway that cannot carry v6, a dual-stack client refuses one
that cannot carry v4. The warning stays asymmetric, because an unclaimed
gateway is a guess in both modes but only one of them is the common
case: every network with a coordinator predating the field has
unclaimed gateways, and warning a dual-stack client about all of them
would fire constantly to describe something rare.

Also: a dns-upstreams --replace list with no IPv6 in it keeps the
operator's own servers instead of being swapped for public ones.
--replace means these and no others, usually an internal resolver
holding names nothing else answers, and IPv4 egress is reachable in this
mode anyway, so the cost is a lookup going around the exit rather than a
wrong answer and the names handed to a third party.

fix(exit-node): one rule for the mirrored prefixes, and track convergence by what we accepted

PREF_FOREIGN was a rule per mirrored prefix, so its count grew with the
co-resident VPN's route count, and the readback that reclaimed them compared
the printed table against our numeric id, which iproute2 prints as a name
wherever rt_tables maps it. That is the same false negative parse_catch_all
had, and here it left rules behind to accumulate on every re-apply.

`suppress_prefixlength 0` on our own table replaces the lot: the lookup
becomes its own selector, matching every mirrored prefix and suppressing our
default, so one rule covers all of them, needs no readback to remove, and
cannot outlive a route that failed to install. Verified against a live kernel
(iproute2 6.1.0): a packet to a mirrored prefix resolves to the foreign
interface whether it is sourced from the physical address or carries our
mark, an ordinary destination still takes the tunnel, and a marked one still
bypasses it. Deleting by full spec leaves the neighbouring rules alone.

Separately, a member tracked convergence by the hash of its own re-encoding
of the group, which only equals the record's while the publisher writes the
bytes we would. rmp-serde reads a struct from a map as well as an array, so a
node that upgrades ahead of its coordinator converges from the old named blob
and then re-encodes it compactly: every poll after that read as "a different
blob", refetched, reapplied, and never reached the converged branch that
syncs the exit offer and drains a pending rename. Convergence is now
`converged_hash`, the hash we accepted; the snapshot stays what we publish.

feat(exit-node): a tunnel carries what both ends carry, and says which

The client tunnel took the families its own data plane routes. The gateway's
claim only ever produced a refusal, which meant a dual-stack node picking a
gateway that can return IPv6 and not IPv4 got no tunnel at all: the family
that worked was dropped to avoid one that never could. In the other
direction, a gateway with no IPv6 uplink was accepted by a dual-stack client
and its tunnelled IPv6 vanished at the far end with nothing said.

Both are the same question, so both get the same answer. `ExitFamilies::
tunnelled` intersects what this node's data plane routes with what the
gateway says it can return, and the tunnel installs exactly that: the routing
rules, the macOS split default, the socket pin and the DNS override all read
it, through one `Daemon::tunnel_carries` so they cannot describe different
tunnels. A family only one end can carry keeps leaving directly, which is the
trade IPv6-only mode already makes with its own data plane, and `ray
exit-node use` warns about it while `ray exit-node status` reports `IPv6
only` / `IPv4 only` standing.

Only a gateway that can return neither family is refused now. An absent claim
still narrows nothing: it is what a coordinator predating the field leaves
behind, and treating silence as denial would stop tunnelling a family that
works.

The convergence fix in `3caa4c5` updated two of three readers and missed the
group poller, which is the periodic one and has no timestamp floor, so the
loop its own doc comment describes was still there. All three now go through
`NetworkState::needs_reconverge`.

Two tests were worthless: the convergence one asserted a field it had just
assigned, and the PREF_FOREIGN one asserted only that 98 < 99. Both now fail
when their fix is reverted. And the rule the second one covers had a real
gap: the readback that reclaimed the old per-prefix rules was deleted with
them, so a host that ran an intermediate build of this branch kept rules that
outlive the routes they depend on.

Also: `Member.exit_families` was inserted above `ipv6_only` rather than
appended, which is what the append-only rule exists to prevent, and the
fixture that was supposed to pin it modelled a struct that never shipped.

Merge pull request #125 from rayfish/feat/exit-node-ipv6-only

feat(exit-node): support exit nodes in IPv6-only mode

refactor(peers): key the data plane on the mesh IPv6

The peer table held three maps: an IPv4 one owning the real dashmap entry
state machine, an IPv6 mirror kept in step by hand, and an endpoint-id
side table pointing back at the v4 key. The v6 is blake3 of the identity,
so the side table was storing what a hash already computes, and the mirror
was two copies of one peer that could drift.

Collapse all three into one Ipv6Addr-keyed map. `by_id` is deleted rather
than re-typed: `derive_ipv6(id)` is the key, and `ipv6_for_id` keeps the
"None until registered" contract every caller relies on by asking the map
whether the peer is there. RosterRouteMap loses its second map the same way.

The data path follows. Ingress anti-spoofing now matches the source against
the peer's derived v6 alone, so an IPv4 source is never a legitimate mesh
source and falls through to the exit-return exemption, where a routable
public address belongs. `ExitSelection` and `ExitContext` carry the v6,
`DisconnectEvent` drops its v4, and mesh SSH takes an Ipv6Addr because the
listener only ever binds our own overlay address.

Mesh IPv4 stops carrying traffic here. Nothing else about it moves yet:
`Member.ip`, the roster, the TUN address and the collision index are all
still in place, and `is_overlay_ip` still matches 100.64.0.0/10 so iroh
keeps a co-resident VPN's CGNAT addresses out of its transport candidates.

The forward tests move to IPv6 packets, which is the same change stated
from the other side: an IPv4 mesh packet is now a spoofed one.

refactor(ipc): report the mesh IPv6 as the node's address

The polarity was backwards: `NetworkStatus.my_ip` and `PeerStatus.ip` were
required IPv4 while the v6 beside them was an `Option`, so every consumer
had a fallback path for the address that always exists and none for the one
that does not. Both become a required `Ipv6Addr` and the v4 fields go, along
with the `Option` on `Created`/`Joined`.

`ray status` loses its dual-stack branch and always prints the v6. The
comment the old branch carried already settled the layout question this
raises ("wider rows are the price; a wrong address is not"), so the address
stays a column rather than being dropped for width. `ipv6_only` stops being
threaded down through `print_network`/`grouped_peer_rows`/`device_row`,
which only ever used it to choose between the two addresses; it keeps its
top-level meaning until the setting itself goes.

`ray network`, `ray connect`, tab completion and the GUI follow. The GUI
reads `ray status --json`, whose keys are serde's, so `p.ip` becomes
`p.ipv6` and `n.my_ip` becomes `n.my_ipv6` there too.

ray-mobile keeps its UniFFI records unchanged and derives the v4 it still
exposes from the identity instead of reading it off a response. That is a
one-step shim: it keeps the committed Kotlin bindings and the CI drift check
green while the app still reads an `ipv4` field, and it goes when the mobile
surface moves.

Two status tests pinned behaviour that no longer exists. The dual-stack half
of `peer_rows_carry_the_reachable_address` is gone and the assertion is now
that the column is the v6; `peer_without_ipv6_falls_back_to_its_ipv4` tested
a fallback with nothing left to fall back to and is deleted.

feat(mesh)!: mesh protocol 4, drop the IPv4 from the roster

The mesh address is blake3 of the identity, so carrying it on the wire was
carrying a value the receiver could compute. `Member.ip`, `Member.collision_index`
and their `ApprovedEntry` twins are gone, and with them the machinery that
existed only because 22 bits of FNV-1a is not enough space: `derive_ip`,
`derive_ip_with_index`, `assign_ip`, `is_reserved_ipv4`, `IpCollision`,
`ensure_in_cgnat_range`, `validate_no_duplicate_ips`, `resolve_ip_tiebreak`,
both `get_by_ip`, and the `collision_index` file that was read and never
written. `MemberList::add` and `ApprovedList::approve` stop returning `Result`:
there is nothing left for them to reject.

Both validators go the same way. `decode_group_blob` used to check that each
member's stored address matched its identity; the address is now derived from
the identity at the point of use, so the two cannot disagree.

`JoinApproved.your_ip`, `MeshHello.ip` and `MemberApproved.ip` leave the
control protocol. These are non-trailing fields in an array-encoded struct, so
`MESH_PROTOCOL_VERSION` goes to 4 and the ALPN gate keeps old peers out. The
mismatch is already surfaced: `mesh_version_from_record` fails the join with
both versions named, and `PeerStatus.incompatible` flags a roster peer whose
dial hit the gate.

`is_overlay_ip` is split rather than trimmed, which is the part worth reading.
Six callers used its IPv4 arm for a reason unrelated to our overlay: the CGNAT
range belongs to whatever other VPN shares the host, and they were keeping
*its* addresses out of iroh's transport candidates, out of our control-plane
nameservers, and out of the resolver's forwarding path. `is_cgnat_range` now
answers that question under its own name. Eleven tests failed when only the
type changed, which is what the split is for.

Config stops storing what it can derive: `MemberEntry.ip`,
`ApprovedConfigEntry.ip` and `NetworkConfig.my_ip`. Nothing rejects the stale
keys in an existing file, so an upgrade reads them and ignores them.

The TUN stops assigning an IPv4 at all, and the SSH NAT holds one address.
Android's CGNAT preflight now has no address of ours to exclude, so anything it
finds in the range is a real conflict.

ray-mobile's UniFFI records follow: `ipv4` leaves `NetworkInfo`,
`NetworkDetail` and `Status`, `PeerInfo` gains the `ipv6` it never had, and
`HealthSnapshot.mesh_ipv4` becomes `mesh_ipv6`. Bindings regenerated; the
Kotlin screens, the share sheet's sort key and the Sentry context follow.

feat(dns)!: answer on the IPv6 magic address only

`HostnameEntry` was `(Option<Ipv4Addr>, Ipv6Addr)` so a peer could withhold
its A record. There is nothing left to withhold: the entry is a bare
`Ipv6Addr`, and an A query for a name the roster holds is always NODATA.
NODATA and not NXDOMAIN, because the name exists and NXDOMAIN would fail the
AAAA lookup beside it. `handle_query` and `handle_ptr_query` lose the mode
parameter they consulted to make that choice.

`resolver_addr()` is now a constant. `100.64.0.0/10` belongs to whatever other
VPN shares the host, so a resolver address there is one it would drop before
the stub ever saw it. That makes `is_magic_dns` and the resolver's own
loop-guard IPv6-only, and it retires `build_v4_reply`: the resolver is reached
at one address, in one family.

**The NetworkManager backend is deleted, not skipped.** It sets nameservers
through `IP4Config.Nameservers`, a `u32` array that cannot carry an IPv6
address at all, so it could never again be chosen. It was already declined on
IPv6-only hosts; leaving an unreachable rung in the detection ladder would have
been worse than removing it. resolvconf and the direct `resolv.conf` writer sit
below it and take either family.

The upstream filter now refuses anything in either overlay *or* the CGNAT
range, not just our own magic address. A co-resident VPN's resolver lives
there and forwards back to us (Tailscale drops only its own service IPs), so
two resolvers can point at each other. Neither range is a place a real
upstream lives.

The TUN stops installing the `100.64.0.0/10` route and the magic-DNS host
route: `200::/7` is the whole overlay and already covers `MAGIC_DNS_V6`.

`MAGIC_DNS_V4` stays as a constant, and only as an upgrade path: the
`resolv.conf` strippers and the macOS capture filter still need to recognise
what an older build wrote so it gets cleaned up rather than captured as an
upstream.

feat!: delete the ipv6-only setting

The mode existed so a node could share a host with a VPN that owns
`100.64.0.0/10`. Nothing to share now: the overlay never claims that range, so
what the setting selected is simply how the daemon works.

Gone with it: the `ipv6-only` config key and its tri-state `Ipv6Only` type
(including the hand-written `Deserialize` that still read the older bare
boolean), `ray up --ipv6-only`, `ControlMsg::Ipv6Only`, `Member.ipv6_only`,
`build_headless_with_setting`, the mode's copies on `Daemon`, `NetworkRegistry`
and `Resolver`, and `src/daemon/mesh/ipv6_only.rs` whole.

The startup CGNAT scan goes too, and with it the `#[cfg(target_os = ...)]` fork
in `run_daemon` that existed only to skip it on Android, plus a block of unsafe
`getifaddrs` FFI. The scan's job was choosing between two modes; there is one.

`ExitFamilies` keeps its four variants but can now only *produce* two.
`from_uplink` reports IPv6 or nothing, because a gateway with no IPv6 uplink
has nothing it can carry for us, and `tunnelled` narrows any claim to its IPv6
half. `V4` and `Dual` stay decodable because this rides the signed roster and a
claim is read as well as written. The partial-tunnel warning goes: a tunnel now
carries IPv6 or it is refused, so there is no half to report.

`Member.ipv6_only` is a second wire change, but no second version bump: mesh 4
has not shipped, so no build has ever spoken it with that field present.

Two tests moved rather than died. The silent-swap guard was pinned to
`ipv6_only`/`exit_node` being an adjacent bool pair; `Member` no longer has one,
so it now pins the property against a local pair of structs, where it cannot
evaporate the next time a field moves. The hostfw fix-command test stops
asserting both families and asserts the one mesh SSH actually binds.

On Android: **`allowFamily(OsConstants.AF_INET)`**. `VpnService` blocks an
address family outright when the Builder names no address, route or DNS server
of it, and this tunnel names none for IPv4 any more. Without that line every
app on the device loses IPv4 internet the moment the VPN comes up, while the
mesh keeps working, so no mesh test would have caught it. The IPv6-only
settings card and its prefs are gone from the app.

docs: the e2e harness, invariants and changelog for an IPv6-only overlay

The shell harness was the dangerous half. `my_ip4` read `.my_ip` from the
status JSON, a key that no longer exists, and jq's `// empty` turned that into
an empty string rather than an error: every comparison against it passed. It
is now `my_ip`, reads `.my_ipv6`, and calls `fail` when it finds nothing, as
does `own_ip`. `peer_ip` keeps returning empty, because several callers test
for a peer's absence.

The exit-node suite tested the wrong thing in three places. Step 4 asserted
srv-b's public IPv4 became srv-a's; the tunnel carries IPv6 now, so it asserts
the IPv4 is *unchanged* and that no IPv4 rule was installed at all, with the
IPv6 egress as the headline. Step 5 probed the revert over IPv4, which was
never tunnelled and so proved nothing. Step 6's deny path did the same, and
would have reported srv-c's untouched IPv4 egress as a leak. All three now
probe IPv6, against a baseline captured before any tunnel exists. Step 9
tested exactly what step 4 now tests, through a mode that no longer exists, and
is gone.

The DNS suite keeps both resolver helpers: `a6` for `.ray` names, which answer
AAAA only, and `a4` for the public names the upstream-forwarding checks use,
which still have A records.

CLAUDE.md loses three invariants and gains two: the address is derived and
never on the wire, and `100.64.0.0/10` is not ours, which is why the predicate
that used to answer both questions is split. The four exit-node invariants are
rewritten around a tunnel that carries IPv6 or is refused.

The changelog's `[Unreleased]` entries described IPv6-only as a mode, and that
mode never shipped, so they are rewritten rather than left describing something
that never existed. Two entries claimed different protocol versions; merged.
Released sections are untouched: they are the record of what shipped.

The listen-address migration is called out where users will meet it: `0.0.0.0`
is the IPv4 wildcard, so a service bound there is no longer reachable over the
mesh, and `ss -tlnp` is how to find out which of yours are.

test: provision e2e fleets with doctl instead of scw

The overlay is IPv6-only now, and the exit-node suite skips its egress
assertions on a host that cannot reach the v6 internet, so a fleet without
IPv6 makes that suite pass without testing the tunnel. Droplets are created
with --enable-ipv6, which is settable only at create time, and provisioning
warns when one comes up without a v6 address.

DigitalOcean injects no SSH key unless --ssh-keys names one, where Scaleway
attached every account key by itself. The provisioner passes all account keys
by default (DO_SSH_KEYS overrides), which is what the harness needs: just scp
runs bare rsync/ssh with no -i, so a host has to accept ssh's default identity.

ZONE/TYPE become REGION/SIZE to match doctl's vocabulary. The .servers format
is unchanged, so the region column still doubles as the backend marker and the
docker backend keeps refusing to touch a cloud fleet.

Also fixes tests/bench/ab.sh, which called a provision.sh that does not exist.

build: give cross builds their own target dir

A native `just release` leaves host-linked build scripts in target/release,
and cross reuses the same target dir inside its container, where cargo finds a
matching fingerprint and tries to execute a binary built against a newer glibc:

  build-script-build: /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.39' not found

The container is Ubuntu 22.04 at glibc 2.35. Any e2e run after a native release
build hit this. android-check already documents the same hazard and solves it
the same way, so cross, cross-musl, deploy, scp and the -dev twins now build
into target/cross.

fix(test): repair three harness bugs the IPv6-only cutover left behind

Found by running the suites on real hosts; none of them could fail a syntax
check, a clippy run or a unit test.

own_ip matched a literal `200:`, but the overlay prefix is /7: only the first
seven bits are fixed, so the leading hextet runs from 200 to 2ff and a real
address matched about one time in 256. Its complaint was invisible too, because
every caller reads it through $(...), which captured the message into the
command line being built instead of printing it. That now goes to stderr.
peer_host had the same pattern in its awk guard. Six suites use these.

start_tcp_listener bound 0.0.0.0 and udp_probe used AF_INET. With no mesh IPv4
left, a socket on the v4 wildcard has no presence on the TUN, so every probe
read CLOSED whatever the firewall did: the allow assertions could not pass and,
worse, the deny assertions passed for the wrong reason. The firewall suite has
seven listener sites and a UDP matrix on top. Binding :: is the same fix a user
hits when a service of theirs stops answering over the mesh.

exit-node step 8 still pinged the peer's mesh address over IPv4. It now checks
that `ray status` reports the address the TUN actually holds.

fix(dns): restore the macOS AAAA marker and the foreign-resolver loop guard

Two things the cutover left half-deleted.

The macOS SCDynamicStore path still read an `ipv6_only` flag whose only setter
call went away with the setting, so it was permanently false and both blocks it
gated were dead: the `InterfaceName` + `ConfirmedServiceID` pair that makes
configd trust our resolver, and `write_service_config` that puts the AAAA flag
on it to carry. Without them configd falls back to merging the default
resolver's flags, which on a Mac with no native IPv6 is A-only, so `.ray` names
resolve to nothing while `dig` against the same resolver answers fine. Both are
unconditional now and the flag is gone.

The resolver's upstream filter had widened from "our own magic addresses" to
"anything that could loop", which swept another mesh's resolver out of the list
entirely and left `loop_guard_allows` unreachable. A host whose only captured
nameserver is in `100.64.0.0/10` then has nothing to ask at all. Split the
predicate back in two: `is_own_resolver` is filtered out, a foreign mesh
resolver stays in and is rate-limited by the guard, as before.

Also drops `Resolver::ipv6_only`, written and never read.

refactor: delete what the IPv6-only cutover left behind

`is_disabled_mesh_ipv4` is unreachable twice over: its flag has no setter left,
and `is_overlay_ip` is v6-only now, so an IPv4 destination never matches. It
still read as live policy. Gone, with `InboundDecision::DropIpv4Disabled` and
`DropReason::Ipv4Disabled`. Such a packet now falls to the exit-transit branch,
where a mesh IPv4 address fails `is_transitable` and is dropped as `DropExit`.

Android: `SegmentedCard` lost its only caller with the setting it rendered, and
`NodeHolder` still explained an Auto mode that `start()` no longer takes.

Also fixes an exit-selection log line that printed an IPv6 address under an
`ipv4` key.

test: stop three checks from passing when they should not

`my_ip` reports a missing address through `fail`, which writes to stdout, and
every caller reads it through `$(...)`. So the variable holds the complaint
instead of an empty string, the caller's own `[[ -n ]]` guard passes, and every
probe below runs against garbage; the tally is lost in the subshell too, so the
suite can still exit 0. This is what 875523f fixed in `own_ip`. Both now go
through `fail_out`, which writes to stderr and leaves the counting to the
caller.

The exit-node scenario never checked whether `ray exit-node use` was accepted,
and gated its deny-path probe on the client's IPv6 rather than the gateway's. A
gateway with no IPv6 uplink refuses the selection, both hosts egress directly,
and the script reports a leak that is really a skipped test. It now aborts with
the refusal when the selection fails, and skips the deny path unless both ends
have IPv6.

Restores `the_split_default_plan_visits_every_family_and_adds_only_what_it_carries`,
which went with the rest of `tun.rs`'s test module. It is the only coverage of
"install is per-family, teardown is never per-family", and the plan still has to
decode every variant the roster can carry.

The ufw arm of `the_iptables_fix_matches_the_family_ssh_listens_on` compared a
call to itself once the family input was gone. Asserts the command now.

fix(cli): exit non-zero when the daemon rejects a command

Every handler that talks to the daemon matched `IpcMessage::Error`, printed it
with `print_error`, and fell through to `Ok(())`. That is exit 0: `ray join` on
a spent invite, `ray exit-node use` on a gateway that cannot carry IPv6, and
forty-odd others told whatever ran them that the command worked. `files.rs`
carried a comment admitting it.

Routes all of them through `fail_with`, which prints the same block and exits 1.
Two sites already did this by hand and now share the helper.

One ordering exception: on `sudo ray up`, a failed activation still grants the
invoking user operator access before exiting, because the service is installed
and running by then and the next thing they will do is retry `ray up` without
sudo.

docs: correct what the cutover left pointing at a deleted setting

Five places still described `ipv6-only` as a mode a host can be in, which since
the cutover it is not.

The one with teeth is in `DirectResolvConf::apply`: an `ensure!` that
`resolver_addr()` is IPv6, which it now is unconditionally, so the guard cannot
fire and its message told the user to set a setting that no longer exists. The
reasoning behind it is worth keeping, so it stays as the comment it always
should have been.

The rest are doc comments: `create` describing an IPv4 address it no longer
assigns, `split_default_plan` and an exit-node test citing `ipv6_only = auto` as
a way a tunnel narrows, `fix_command` documenting a `v6` parameter it does not
take, and an orphaned line in `config.rs` that had drifted onto `TransportMode`
and was documenting it as the ipv6-only tri-state.

test: pin the three behaviours the last round changed but left unasserted

`evaluate_inbound` had no test that built an IPv4 packet at all, so nothing said
what happens to one now that `DropIpv4Disabled` is gone. It is `DropSpoof`, and
only that: an IPv4 destination makes the whole packet IPv4, so its source is
IPv4 too and can never be the peer's derived IPv6, while the exit-return
exemption compares an IPv6 destination and cannot fire either. (The commit
message on 41391b8 said such a packet reaches the transit branch and is dropped
as `DropExit`. It does not get that far. The outcome is a drop either way, but
the reason on the record was wrong and nothing pinned the real one.)

`DropReason::ALL` is hand-maintained and is the only thing `total_drops` and the
metrics snapshot iterate, so a variant left out of it is invisible in both and
still compiles. Iterating `ALL` cannot catch that; an exhaustive match beside a
count can, at build time.

And the upstream filter split changed `set_tunnel_upstreams` too: another mesh's
resolver used to be dropped from a tunnel override and now survives it, same as
on the capture path. That was untested in either direction.

test: guard two more e2e paths that pass without asserting anything

The unpair scenario reads srv-b's mesh IPv6 through `own_ip` but only used it
behind an `&&`, so a miss skipped the baseline probe silently. Step 5 then
pings that empty address, reads the empty loss figure as "no route", and passes
the revocation assertion against a peer it never reached. Same shape as the
`my_ip` bug, one scenario over: a hard guard, not a skipped probe.

In the exit-node scenario the `exit-node use` guard added last commit could not
fire, because `ray` exited 0 on a refusal until the CLI fix. Now that it can, it
reverts before disarming the failsafe (disarming only touches the flag file, so
doing it first on a half-installed tunnel removes the automatic revert without
performing one) and reports rc 255 as the lost SSH session it is rather than as
a refusal.

Steps 4 and 5 are now skipped rather than fatal when the gateway has no IPv6
uplink, matching how step 6 treats the same condition, so a fleet without IPv6
still runs the steps that never needed it. `pub6` gets a second service like
`pub4` has: it decides whether those steps run at all, so one flaky probe would
turn them into skips whose message claims something about the host that was
never established.

fix(cli): do not abandon a loop's remaining work on the first rejection

Two of the 43 sites converted last commit sit inside loops that were written to
keep going, and `exit(1)` in them abandons the rest.

`ray send <peer> a b c`: `ipc_send_files` runs one IPC round-trip per file and
accumulates failures, as its own doc comment says ("a failure on one file still
sends the rest"). Exiting inside it dropped every file after the first the
daemon rejected, and made the accumulator dead code for that whole class of
failure. It returns the error now and the caller reports it with the file's name.

`ray exit-node none`: resolved client-side into one request per network with a
live selection. Exiting on the first failure left the remaining networks still
routing through their exit nodes, having reported only the one it reached. That
is the opposite of what the command was asked to do, so every network is now
attempted and the exit code comes at the end.

Also converts three arms the last commit missed (`ipc_firewall_pending`'s fetch,
`clear_all_exit_selections`'s status query, and `config_row`, which returned
`Ok(None)` and had both callers quietly succeed), routes the four hand-rolled
`print_error` + `exit(1)` pairs in `main.rs` through the same helper, and drops
a comment in `files.rs` describing the behaviour that is now gone.

fix(dns): a resolver on a mesh peer is an upstream, not a loop

`is_own_resolver` filtered the whole `200::/7` when it meant "the address we
answer on". Only `200::53` comes back to us: `forward::is_magic_dns` intercepts
that one address and nothing else, so a query aimed at any other overlay address
is routed out to the peer that owns it, which is a real second party. A test
beside it already asserted exactly that about `200::9`.

So a user running unbound or a pi-hole on a mesh peer and naming it in
`dns_upstreams` had it dropped. Worst under a full tunnel, where a mesh address
is the *best* upstream available, being reachable only through the tunnel by
construction: `set_tunnel_upstreams` filtered it, the empty result became `None`,
the forwarder fell back to the captured IPv4 servers, and every off-mesh lookup
left around the exit. Silently, since the warning for a missing override is
guarded on the override existing.

Back to the two magic addresses, which is what master filtered. The doc comment
already said "the magic IPs" and only the body disagreed.

test: say what the DropReason tripwire actually catches

It claimed to fail when a variant goes missing from `ALL`, and does not: the
loop iterates `ALL`, so a variant absent from it is never seen, and the count
assertion adds nothing the fixed array length does not already enforce. Adding a
variant and its match arm while leaving `ALL` alone compiles and passes.

The mechanism is still worth keeping, so the name and the doc now describe it
honestly: the exhaustive match makes a new variant a compile error in this file,
three lines from the `ALL` it has to be added to. A real assertion needs the list
generated from the enum instead of typed out twice, which is a derive this crate
does not depend on yet.

test: stop three more e2e paths from asserting less than they report

`device-cert` read three mesh addresses with no guard, and its four reachability
probes are `&&`-guarded on them, so a miss made all four vanish rather than fail.
The distinctness check above them still recorded one failure, so the run came
back saying one thing was wrong when in fact the scenario asserted nothing.
`ssh` counted the same miss and then carried on into a ping and the SSH checks
built on it. Both stop now.

Also fixes the step-6 skip message added last commit, which named the host with
`${A_PUB_V6:+srv-c}${A_PUB_V6:-srv-a}`. `:-` expands to the variable's value
when it is set, so the two halves concatenated and it printed `srv-c` followed
by an IPv6 address.

fix(macos): dial the exit peer by its mesh IPv6

The macOS full-tunnel path still read `ExitSelection::ipv4`, which the
cutover deleted, so the macOS target did not compile at all: four E0609s
in `nudge_all_peers` and `exit_peer_conn`. Only the macos CI job builds
that code, and `cargo check` on Linux never sees it.

Not only a compile fix. `exit_peer_conn` asked
`resolve_route(IpAddr::V4(..))`, and that arm now returns `None` for
every v4 destination, so the dial-when-absent half would have been dead:
picking an exit node while the connection is idle-closed would fall
through to no connection, skipping the direct-address exclusions and
leaving the exit path on the relay.

Also drops a duplicated comment paragraph in `exit_peer_conn` that
predates the branch.

refactor(connect): carry a message, not a whole reply, out of target resolution

`resolve_connect_target` returned `Result<EndpointId, IpcMessage>`, and
clippy in Rust 1.98 (released 2026-08-20, which CI installs fresh each
run) fails `result_large_err` on it: the `Err` variant is 208 bytes. Not
something this branch introduced, and master trips it too.

Every failure in there was already an `ipc_err`, so the error type is a
`String` now and the single caller builds the reply. No boxing, no
`allow`, and the function no longer names an IPC type it does not need.

docs: drop the mesh-IPv4 wording the cutover left behind

`ExitFamilies::V6` and `Neither` still explained themselves in terms of
an IPv6-only *mode* and a mesh IPv4 with no return path, and
`route_default_via_tun` said "in IPv6-only mode" for what is now the only
mode there is. Same for the rest: the overlay carries no IPv4, so V6 is
the whole of a working gateway rather than half of one.

fix(exit-node): stop a gateway claiming the IPv4 the overlay dropped

`enable()` still set `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` and installed an IPv4 NAT rule
for `100.64.0.0/10` beside the IPv6 ones, on both platforms. The cutover took
away everything those could act on: no mesh IPv4 is assigned, none is routed,
and an inbound IPv4 packet is dropped as spoofed before it could reach the TUN.

The pf half is the one with teeth. `nat on {iface} inet from 100.64.0.0/10`
matches on `default_interface("-inet")`, the *uplink*, not our TUN, so pf applies
it to anything leaving that interface from that range. Ours used to be in it;
now the only thing that can be is a co-resident VPN's. CLAUDE.md says the host's
IPv4 egress is left "with whoever owns `100.64.0.0/10`" and that claiming it
would take IPv4 from that VPN, which is what the rule does.

Sharpest on a Mac with no IPv6 uplink: `nat_rules(Some("en0"), None)` returned
`Some`, so `enable()` succeeded, turned on IPv4 forwarding and loaded the rule,
and then published `ExitFamilies::Neither`, which every client refuses. Host
posture changed, nothing delivered.

`nat_rules` takes only the v6 uplink now and returns an empty ruleset rather than
`None` when there is none: that host has nothing to masquerade, but it is not an
error, and failing there would clear the offer and leave clients reading "does
not advertise an exit node" instead of the reason the refusal gives them. The
nft ruleset moves into `server_nft_ruleset` so a Linux test can pin it, the way
`nat_rules` already was.

The `v4` snapshot field and `disable`'s restore of it both stay: an older build
did set the sysctl, and teardown may not assume which build turned it on.

Three comments said a gateway with no IPv6 "is still a perfectly good IPv4 exit
node, which is why this is advertised rather than refused". `from_uplink` has
reported `Neither` for that host since the cutover and every client refuses it,
so the reasoning that kept these halves alive was already false in the file.

fix(dns): re-check the upstream after quieting NetworkManager

Deleting the NetworkManager rung sent one host to `DirectResolvConf` that never
reached it before: NM in `dns=dnsmasq` mode, with no systemd-resolved in the
resolution path and no `resolvconf` binary. `nm_supports_split_dns` matched
`"dnsmasq"`, so that host took the NM rung on master.

There it walks into the black hole the backend's own `ensure!` exists to refuse,
by ordering rather than by an empty capture:

  - `new()` reads `nameserver 127.0.0.1`, which is NM's own dnsmasq, and
    `live_upstreams` keeps it because it is answering at that moment.
  - the `ensure!` in `apply()` passes on the strength of it.
  - `apply()` then calls `nm_quiet_install()`, which writes `dns=none` and
    reloads NM: the instruction that stops that dnsmasq.

The file we write names `200::53` and then a resolver we just shut down, so every
name outside `.ray` fails until `ray down`. The guard read a set that was true
when it was taken.

So take it again, after. `nm_quiet_outcome` classifies before against after:
nothing died is `Proceed`, some died (or all did while `dns_upstreams` still
gives the forwarder somewhere to go) is `Degraded` and warns with the dead
entries, and all died with nothing configured is `Abort`, which restores the file,
un-quiets NM and bails with the reason. That leaves the host with working DNS and
no Magic DNS, which is the trade the original guard chose.

Split out as a function because the ordering is not otherwise observable: the
capture is in `new`, the kill is in `apply`, and neither end has a seam a test can
reach.

fix(cli): exit non-zero on a reply the command cannot read

The exit-code sweep converted every `IpcMessage::Error` arm and left the `other`
arm beside it printing to stderr and falling through to `Ok(())`. That is the
same bug one match arm over, in 45 places: `ray join` against a daemon that
answers something it does not recognise told its caller the join worked.

Not a hypothetical arm. IPC has no version negotiation, and CLAUDE.md says why:
the binary is swapped before the service restarts, so a CLI and a daemon on
different versions is the routine case rather than an exotic one, and it is
exactly what puts a reply here.

`fail_unexpected` prints the reply and names the skew as the likely cause. Two
sites do not use it:

`service.rs` is the `sudo ray up` ordering exception. Exiting there would skip
`grant_operator_to_invoking_user`, which is the whole point of the carve-out, so
an unrecognised reply becomes a message and takes the existing failure path after
the grant.

`logs.rs` calls `sink.finish()` first, as its error arm already does: it waits on
the pager, and exiting out from under one leaves the terminal to its mercy.

style: rustfmt

`cargo fmt --all` was clean on master and had 69 diffs here. Most are collapses
that became possible when the cutover deleted an argument, so they are the
cutover's own residue rather than drift. CI runs clippy and not fmt, so this was
never going to show up as a red build.

fix(dns): restore the cfg the NmQuietOutcome enum was inserted under

`0304f21` put the enum between `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]` and the item it
gated, so both cfgs bound to the enum and `impl DnsConfigurator for
DirectResolvConf` was left with only `#[async_trait]`. `DirectResolvConf` is
Linux-only, so every non-Linux build fails on an impl for a type that was
configured out. Linux sees nothing wrong, which is why check, clippy, test and
fmt were all green: only the macOS CI job compiles that combination, the same
way `e338963` went unnoticed until it ran.

Also stops the abort retrying forever. `DnsService::configure` hands a failed
detection to `spawn_configure_retry`, which backs off to a 60s ceiling and never
gives up. The `ensure!` it was modelled on is safe to retry because it bails
before touching anything; this one is not, because reaching the verdict means
installing the `dns=none` drop-in and reloading NM, then removing it and
reloading again. The host would pay two reloads and the DNS gap between them
every minute for the daemon's lifetime, to re-derive an answer that follows from
NetworkManager's static configuration. `NM_TAKEOVER_UNSAFE` records it and the
next attempt bails alongside the original guard, before `backup_file`.

And two tests that the cutover had turned into tautologies:
`strip_removes_either_magic_address` had the same IPv6 string in both halves, and
