thing they exist to hold down: that filter is the whole reason the constant
survived the cutover.

fix(cli): stop fail_unexpected abandoning the two loops written to continue

`12752d5` converted the `other` arm beside every `IpcMessage::Error`, and two of
them sit in the loops `056fd8b` had just converted *away* from exiting, for
exactly this reason. Both have the reason written directly above the line:

`ray exit-node none` resolves client-side into one request per network with a
live selection, under a comment reading "Every network is attempted even after
one fails... Stopping at the first would leave the rest still routing through
their exit nodes, which is the opposite of what was asked". Exiting there also
made the `failed` counter and its `ensure!` dead for that class.

`ipc_send_file` is called once per file by `ipc_send_files`, under "Returned, not
exited... ending the process here would drop every file after the first rejected
one". `ray send peer a b c` would have sent only up to the first unreadable
reply.

Both now do what the arm above them does: count it, or return it. The shared
wording moves into `unexpected_detail`, which `fail_unexpected` also renders, so
the two paths cannot drift.

The remaining 45 sites are checked to be outside any loop.

docs: four more mesh-IPv4 references in the registry

`DialTarget` said it carries "our mesh IPv4 on it" for a struct holding only a
name and a key. `resolve_peer_name` and `resolve_peer_flexible` both listed
"mesh IPv4" among the forms they accept, and the second had it backwards: it is
the mesh *IPv6* that resolves against the roster including offline members,
because it derives from the identities the roster already holds.

The fourth was a trailing comment stranded inside a `Member` literal, explaining
that our own entry "already tells peers not to use our mesh IPv4" from a
position where it read as a note on `exit_families`. Replaced with what that
field's `Unknown` is actually saying there.

fix(firewall): refuse IPv6 extension headers instead of misreading them

`parse_ipv6` read the upper-layer protocol out of the next-header field and the
ports at a fixed offset 40. For a packet carrying an extension header that is
wrong twice: the protocol is the extension header's number, and offset 40 is the
extension header rather than the ports.

Cosmetic in the parser, load-bearing in the conntrack. `Flow` is keyed on
`(proto, local_port, peer_port)`, so a fragmented TCP segment becomes
`(44, 0, 0)`: a wildcard entry matching every fragmented packet from that peer,
whatever reassembles inside it. `track_outbound` inserts it (its ICMP guard asks
`is_icmp`, which 44 is not), and on the way back `conntrack_eligible &&
flow_active` returns `Allow`. One outbound fragment, which any UDP send past the
1280 MTU produces, then holds a 30-second hole through which that peer reaches
any local port. That is the inbound default-deny gone, between peers that share
a network but have no rule permitting each other.

Not this branch's doing and not new: master is the same. What the cutover changed
is that IPv6 was the second family and is now the only one, so this stops being a
corner of the data path and becomes all of it.

Fail closed rather than walk the chain. Walking it to the real protocol is the
complete fix and wants its own tests for nested headers and first-fragment-only
ports; refusing is a line, and `evaluate_inbound` already turns `None` into
`DropMalformed`. The cost is that IPv6 fragmentation over the mesh stops working,
a visible failure the user can act on, where a mis-keyed conntrack entry is not.

`packet_spec` filters these out, since they are no longer packets the round-trip
property can hold for, and a new property asserts the refusal directly. The same
protocol numbers over IPv4 are untouched: they are only extension headers in v6.

fix(exit-node): a gateway is not a way onto the gateway's own network

Two things a gateway got wrong about its own uplink.

`is_transitable` refuses `is_private()` for IPv4, which is where a v4 LAN lives
by definition, and the IPv6 arm has no equivalent because there is none to have:
a home or office IPv6 LAN is a *global* /64 delegated by the ISP, indistinguishable
from any other global address. So a client of an exit node could reach every other
machine on the gateway's LAN, and `forward.rs` promised the opposite in as many
words ("not our LAN"). Before the cutover that promise was still true for the
family a v4 LAN uses; now IPv6 is the only family an exit node carries, so the
protection was gone rather than halved.

The answer has to be read from the host instead of derived, so it is:
`parse_on_link_prefixes` takes the prefix lengths out of the interface listing
`host_addresses` already reads, and `ExitServer::is_on_link` refuses transit into
them alongside `is_self_addr`. Bounded on the side that keeps traffic flowing:
global unicast only, `32 <= len < 128`, since a misparse yielding a short prefix
would refuse most of the internet and break the exit node outright.

Second, `has_v6_uplink` on the BSDs asked `route -n get -inet6 default` with no
filter. On a host that both offers an exit node and uses one, the client tunnel's
`::/1` is more specific than `::/0`, so that query answers with our own utun as
soon as the tunnel is installed. `refresh_v6_uplink` re-probes after the client
install, so the gateway would publish `ExitFamilies::V6` for an uplink it does
not have and `enable()` would masquerade transit onto the tunnel it is itself
carrying. `capture_physical_defaults` documents this exact trap ten lines up and
filters it with `usable_pin_iface`; this call did not. The predicate is now
shared and named, and a false claim is the one outcome `ExitFamilies` exists to
prevent, since `ipv6_gateway_refusal` never fires on it.

fix(dns): three ways the resolver outlived what it was pointing at

**macOS `ray down` re-armed the configuration it had just removed.**
`DnsService::revert` runs the backend's own revert, which drops all three
SCDynamicStore keys, and then calls `clear_search_domains`. On macOS the only way
to set search domains is `write_dns_config`, which also writes `ServerAddresses`
and, while the full-tunnel flag is up, the empty catch-all match domain. So a
*clear* went through the *set* path and put the keys back, naming a `200::53`
that stops answering the moment the TUN goes down. With an exit node selected it
was the catch-all that came back, so the whole machine's name resolution pointed
at it, not just `.ray`. `deactivate` reverts DNS well before `apply_exit_client`
clears the flag, so the tunnel was always still "up" at that point. macOS now
clears by removing the keys, which is what clearing means there; the sole caller
is `revert`, so there is no path that wanted the old behaviour.

**The re-assert tick was an idle timer.** The 30s `sleep` was constructed inside
the loop, and the inotify arm fires on any `CLOSE_WRITE`/`MOVED_TO`/`CREATE`
under `/etc` (the name filter decides whether to re-assert, it does not stop the
arm completing). On a host that writes to `/etc` more often than every 30s the
tick never elapsed, and that tick is the only thing that probes the resolver we
share the file with: `shared_misses` never incremented, so `SharedResolverGone`
never fired and the daemon kept declining off-mesh names while pointing the stub
at an address that had stopped answering. Now a deadline, reset only when it
actually fires.

**A degraded upstream set was reported and then discarded.** `nm_quiet_outcome`
computed which captured servers died when NetworkManager was quieted, warned
about them, and left them in place; `fallbacks()` rendered them into the file and
`captured_upstreams()` seeded the forwarder with them, costing a full lookup
timeout each on every off-mesh name. The field is an `ArcSwap` now so `apply` can
narrow it to what actually answers, which is the whole point of having probed.

docs(changelog): the round-two fixes

Four user-visible entries: the IPv6 fragment firewall bypass (with the
behaviour change it costs, since traffic relying on IPv6 fragmentation over the
mesh now stops rather than falling through), the exit node's route onto its own
LAN, and the two macOS ones (`ray down` leaving a dead resolver, and a host that
both offers and uses an exit node advertising IPv6 it cannot carry).

fix(forward): count the outbound packets the parser refuses

Refusing IPv6 extension headers closed a conntrack hole, but the outbound
side of that refusal was a silent `continue` in two places: the main loop
and the flush of packets buffered during a dial. A UDP send past the 1280
MTU comes back from the kernel as fragments and now stops there, so the
drop needs a counter or the traffic disappears with nothing in `ray
status` to say why. Both sites record `Malformed`, which is what the
inbound path already uses for the same condition.

The main loop also logged "not IP, dropping" for a packet that is IP.

fix(mesh): announce handles to the address the peer is registered under

`handle_frame` returns the peer's mesh address, which is the peer table's
key, and the call site threw it away and derived one from the QUIC
transport key instead. Those agree for every current build, but a
`MeshHello` may claim a cert-bound identity other than the dialing key,
and `handle_mesh_hello` registers that peer under the claimed identity's
address. The derived one would then miss, announcing an empty handle
table to a peer that could decode none of the datagrams we tag for it.
chore(android): regenerate the UniFFI bindings

refactor(cli): config_row has no "no value" case to return

A daemon-side error ends the command, so the Option the caller unwrapped
could only ever be Some. An absent row renders as the empty string, which
is how every settings key already spells unset, and both call sites
already treated it that way.

refactor(mesh): derive a peer's address rather than passing it

A peer's mesh address is blake3 of its identity, so every caller of
dial_peer_once and spawn_reconnect was computing the same value from the
same input and threading it alongside. A parameter that can only ever
hold one value is a parameter that can be handed the wrong one, so both
now derive it themselves.

Same reasoning for the stale-member pruner, which carried (identity,
address) pairs where the identity alone says everything, and for the kick
path's DNS prune, which looked the member up only to decide whether to
call a retain that costs nothing when the name was never there.

fix(firewall): walk the IPv6 extension-header chain to the real protocol

Refusing every chained packet closed the conntrack hole but took ordinary
traffic with it. The parser now walks hop-by-hop, routing, fragment,
authentication, destination-options, mobility, HIP and shim6 to the
header that really is the upper-layer protocol, and classifies the packet
on its own ports.

The Authentication Header is the one link measured in 4-octet units, and
minus 2 rather than plus 1 (RFC 4302 2.2); getting that wrong walks into
the middle of the payload and reads two arbitrary bytes as the ports, so
the arithmetic is pinned by a test rather than left to review. The walk
is capped at eight links and every read is bounds-checked, so a crafted
chain is refused rather than followed.

One case stays refused: a fragment after the first, which carries no
transport header at all. Guessing zero there is what rebuilt the wildcard
conntrack entry in the first place. The first fragment does carry one and
is now keyed on its real ports, which is what stops every fragment from
collapsing into a single entry. A port-bearing protocol with no room for
its ports is refused for the same reason.

IPv4 gets the same non-first-fragment guard. Nothing on the mesh produces
IPv4 any more, so it guards a path rather than fixing a live bug, and it
costs one comparison.

The changelog entry moves to Security along with the exit-node LAN-transit
one, which was filed under Fixed by mistake.

fix(dns): two strikes before the NetworkManager takeover latches off

The abort is inferred from a pair of liveness probes either side of
quieting NetworkManager, and it latches NM_TAKEOVER_UNSAFE for the life
of the daemon. Both halves of that pair are network measurements that can
be wrong once, so a permanent decision was resting on a single pair.

Two things were missing. The "before" set was the capture from `new`,
which may be minutes old: a host that lost its DNS in the meantime (a
boot, a link still associating) presents exactly the evidence an NM
forwarder does, everything answered then and nothing answers now, and
attributing that to the quiet cost Magic DNS until the next restart. It
is now re-probed immediately before the kill, so the verdict is the
difference between two probes taken seconds apart and nothing else; a
host with no working DNS to begin with is refused ahead of backup_file
as an ordinary retry, which is what it is.

And the verdict now has to hold twice, the same two strikes
run_resolv_reassert gives the resolver it shares the file with. The retry
loop backs off to 60s, so a second look costs one cycle.

The re-probed set is also kept, for the reason the Degraded arm already
keeps its own: it is what fallbacks renders into the file and what
adopt_configurator seeds the forwarder with, and a server that has
stopped answering costs a full lookup timeout in either.

fix(mesh): tell a kicked member which network it left

`ray kick` pruned the roster, republished, and then closed the victim's
connection with KICK_CODE. A close code cannot name a network, so it is
not a kick the victim can act on: confirm_kick_and_leave runs off the
in-band, network-scoped ControlMsg::KickedFromNetwork, and this path
never sent one.

The victim therefore learned of its own removal only from the group poll,
whose ReconvergeOutcome::Departed does nothing but stop polling. The
network stayed in `ray status` and on disk with a roster frozen at the
moment of the kick: joined-looking, carrying nothing, and clearable only
by a manual `ray leave`.

remove_member_roster_only's doc has always said it is shared by the
manual kick handler and the ephemeral pruner. Only the pruner used it.
Routing the kick through remove_member_roster_only + finalize_removal
makes that true and sends the message; finalize_removal also leaves the
connection open on purpose, so the message cannot lose a race with its
own teardown.

Other members were never affected: they reconverge from the published
roster either way. Covered end to end by tests/e2e/churn, which kicks a
member while a third node is offline.

test(e2e): a churn scenario for flap, kick and nuke

The other scenarios each take one lifecycle event on a quiet mesh. This
one takes those events while the mesh is moving: three hard flap rounds
of one member, a simultaneous flap of two, a coordinator flap, three
`ray down`/`ray up` cycles, and a kick and a nuke each delivered while a
member is offline. It ends with a sweep for panics and crash-restarts.

Two roles carry the weight. srv-b never restarts, so a convergence check
is never read from a node that was itself mid-restore. srv-c is offline
for every roster change, so what it knows on return came from the signed
blob and not from a broadcast it received, which is the invariant the
scenario exists to test.

Found the kick bug fixed in the previous commit: the assertion that a
kicked node leaves the network was the one check that failed.

Runs on both backends. The README table was listing 7 of the 12
scenarios, so the missing rows are filled in too.

docs(changelog): use a placeholder hostname in the macOS AAAA entry

The entry named a real mesh host in a public repo. It is only ever an
example of a `.ray` name, so it reads the same as a placeholder.

feat(android): notify about an incoming file offer

Notifications were driven only from the transfer registry, and on the
receiving side a transfer exists only once the file has been accepted.
An offer from a peer that is not one of the user's own paired devices is
never auto-accepted, so it sat in the pending queue with no transfer
behind it and nothing to report: the only place it surfaced was the
HomeScreen row, painted only while the app is open. Sent while the app
was closed, a file arrived in silence.

OfferNotifier reconciles the pending offers into notifications, on its
own channel at default importance (the transfers channel is
IMPORTANCE_LOW on purpose, so it would never alert) and in its own id
range. It posts once per offer so a swipe-dismiss stays dismissed,
cancels when the offer leaves the core's queue, and sweeps stale
notifications once per process: pending offers do not survive a restart
and offer ids restart at 1, so a leftover Save button could otherwise
point at a different file.

Save and Reject are handled by ReceiveService, foreground for the same
reason SendService is: acceptFileOffer blocks for the whole download,
far past what a BroadcastReceiver may live. Starting it from a
notification action is what makes the background start legal. It reuses
the DownloadsOutcome bookkeeping so the result names the right location,
and leaves progress and the result to TransferNotifier.

Driven by both existing pollers, so it works with the app closed and in
standby. Acting on an offer from the app's own row takes the
notification down too.

formatSize was duplicated with binary units against HomeScreen's decimal
one, which would have printed different sizes for the same file
depending on where it was read; it is now one definition in Files.kt.

fix(firewall): refuse every fragment, not only the ones after the first

A fragment after the first carries no transport header, so it was already
refused. The first one was classified and forwarded, which only earned the
right to put a datagram on the wire that the peer can never reassemble: it
holds an incomplete reassembly until timeout, and outbound we opened a
conntrack entry on the strength of a send that never completes. The mesh
already promises a fragmented datagram does not cross it; this keeps the
promise rather than half-keeping it.

Also pins the TLV header length, which nothing covered: every chain test
used hdr_ext_len 0, where (n + 1) * 8 and a hard-coded 8 agree. A
hop-by-hop header carrying one option is n = 1, and reading its ports 8
octets early lands inside the option data.

fix(dns): finish aborting a takeover when restoring resolv.conf fails

The abort arm is the one that hands the host back to NetworkManager, and
`restore_file(path).await?` short-circuited the rest of it. A failed
restore left NM quieted with the `dns=none` drop-in installed and no
resolver of ours in the file, so the host had neither, and nothing removes
that drop-in until a `ray down`. It skipped the abort counter too, so the
two-strike latch could never trip.

The cleanup now runs whatever the restore did, and the restore error is
reported alongside the reason for the abort instead of replacing it.

fix(test): three harness bugs that lost fleets or passed on nothing

provision.sh kept a half-created fleet through an EXIT trap reading $tmp,
a function local. Bash pops locals before running the trap when `set -e`
kills the shell rather than an explicit `exit`, so under `set -u` the trap
died on an unbound variable and kept nothing. A `doctl create` failing
partway is exactly that path, and it leaves the earlier droplets running
and billed while teardown says there is nothing to remove.

exit-node's loop-prevention check grepped for "0% packet loss", which is a
substring of "100% packet loss". That is the one assertion the SO_MARK
fork chain exists for, and a completely dead mesh under the full tunnel
reported PASS. It reads through ping_loss now.

churn's daemon_start slept a fixed 5s, ran `ray up`, and only then waited
for IPC: the wait ordered after the command that needs it, with the
failure swallowed, so a slow droplet came back in standby and every
data-plane assertion of that round failed spuriously. Its health sweep
also read the whole journal, and .servers fleets are reused by design, so
one panic failed every later run on that fleet; a failed ssh read as a
pass for the same reason. Both counts are now bounded by the run's start
and distinguish reading zero from reading nothing.

fix(android)!: require Android 8.0, where the notification APIs exist

minSdk was 24, but every notification the app posts goes through
`Notification.Builder(Context, channelId)` and a NotificationChannel, both
added in 26. On 24 and 25 the builder threw NoSuchMethodError, the
surrounding runCatching swallowed it, and transfers and incoming files
were announced by nothing at all on a build that otherwise looked like it
worked. The pre-O branches meant to cover that could not: they guarded the
channel, never the builder.

Keeping a tier where the app is quietly half-functional is worse than
dropping it, so 7.x goes and the branches that only existed for it go with
it.

fix(android): stop an offer notification outliving or misnaming its file

Three separate ways the incoming-file path went wrong.

ReceiveService: `stopSelf(startId)` stops the service when the id *is* the
most recent start, which is the opposite of what the comment beside it
assumed. Save a large file (start 1), then Reject another offer (start 2):
the reject finishes in milliseconds and its own `stopSelf(2)` destroys the
service while the accept is still downloading, which is what the inFlight
guard one line above was written to prevent. Teardown is now inside that
guard and names the newest start, or the accept finishing second would
call `stopSelf(1)` while 2 is current and never stop at all. Going
foreground and leaving it now share a lock, so a finishing worker cannot
undo a starting one, and the no-op path no longer tears down a live
transfer.

OfferNotifier: the Save and Reject PendingIntents carried FLAG_IMMUTABLE
alone. Matching ignores extras, the request code comes from the offer id,
and offer ids restart at 1 each process, so offer 1 of this run reused the
record left by offer 1 of the last one and handed ReceiveService the
previous file's name, peer and size.

HomeScreen: both row handlers marked an offer acted-on and never undid it
when the call failed, unlike ReceiveService. A failed reject leaves the
offer pending, so it stayed live and stayed suppressed, and no
notification was ever posted for it again.

Also wraps a row's value to two lines: a node's only address is now a full
mesh IPv6, which did not fit beside its label and was ellipsised in the
middle, so the row showed an address nobody could read or check.

fix(status): register a version-incompatible network instead of dropping it

Restoring a saved network stopped at the mesh-version check in
resolve_and_fetch_blob, before the roster blob was even fetched, so a
network whose record advertised another protocol version never
registered and `ray status` listed it nowhere at all. It read as gone
rather than as out of step.

The check is a VersionGate now and the calling path decides what a
mismatch means. A fresh `ray join` still refuses with the same message:
admission needs a mesh connection the versioned ALPN blocks, so there is
nothing to register. A restore fetches the blob anyway (it rides the
unversioned blobs ALPN), registers through dial_reconnect's cold-restore
fallback, and flags the NetworkHandle incompatible. The restore loop
stays alive watching the record, and rebuilds only on a republish at our
version, so the flagged registration is not torn down on every retry.
Peer rows need nothing: their dials fail the ALPN gate, which already
marks them. The gate itself is unchanged and nothing new crosses it.

Second fix behind the same symptom: the CLI's inactive-network fallback
read config::load(), which resolves the calling user's config directory.
On macOS the daemon runs as root, so its config is under /var/root while
`ray status` read (and created) an empty one in the user's home, and
every failed restore rendered as no mention at all. The daemon reports
saved-but-unregistered networks in StatusResponse now, with the last
restore error, and the CLI drops the read. config_dir_for_read /
load_for_read cover the one remaining CLI-side read (daemon down) and
create nothing.

No wire change and no mesh version bump: NetworkStatus and
StatusResponse are named-encoded IPC.

fix(android): send the diagnostics with the diagnostics report

`Sentry.withScope` (SDK 8.47.0) dropped every scope write made inside it.
Twelve of twelve reports over a month arrived with no `install_id`, no
`transport`, no `rayfish` health context and no log attachment, which is
everything that makes a report worth reading. The button said "Diagnostics
sent" each time, and it had: the event went through, empty.

The writes did not vanish. They landed somewhere longer-lived and surfaced
on an unrelated ANR captured sixteen seconds after one of these calls, so
the old shape also put a device id on an event that had no reason to carry
one, with `isSendDefaultPii` off two lines above.

Both capture paths now use the `ScopeCallback` overloads, which apply the
callback to the event being sent and to nothing else. `captureStartFailure`
had the same shape and the same loss, and it is the one nobody is around to
notice is empty.

While here: read `healthSnapshot()` before the capture so a failure to read
it is distinguishable from never setting it, skip a zero-byte attachment
rather than send one ingest may drop, and return null on `EMPTY_ID`. The id
was stringified before the check, so a refused capture read back as a
successful send.

Compiles; that the fields actually land needs a send from a device.

fix(android): resolve .ray names in Chrome on an IPv4-only network

Chrome gates AAAA lookups on an IPv6 reachability probe, a connect() to
2001:4860:4860::8888 that needs a route but sends no packet. With only
200::/7 on the tunnel and no IPv6 on the underlay that probe failed, so
Chrome dropped AAAA from the query set and asked for A alone. The overlay
is IPv6-only, so every .ray name came back empty and the browser showed
DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN, while the same name resolved fine for any app
that asks for AAAA directly.

Route the two probe targets (Chromium's and bionic's) when the underlay has
no global IPv6 of its own. Real IPv6 destinations stay unrouted, so they
keep failing instantly with ENETUNREACH rather than blackholing in the
tunnel, and a network with genuine IPv6 is left untouched.

feat(hostname): join under this machine's name, not a random noun

A create or join with no --hostname fell back to a word from NOUNS_B, so

a box. The name the machine already answers to is the better default and
the only one nobody has to look up.

The OS name is folded into a mesh one first: first label, lowercased,

And a name the network already holds falls back too, since laptop-1
reads as the name of the laptop that is already there. The joiner has
the signed blob in hand before it dials, so that clash is settled
locally and needs no wire field; create has no roster yet, and a direct
network's roster is the one peer.

`ray up --hostname` still wins over both: that one is a choice, not a
guess, and its collisions stay the coordinator's suffix to resolve.

feat(bridge): reach IPv4-only listeners over the mesh

The overlay is IPv6-only, so a peer reaches a service at [<mesh ip>]:<port>
and a program listening on 0.0.0.0 never saw the connection: the port was
open in the firewall, the name resolved, and the connection was refused with
nothing saying why. No packet filter closes that gap, since neither nftables
nor pf translates between address families, so the daemon binds the mesh
address for those ports itself and splices each connection to 127.0.0.1.

Only a wildcard listener is bridged. One bound to 127.0.0.1 is deliberately
local and is left alone, so nothing the host was not already offering on
every other interface becomes reachable. The firewall sits ahead of the
socket on the packet path, so it still decides who gets through, and the
bridge binds every qualifying port rather than consulting it. What is lost
is the peer's address inside the service, which sees 127.0.0.1: per-peer
policy belongs in `ray firewall`, not in the application.

Enumerating the host's listeners is per-OS and has no answer on Android, so
an unreadable listing bridges nothing and stays quiet. A port the bridge
already holds is excluded from the coverage check, or its own listener reads
back as the service having grown IPv6 support and it unbinds and rebinds on
every scan.

Off with `ray config set v4-bridge off`.

test(e2e): cover the IPv4-only listener bridge end to end

Two peers, one of them running a service bound to 0.0.0.0 and another bound
to 127.0.0.1. None of this is reachable from a unit test: it needs a real
TUN, a real host listener table and a real peer on the other side.

Reachability and "is it bridged" are asserted separately, from a TCP
handshake over the TUN and from ss on the far host, because they can
legitimately disagree. The firewall closes the first with the second still
true, and that is what makes the two negative steps mean anything: the
deny-by-default probe fails with the bridge's listener demonstrably up, so
the bridge is not a way around the firewall, and the loopback-only service
stays unreachable with its port explicitly allowed, so the refusal is the
bridge declining rather than the packet path.

Step 7 is the regression that shipped: a bridged port is itself an IPv6
listener on the mesh address, and a scan that does not recognise its own
socket unbinds and rebinds it every cycle. A single probe passes straight
through that, so the check waits out two rescans and probes again.

The rest is lifetime: the bridge follows the service, the setting, and the
data plane. The shared start_tcp_listener keeps binding `::` on purpose, and
its comment now says which scenario a 0.0.0.0 listener belongs to.

feat(bridge): take listener changes from the kernel, not a poll

The v4 bridge re-read /proc/net/tcp every 15s to notice a service
starting or stopping. That paid for a scan whether or not anything had
changed, read every socket on the host to learn about the few that
listen, and made the interval itself the worst case for how late a port
could be bridged.

Linux will report the change instead: the sock:inet_sock_set_state
tracepoint, read through a private ftrace instance. That needs no eBPF,
no new dependency and no privilege the daemon lacks. Events are triggers
and never data, so the socket table still decides what to bridge.

The filter names both endpoints of a transition. oldstate==10 on its own
reads as "a listening socket changed" but also matches TCP_LISTEN to
TCP_SYN_RECV, which is every inbound connection the host accepts, and
would scale with the host's traffic rather than with its listeners.

The timer stays as a 300s backstop rather than being deleted: every way
an event can go missing is silent, and a missed close is the worse
direction, leaving us holding a port whose service has moved out of
reach. macOS and any host without tracefs keep the 15s timer as the
mechanism.

fix(report): keep a diagnostic bundle private to whoever asked for it

The finished archive was chmodded 0644 unconditionally, including on the
path that had just chowned it to the requester. IpcMessage::Report is in
the open-reads arm of check_authorized, so any local user can ask for a
bundle, and collect_recent_logs packs /var/log/rayfish/* precisely
because those are root-only. One user running `ray report` therefore left
the daemon's debug logs, status dump, peer ids and mesh IPs in /tmp for
every other user to read. It now stays 0600 whenever there is a requester
to own it, and widens only in the fallback where it is still root-owned
and would otherwise be unreadable by its caller.

The fchown had also become fatal, so a daemon without CAP_CHOWN, or a
/tmp that refuses ownership changes, deleted the finished archive and
failed the request instead of returning a working root-owned bundle. It
is best-effort again, and logs when it fails.

Tests cover both modes, and the symlink case now includes a dangling
link: the existing test's target exists, which O_EXCL refuses on its own.

Merge pull request #130 from lambadalambda/fix/report-symlink

fix: secure diagnostic report creation

fix(mesh): restore coordinators from durable snapshots

Persist every complete coordinator-authored GroupBlob before publishing
it, with an exact recovery hash and published/unpublished provenance, and
restore from the newest safe complete source: an interrupted local
generation, the current signed record, or the last retained complete blob
during a pkarr outage. The lossy config roster is never reconstructed,
welcomed or published as network truth.

Exact signed state is carried through direct admission and reconnect, so
a co-coordinator key grant stays bound to the generation it was admitted
under. Snapshot storage, recovery-pointer durability, publication,
reconvergence and admission retries are serialized, and an ambiguous
atomic-write outcome stays pending until a durability barrier succeeds.

Bumps MESH_PROTOCOL_VERSION to 5 for the two appended direct-admission
fields on the wire.

fix(config): put settings.toml under the transaction boundary

The network shards got a transaction in #137 and settings.toml did not,
so eleven load() -> mutate one global -> save_settings() sites still
raced. Each wrote the whole file back, reverting whatever another task
had changed in between: `ray firewall ssh on` could restore an
operator_uid that had just been cleared, and neither command failed.

update_settings holds the exclusive guard across the read and the write,
mirroring update_network, and skips the write when the callback changed
nothing so a no-op does not cost an fsync. All eleven callers move to it,
ray-mobile's set_default_hostname included, which leaves save_settings
with no users; it is removed rather than left as a footgun that reads as
if it were guarded.

fix(completions): install the zsh stub where zsh actually looks

The install wrote `_ray` to /usr/share/zsh/site-functions on every Linux.
Arch and Fedora search that directory; Debian and Ubuntu do not. Those
build zsh with its site directory under /usr/local and hand packages
/usr/share/zsh/vendor-completions, so the file landed somewhere nothing
autoloads it. Writing it succeeded, the install reported success, and
pressing tab did nothing, with no step able to tell.

Read the real fpath off the zsh on the box instead of assuming one path
fits every distribution, and take the first entry that is a site or
vendor completions directory. zsh's own functions/Completion tree is on
fpath too and is excluded: a file there belongs to the next zsh upgrade.
No zsh to ask falls back to the previous path.

Installing also sweeps a stub an earlier version left in one of the other
candidate directories, since that is exactly the box where completion has
been quietly dead, and `ray up` and `ray update` both come through here.
The sweep compares content first, so a `_ray` somebody else put in a
shared directory is left alone.

The per-user install has the same problem with no fix available: no zsh
searches anything under a home directory. It now checks and says so
outright, with the lines to add to ~/.zshrc, rather than hedging with an
"if tab completion does not work" the answer to which was always yes.

Detection runs at install time only, never on the completion keystroke
path.

Windows takes the main thread's stack from the PE header and defaults to
1 MiB. Building the clap command tree does not fit in that unoptimized, so
every command in a debug build, `--version` included, overflowed the stack
and died with 0xC00000FD before it parsed an argument. Reserve 8 MiB, the
same as Linux hands a process, from build.rs so it applies to the binary and
not to the test harnesses, which get their stacks from the threads libtest
spawns them on. Reserve is address space and pages commit as the stack
grows, so the headroom costs no memory.

A release build fits in a quarter of the old default, which is why the MSI
never showed it and only CI and a local build did. The contract test reads
the header out of the built image rather than asking the running process,
since a test target keeps the default reserve either way.

fix(build): gate the listener module on the desktop feature

`bind_listener` moved out of `ssh` into a module of its own, which is where
it has to live: `ssh` is Unix-only and `v4bridge` is not. The new module
carried no gate, so a build without `desktop` compiled it with no caller and
failed dead_code on `bind_listener`. Both users are `desktop`-only, so the
module is too.

Nothing in CI caught it. The clippy jobs pass `--workspace`, where feature
unification turns `desktop` on, and the Android lane runs `check` without
`-D warnings`, so it showed up only as a warning on Android builds.

cargo clippy --no-default-features --all-targets -- -D warnings clean;
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings clean; 838 tests pass.

fix(windows): ask for the service access the restart policy needs

`apply_own_failure_actions` opened the service with CHANGE_CONFIG and
QUERY_CONFIG. `ChangeServiceConfig2` also requires SERVICE_START whenever the
actions include SC_ACTION_RESTART, which is the SCM asking whether the handle
could start the service it is being told to restart. `failure_actions()` is
three Restart entries, so the call was failing ACCESS_DENIED on every start,
and the caller logs that at warn and carries on. Nothing looked wrong until a
panic, at which point nothing restarted the daemon: the exact outcome the
policy exists to prevent, on both the MSI and `ray install` paths now that the
WiX element is gone.

QUERY_CONFIG goes: both calls reach `ChangeServiceConfig2` and neither reads
the config back.

Also applies the policy after the Running report rather than before it. Three
blocking SCM calls about our own service, made while the MSI's `ServiceControl
Start="install" Wait="yes"` has the SCM inside StartService on that same
service, do not belong on the start path. Nothing reads the policy until the
next failure.

fix(report): keep one principal's bundle out of another's sweep

Two Windows-only defects in `ray report`, both from the same assumption that
the pipe DACL admits one principal.

The sweep deleted every `rayfish-report-*.tgz` in the directory. Its comment
argued that the DACL limits callers to Administrators and the operator so
there is no other account's file to protect, but that is two principals or
more, and `create_report_file` grants read to exactly one of them per bundle.
An administrator running `ray report` unlinked the bundle the daemon had just
handed the operator, who then opened a path that no longer existed. Bundles
now carry a tag naming the principal they belong to and the sweep matches on
it. On Unix the uid check stays and is still the decision; the tag is a hint
there, since any account can create a name in /tmp.

`to_io` flattened the anyhow chain with `io::Error::other`, so the kind became
`Other` and `create_report_bundle`'s 16-attempt retry, which distinguishes a
name collision by `ErrorKind::AlreadyExists`, ended on its first iteration and
reported the collision as a hard failure. The kind is now recovered from the
chain. Reachable because the daemon's temp directory is one where any local
account may create files.

The guard test asserted nothing about scoping on Windows: its "unrelated" file
failed the name prefix anyway. It now plants a second bundle belonging to a
different principal, which the old code deleted on both platforms.

fix(windows): correct what the port claims about completions and reuse

The changelog said tab completion "installs for the current user rather than
machine-wide" on Windows. It installs nothing: `install_system_under` returns
empty there, `Shell::from_env` reads $SHELL which PowerShell does not set, and
`user_path` has no arm for PowerShell because it loads completions from a
profile script rather than a directory. Every route ends in an error or a
no-op, so say that instead.

`install_with_service` called `is_root()` with no `HAS_SYSTEM_DIRS` guard,
which on Windows meant duplicating a token check to decide whether to write
files to a set of directories that does not exist there. Guard it, which also
makes `is_root`'s own doc true.

`bind_listener`'s comment read as a clearance for the next caller: SO_REUSEADDR
on Windows does not mean what the Unix pair means, it lets any process on the
machine bind the same address and take delivery, which is why
SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE exists. Nothing binds through here on Windows yet; say what
the next caller has to do.

The PE header test indexed slices directly, so a truncated or non-PE image
would fail as a slice-index panic instead of naming the field that ran off the
end.

test(windows): give the descendant test time to publish its pid

The kill-on-close test budgets three seconds for the parent to spawn a
descendant and write its pid, then asserts on the pid file. Everything
before that write is on the clock, including powershell's own engine
start, which is under a second idle and several seconds on a loaded CI
runner. When it lost that race the test failed on a missing file rather
than on the descendant it exists to check.

Widen the budget to twelve seconds, put the sleeps well past it so a
dead descendant means killed and not finished, and say the budget in the
panic message.

fix(windows): build the msi when the output path is a drive root

New-Item -ItemType Directory rejects a drive root even with -Force, so
passing -OutputPath C:\something.msi killed the script before cargo ran.
Only create the output directory when it is missing.

feat(windows): sign the msi and the ray.exe inside it on release

Tagged releases go through SignPath, which signs the executable nested in
the package and then the package itself. Signing only the MSI would leave
the installed ray.exe unsigned, so every UAC prompt, firewall dialog and
service start after the install would still say unknown publisher.

Pull request artifacts stay unsigned. Fork workflows cannot read
repository secrets, and with the token unset the signing steps skip and a
release publishes the same assets it does today.

The sha256 sidecar moves into its own script so it can be written after
signing. Signing rewrites the file, so a hash taken at build time
describes something nobody will ever download.

For a key reachable from the build machine, a cloud HSM through signtool
or a test certificate, -SignTool and -SignArgs sign in place instead.

fix(dns): coerce Windows NRPT NameServers to strings

`Get-DnsClientNrptRule` hands `NameServers` back as `IPAddress` objects, so
`ConvertTo-Json` writes the whole object where the snapshot expects
`["200::53"]`. The snapshot then fails to parse, and it only parses at all
while no rayfish rule exists yet, which is exactly the first apply on a clean
machine. So DNS looks fine once and every reconcile after it dies, leaving
stale NRPT rules and search suffixes behind on leave and on stop.

Coerce them in the script, and accept both shapes when deserializing: the CIM
typing has differed across Windows builds and the failure is quiet enough to
be worth the belt and braces.

fix(windows): reject a group as the operator account

`LookupAccountNameW` resolves a group name as readily as a user's, and the SID
it returns goes straight into the IPC pipe DACL. `ray set-operator Users` would
have granted mutation rights to every account on the machine, which is the
opposite of what naming an operator is for.

Require SidTypeUser.

fix(windows): put the install dir on PATH

The MSI installs per-machine and nothing else adds the directory, so `ray` was
only runnable by full path after a fresh install. Add a system-scope
`<Environment>` entry, removed again on uninstall.

fix(status): do not report a reachable daemon as down

`ipc_status` threw away the reason the connection failed and printed "daemon
not running" for every one of them. The IPC layer already tells absence from
refusal apart, so a user who is not allowed to talk to a running daemon was
told there was nothing there, and went looking for the wrong problem.

Keep that answer: say plainly that the caller is not authorized, and how to
grant it.

fix(windows): open IPC reads to any local user

The pipe DACL named LocalSystem, Administrators and the operator, and nothing
else, so a standard user was refused at open() and the reads-are-open-to-
everyone arm of `check_authorized` was unreachable on Windows. `ray status`
worked for administrators only, and told everyone else the service was down
while it was running.

Grant Authenticated Users GENERIC_READ | GENERIC_WRITE: enough to open the
pipe and run one request/response, not enough to change the pipe or rewrite
its ACL. That is the Windows spelling of the 0666 the Unix socket already
gets, and for the same reason: reaching the daemon is not authority over it.
Every mutation is still authorized per connection, and still demands
LocalSystem, an elevated Administrator, or an exact operator SID.

That alone was not enough. The client proves the far end really is the service
before it says anything to it, and it did so by opening the server process,
which a standard user may not do against a LocalSystem service: every
unprivileged command failed there instead, after opening the pipe perfectly
well. Ask the kernel who owns the pipe instead, which needs only the
READ_CONTROL that GENERIC_READ already carries.

Stamp that owner rather than inherit it. A token's owner is a separate field
from its user, and where the "default owner for objects created by members of
the Administrators group" policy names the group, the service's own pipe comes
out owned by S-1-5-32-544. Left to default, the check refuses the real daemon
on those machines.

ci(windows): gate MSI packaging on a label, not a variable

`vars` is empty in a workflow run triggered by a pull request from a
fork, so the packaging job could never run on the pull request that
brought the port in. Labels are part of the event payload and readable
there, so gate on `windows-packaging` and listen for `labeled` so
applying it starts a run.

fix(android): let an inbound firewall rule name a peer

The add-rule dialog asked for a protocol and a port and passed null for
the peer, so every rule the app could write applied to the whole network.
firewall_add already takes a peer and resolves a hostname, mesh IP or
endpoint id, so this is a missing field in the UI, not a missing feature.

Add a peer dropdown listing the network's members (any peer by default),
sending the full node id, and name the peer in the rule list instead of
printing the daemon's short id.

fix(android): keep identity keys out of Android Auto Backup

The app set allowBackup with no exclusion rules, so getFilesDir() went to
the account's cloud backup on Android's own schedule. That directory is
the core's config dir: the Ed25519 identity, the device certificate and
the coordinator's per-network secret keys all sit there in the clear.

Restoring such a backup onto a second phone was also incoherent for the
mesh, not just for privacy. Both handsets end up holding one identity,
which means one EndpointId and one mesh address between them, and the
pairing model exists precisely so a second device gets its own key.

Exclude the whole file domain from cloud backup and from device-to-device
transfer, rather than naming the two files: a secret added to the config
dir later is then excluded by default instead of by someone remembering
to come back here. SharedPreferences still back up, which is what Auto
Backup is good for and holds no key material.

feat(android): back up and restore the identity from a file

Losing the phone lost the identity, and the only way to keep a copy was
to have made one on a desktop with `ray pair backup`.

Move the enc1 codec out of the CLI into a keybackup module so the mobile
side can reach it: it lived in src/cli, which is binary-only, and prompted
for its password inline. The format is unchanged, so codes made by either
side restore on the other. Also fold the secret_key path back into
identity::store_secret_key, which three call sites had started spelling
out for themselves.

Node gains backupIdentity/restoreIdentity plus three error variants the
UI can act on rather than print: a wrong password is retryable, an
identity already on the device is a question for the user, and a running
node has to be stopped first (the endpoint is bound to the old key).

The Android side uses the storage access framework on both ends, so
Drive, OneDrive, Files and any password manager registered as a document
provider all appear in the picker with no Play Services, no OAuth client
and nothing that would break the F-Droid build. The blob is encrypted
before it leaves the process, so the provider is trusted with nothing.

feat(android): offer the identity restore before first run

Restore was reachable only from the You tab, which is the wrong place for
the one moment it matters: a new phone. Worse, it could not work cleanly
there. Everything that touches the app starts the node, the first start
mints an identity, and restore_identity then called load_or_create to
find out whether one existed, minting a second. A restore onto a genuinely
empty device therefore always asked permission to overwrite a key created
moments earlier, and replace_existing had no reachable false case.

Add identity::load_existing, which reads or returns None and never
creates, and have the restore path use it. Node.has_identity exposes the
same answer to the platform: it reads a file, starts nothing, and is the
"has this person used the app" question, so it drives the first-run screen
with no onboarding flag to keep in step and no migration for installs that
already have a key.

The welcome screen sits in front of the startup effect, since anything
after it would already have minted. Backing out of it (cancelled picker,
wrong password) leaves the device untouched and the screen shows again
next launch, so nobody gets stranded past the only offer. The restore flow
is now shared with the You tab rather than copied, and restarts the node
only if it stopped one, which is what keeps a mistyped password from
minting the key the restore was meant to replace.

docs(ssh): say why a node cannot SSH to its own mesh address

Connecting to your own mesh address from the box it belongs to is
refused, and nothing said why. Self-traffic is delivered over loopback,
so it never enters the TUN and the port rewrite that puts mesh :22 on
the embedded server never runs; the connection lands on :22, where
nothing is bound.

`ray firewall ssh show` now says so and points at `ssh localhost`, and
the ssh module doc records why binding :22 as well is not the fix: the
`none` auth method is safe only because the mesh link proves who the
peer is, and a loopback connection proves nothing beyond "some account
on this box".

feat(status): show a saved group before its coordinator answers

Restoring a saved network needs its signed pkarr record and a coordinator
that replies, which after a reboot is up to a minute of backoff. Until the
restore landed the group rendered as a bare name over one line of apology:
no address, no members, no join code, even though the config on disk holds
all three.

The daemon now projects an unregistered network's saved config into the
same NetworkStatus shape a live one has, and the CLI draws it with the same
block, marked `connecting...` until an attempt has actually failed and
`offline` with the reason after. Every peer on it reads offline, and
pairing is left unresolved: the device/user map is only filled by applying
a verified roster, which has not happened yet.

No daemon behaviour changes; the restore loop already retried and synced.

IPC is the to_vec_named exception in the wire rules, so appending an
optional field to InactiveNetwork needs no version bump. A daemon that
sends none falls back to the old terse block.

ci(windows): build ray.exe for arm64 on a native runner

Windows on ARM is its own target rather than a variant of the x86_64 one:
its C dependencies (ring, blake3) select different sources there, so a
green x86_64 job says nothing about it.

Built natively on windows-11-arm, which is free for public repositories.
Cross-compiling the target from Linux works but needs an out-of-tree
clang/lld toolchain, because ring forces the GNU clang driver on
Windows/AArch64 while the MSVC CRT ships NEON headers clang cannot use.

The MSI stays x86_64 only; this job publishes the bare exe.

ci(nightly): publish the ARM64 Windows binary

The nightly release had no Windows ARM64 asset, so an ARM laptop had
nothing native to download.

Ships the bare exe with a checksum sidecar rather than a second MSI:
build-windows-msi.ps1 validates the x86_64 target and pins the amd64
Wintun, so an ARM64 installer is its own piece of work.

`ray update` still has no Windows ARM64 path (release_asset_name bails
on the arch), so this is a manual download until that follows.

ci: fold the Windows workflow into CI

The Windows jobs were a workflow of their own for no reason the other
per-platform jobs do not share: macOS and Android already sit in CI as
the jobs that cover code no Linux build compiles, and Windows is the
third of those.

The pull_request trigger grows the `labeled` type, which the Windows
workflow carried so applying `windows-packaging` starts a run on its own.

Cache keys now name the target triple rather than the job, so the x86_64
and ARM64 legs cannot land on one key.

ci: key every rust-cache by the target triple

rust-cache's own key carries the runner os and arch but not the triple,
so the shared-key is the only thing separating two jobs that build
different targets. The keys were named after the job instead, which said
nothing about what the cache holds.

Both Android jobs build two ABIs at once, so no single triple names them;
those key on the platform.

feat(install): add a Windows installer

install.sh covers Linux and macOS and dies on anything else, so Windows
had no scripted install at all: x64 users found the MSI by hand and ARM64
users had nothing.

install.ps1 takes the two architectures by the routes they are published
on. x64 downloads and runs the MSI, which already registers the service,
sets PATH and records the release identity. ARM64 has no MSI, so the
script places the bare exe and does the part the MSI would: the Wintun
DLL has to sit next to ray.exe or the tunnel cannot be created, and it is
the arm64 build of it, not the amd64 one the MSI pins.

release.yml grows the ARM64 leg nightly.yml already had, so a stable tag
publishes the binary the installer downloads.

CI parses install.ps1 on the Windows runner. Nothing else in the tree can:
a piped installer's syntax errors otherwise land on the user.

fix(cli): keep styled values readable on light terminals

Value and headline text used fixed near-white xterm grays (38;5;252 and
38;5;255) that vanish on light backgrounds. Render them in bold with the
terminal's default foreground, which is theme-adaptive, so the output stays
legible on light and dark themes without any background detection.

The app listed only the networks the daemon had finished registering, so a
cold start showed an empty Networks screen until every restore landed, and a
network whose restore kept failing was absent with nothing to say why.

The daemon already reports these as `inactive_networks` on its status reply,
with the roster it last saved and the one-line reason the restore failed;
`ray status` has always rendered them. `Node::status` was destructuring the
reply with `..` and dropping the field.

`NetworkConnState`: `Connecting` while the restore is in flight and has not
failed yet, `NotConnected` with the reason once it has. Also stop returning a
blank snapshot when the IPC reply is not the one we asked for, since an empty
list reads as "you have no networks".

fix(forward): bound the lazy-dial packet buffer

Packets held while an on-demand dial is in flight went into an unbounded
per-peer VecDeque, so traffic aimed at a peer that stays offline for the
five-second dial timeout was retained in full. Cap retention per peer
(64 packets / 128 KiB) and daemon-wide (512 packets / 1 MiB), dropping
newest so the oldest packets, the ones a handshake needs, survive.

fix(clippy): group the bind and member-restore parameters

Three functions crossed clippy's seven-argument limit and broke the
check, macos and windows jobs with -D warnings.

`bind_endpoint` now takes a `BindConfig` holding everything a bind
attempt needs; `port` stays a plain argument because it is the only
value the ephemeral-port retry varies. `restore_member_network` and
`warm_resume_member_network` take a `SavedMemberNetwork` carrying the
seven saved-network fields both of them read off the config.

No behaviour change: the values and their order at each call site are

fix(e2e): stop the harness clobbering $KEY and sharing one tracefs

Two failures in a full docker run that were the harness, not the daemon.

closed-net assigned the reusable join code to `KEY`, which is
common.sh's SSH private key, so every `on` after step 5 ran
`ssh -i <join-code>`. Docker survives it because the nodes accept any
default identity; a fleet that only accepts a non-default SSH_KEY would
not. Renamed to `REUSABLE`, and dropped the docker.sh comment that
recorded the collision as a constraint.

tracefs is not namespaced, so every node container shared the host
kernel's one /sys/kernel/tracing: all the daemons opened the same
instances/rayfish and read the same consuming trace_pipe, and one node's
listen event was delivered to another node's daemon. v4bridge step 12
then failed by fleet-size accident, with the node that opened the socket
falling back to its 15s timer. The image masks the tracefs mounts, so
every node takes the timer path deterministically and the scenario
reports the kernel-event path as uncovered, which it is here either way.

The README said tracefs was simply unmounted in a privileged container;
systemd mounts it, so that was wrong about the cause.

test(e2e): cover unprivileged-client authority with an operator scenario

The daemon runs as root and its IPC socket is world-connectable on
purpose: authority is a per-request SO_PEERCRED check, not the socket's
file mode. Nothing below the process boundary can test that, and no
scenario covered `ray set-operator` at all.

Two hosts, two real unprivileged users on the coordinator. Reads are
open to any local user and carry the daemon's roster; a read builds no
config tree of its own and leaves /etc/rayfish untouched; `config set`,
`firewall add` and `down` are refused with the fix named; a non-root
user cannot grant itself operator. After the grant, a rule the operator
installs flips a port from closed to open on the other host's packets,
the second user is still denied, the operator cannot pass the grant on,
and the grant survives a daemon restart. Last, `ray report` is an open
read whose bundle lands 0600 owned by its requester, which until now had
a unit test but no end-to-end one.

Refusal wording is asserted alongside the exit status: a denial that
does not name `ray set-operator` leaves the user with nowhere to go,
which is the failure the message exists to prevent.

fix(mesh): seat a member's paired devices and kick by identity

Pairing shares a user identity, and the daemon was applying that in one
direction only. `ssh` and the firewall resolve a device to its user
(`device_user_map`) and grant it everything the user has, while admission
keyed on the device id alone: `members.is_member(&remote_id)`. The one
cert-based shortcut, `owner_admits`, fires only for devices paired to the
coordinator's own identity. So on a closed network a phone paired to a
laptop that is already a member arrived as a stranger and queued for an
approval, which reads as a bug the moment you know what pairing means.
`member_admits` closes that: a valid cert naming a seated user is admitted
directly. It grants nothing new, since the user key that signed the cert
could seat a device anyway.

The same split made `kick` ambiguous, and it resolved the ambiguity by
taking whichever roster row matched first. A secondary has no row of its
own, so the name resolved to the user identity and matched the *primary*,
which is normally seated earlier: kicking a phone removed the laptop and
left the phone in the network. It is order-dependent, so nothing about the
outcome was visible from the command.

`kick_targets` removes every row for the user instead, on one published
record, and reports the count. That is the only reading consistent with
what the rest of the daemon does with a pairing, because access cannot be
withdrawn one device at a time when policy resolves to the user. Revoking a
single device stays `ray unpair`, which nullifies its cert mesh-wide rather
than editing one network's roster; the nullifier check on the admission
path is what keeps a revoked device out, and this change does not touch it.

Pulled out as a free function so the selection is unit-testable: the four
cases are a secondary, a primary, an unpaired row (a stale entry left by a
reinstall, which must stay kickable on its own id), and a stranger.

ci: cut duplicate compiles and stop PR runs from evicting the cache

Three things, all in ci.yml.

`save-if` on master only. Every job here saves half a gigabyte or more of
target dir, and a cache written on a pull request branch is readable from
that branch alone, so master never sees it. Those writes only pushed the
repo past the 10 GB per-repo budget, where GitHub evicts by last use and
takes out the master caches these jobs restore from: a recent nightly
restored a five-day-old cache and spent 349s rebuilding. Restores on pull
requests are unaffected.

The `check` job ran `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` and then
`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`. Clippy runs rustc's checks
before its own lints and keeps a separate fingerprint, so that compiled
the tree twice.

The windows job's "cross-target compile" was not cross: windows-latest is
already x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, so naming `--target` only moved the
output into target/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and rebuilt every dependency
there instead of sharing with the test and clippy steps. The clippy step
covers the `ray` bin, `desktop` being a default feature.

fix(dns): re-assert macOS DNS after another VPN deletes it

Mullvad's talpid_dns walks every service in the dynamic store when it
connects, ours included, writes its own resolver over each one, and on
disconnect removes them instead of restoring what it found. Our key is a
session key, so nothing reclaimed State:/Network/Service/rayfish/DNS for
us: .ray went quiet when the other VPN was switched off, not while it was
up, and stayed that way until the next `ray up`. Nothing in the daemon
could see it, either, since the key is written once at apply().

Poll the key every 5s and re-apply when it is gone. A key somebody else
is holding is left alone and logged once: a VPN that owns DNS for the
length of its tunnel re-asserts on a notification of its own, so writing
over it would be two daemons overwriting each other until it disconnects,
which is the fight MERGE_COOLDOWN avoids on Linux. Polling rather than
SCDynamicStoreSetNotificationKeys because a notification needs a store
with a callback context and a thread running a CFRunLoop, and this
backend's store is deliberately built without one.

reassert_os_config now reinstalls the search domains after applying, and
takes the TUN name to do it. apply() writes the whole key from scratch
with `.ray` as its only search domain, so every re-apply dropped the
per-network ones that make a bare `box` resolve until the next join or
leave. That was already true of the exit-node full-tunnel flip, its only
previous caller.

fix(tun): set the Linux TUN link state over netlink

`set_link_state` shelled out to `ip link set` while the address and route
helpers beside it went straight to the kernel. On a host whose service
PATH has no iproute2 that one step failed and everything around it
succeeded: the link was never brought up, so the kernel flushed the
address that had just been assigned and refused the connected route, and
the daemon logged "data plane activated" onto an interface that could not
carry a packet. `ray ping` kept answering, since that rides QUIC streams
on the host's real interfaces and never touches the TUN, so the node
looked reachable while everything through the tunnel vanished. Standby
had the mirror of it: the link stayed up with `200::/7` still routed into
a TUN whose writer drops everything, so traffic black-holed instead of
failing fast.

Link state now goes over netlink through the same `with_tun_link` handle
the address and route already use, which is one fewer binary the daemon
has to find at runtime.

A failed link-up no longer joins the warning list. Nothing after it can
work without it, so activation returns an error and puts the node back on
standby, where `ray status` reporting `active: false` is at least true.
Warnings from a partial activation are logged as well as returned: at
service start nobody is holding the socket to read the reply, so every
one of them was thrown away. And these sites log the whole cause chain
now; `error = %e` on an anyhow error prints only the outermost context,
which is why the one line that did reach the log said "run ip link set"
and not the ENOENT underneath.

The churn scenario repeats its data-plane flap with the host's `ip` binary
moved aside, asserting the link goes down, comes back up, gets its route
and carries traffic, with nothing in the journal about link state.

Found in https://github.com/rayfish/rayfish/issues/144

fix(transport): drop direct-address candidates the host cannot route

A co-resident VPN can take one IP family down without removing its
addresses. Mullvad with IPv6 disabled pulls the v6 default route and
leaves the interface addresses in place, so every v6 send fails with
EHOSTUNREACH while iroh keeps publishing those addresses as ways to
reach the node. Peers dial them, the path opens and immediately closes,
and the two ends churn for as long as the VPN is up.

The candidate filter now asks the routing table before publishing, using
a UDP connect() as a pure route lookup. The probe carries LoopPrevention
because iroh's own sockets do, or the lookup would answer for a table the
transport never uses, and it fails open so only an explicit no-route
verdict drops an address.

Only globally routable candidates are probed. The question is about
reaching the internet, and a LAN-scope address is a path to an on-link
peer regardless of the answer, so probing those would drop a working ULA
on a home network that has no IPv6 from its ISP.

fix(dns): stop the OS-DNS retry loop when the node goes offline

The loop spawned when system-DNS configuration fails is cancelled by
`configure` and `revert`, and by nothing else. Neither runs when a node
goes fully offline: `shutdown_and_close` cancels the daemon token, but the
loop watches its own, and it holds an `Arc<DnsService>` on a runtime that
outlives the daemon. An embedder that rebuilds in-process therefore strands
the whole service on every stop/start.

Android never accepts the handover ("DNS configuration not supported on
this platform"), so a stranded loop never exits on its own: it wakes the
device once a minute for the life of the app and fills the diagnostics ring
with its own retries. A report from a device with three of them had them
crowding out most of the log they were meant to leave room for.

Also cancel in `spawn_configure_retry` rather than only at its call sites.
`configure` and `revert` cancel before calling in, but `recapture` does not,
and a token replaced without being cancelled leaves its loop unreachable.

Ship the app's own logcat with Android diagnostics too. Everything that
decides whether a tunnel comes up at all happens on the Kotlin side, so a
report sent because Rayfish would not come back on arrived showing a healthy
core and no trace of the attempt that failed.

fix(macos): keep the mesh alive under another VPN's kill switch

Connecting Mullvad took the mesh down on the spot and kept it down for as
long as it stayed connected, while the daemon, its routes and its transport
were all healthy. Its pf anchor ends in a catch-all block and everything it
permits is enumerated: its own tunnel and resolvers, and, with local network
sharing on, the private IPv4 ranges plus fc00::/7. The overlay's 200::/7 is
on none of those lists, so packets were dropped on the mesh interface before
they ever reached the TUN reader. Tailscale is unaffected on the same host
only because its ULA falls inside fc00::/7 by chance.

pf evaluates anchor "com.apple/*" before any anchor such a VPN inserts on
connect, so a quick rule loaded under Apple's wildcard terminates evaluation
before that VPN's block is reached. Load one passing traffic on the mesh
interface, alongside the peer-range route, and flush it on the way down.

The rule is stateless on purpose. pfctl applies keep state to a bare pass,
and flushing an anchor leaves the states its rules created, so a 1/sec flow
refreshes one indefinitely and teardown appears to do nothing.

pf is never enabled for this and no starter token is taken: a host with pf
off has nothing blocking the mesh, and turning it on would impose a firewall
the operator did not ask for.

New pf-passthrough setting, on by default, with its own setter so the live
anchor follows it instead of waiting for a restart. Turned off on a host that
is in fact default-denying, activate names the ruleset doing it.

fix(windows): stop the five-second network-record republish loop

Windows implements `sync_all` as `FlushFileBuffers`, which needs a handle
with write access and returns ACCESS_DENIED without one. The durability
re-sync that runs when a config save has nothing to change opened the
file for reading, so on Windows it failed every time.

A coordinator reads that failure as an unsaved roster and retries. It
republished its pkarr network record every 5 seconds instead of every
150, once per network, for as long as the daemon ran, and logged a
warning on each pass.

Open the file for writing instead, and cover the no-op update path with
a test so the workspace run on the Windows runner catches a regression.

fix(join): report why fetching the group blob failed

`ray join` said only "could not fetch group blob from any peer", and the
per-seed warning behind it logged the outermost context alone, which for
a dial failure is a flat "failed to connect to peer". The same applied to
the publish warning that carried the config error above.

Format these with `{e:#}` so the cause chain survives, and name the last
seed and its reason in the message `ray join` prints.

fix(ssh): drop a mesh SSH connection that never authenticates

russh has no equivalent of sshd's LoginGraceTime. Its inactivity timeout
covers an idle established session, is an hour long, and is reset by every
packet that arrives, so nothing bounded the stretch between accepting a
connection and logging in: a peer could hold the socket and the task behind
it for as long as it kept the connection alive without ever proving it was
allowed in. The same gap hid a real failure, where a mesh path stops
carrying the flow partway through the handshake and the server sits on the
half-open connection with nothing in the log after the accept line.

Bound accept to authentication at sixty seconds. The two halves need
separate handling: the version exchange runs inside `run_stream`, before
there is a session, so it is bounded by dropping that future, which takes
the socket with it, while everything after it runs in a task russh owns and
nothing here can cancel. What ends that one is `shutdown(2)` on a duplicate
of the socket, so its next read fails and it drops the handler, and with it
the connection's channels, forwards and agent sockets.

Log the drop at warn with the peer and where it came from, and put the
source port on the accept line so a session that stalls before it
authenticates can be matched to a socket in `ss` output.

fix(dns): name our interface in the macOS Setup: store

Another VPN can read our service's DNS key and still refuse to believe
it. Mullvad's talpid-dns derives Setup:/Network/Service/<id>/Interface
from the State: key it found, and a service without one loads as "no
DNS". Nothing it writes can ever equal that, so every pass decides our
service still needs writing and each write re-triggers the store
notification it is reacting to: every service's resolver, its own and the
physical link's included, rewritten a few times a second for as long as
the tunnel is up. Host name resolution never settles, so the machine has
no working DNS at all, and ours is not the part that breaks.

The same read is what it puts back on disconnect. Without the key it
records "no DNS" for us and removes our resolver on the way out instead
of restoring it, which is the disconnect breakage run_sc_reassert exists
to repair from the other side. With it, the resolver is restored and that
watcher goes back to being a safety net.

Publish the key with the tunnel's device name, and drop it with the rest.
It is not a declared network service: a session key in the dynamic store
is not a preferences entry, and it joins no service set or service order.

fix(dns): re-point the forwarder at resolvers that still answer

The upstream set is captured once, when the OS DNS backend is detected,
and without this it stays that way for the life of the backend. Every way
the host's DNS can move afterwards breaks it: changing network leaves the
old router in the list, and another VPN connecting or disconnecting swaps
the resolvers wholesale. The damaging order is connecting that VPN and
then restarting, because the capture takes its resolvers and keeps
forwarding to them after it goes, so every non-.ray name dies with the
tunnel that is no longer there.

Poll every 15s and probe rather than read the configuration, because the
two disagree in exactly the case that matters: under another VPN's kill
switch the captured resolver is still named by the system and still
route-reachable, and simply never answers. Probing also gets the ordering
right for free, a dead entry at the front otherwise costing every lookup
a full timeout before the working one behind it is tried. A pass that
finds nothing alive changes nothing, since replacing a set that is merely
unreachable this second with an empty one turns a slow forwarder into a
broken one.

macOS only for now, where a foreign VPN moving DNS under us is the case
this came from. The loop shares the re-assert token: both watch the same
host DNS and both are meaningless once the data plane is down.

fix(dns): treat a loopback upstream as a possible loop back into us

Mullvad runs its resolver on a 127.0.0.0/8 address and makes it the
host's only nameserver, so the capture finds it and we forward there.
Point its custom-DNS setting back at us, which is what makes .ray resolve
while its tunnel is up, and the two forward to each other with the host's
whole DNS in the cycle.

Rate-limited rather than dropped, for the reason a foreign mesh's
resolver already was: with that VPN on its default DNS settings its
resolver is the only upstream the capture can see, and it forwards into
the tunnel perfectly well.

feat(tun): name the Linux interface rayfish0 instead of tun0

The kernel's default name says nothing about which program owns the
device, and on a host running more than one tunnel it went to whoever
started first. The builder now asks for `rayfish%d`, TUNSETIFF's own
placeholder, so the kernel still picks the index and a second device
becomes rayfish1 rather than failing with EBUSY.

Nothing inside the daemon assumed the name; it reads back off the fd and
flows through the firewall, DNS and exit-node paths as a string.

macOS numbers its own utunN and will not take another name, and the
FreeBSD tun cloner insists on a tun prefix, so both are unchanged.
Windows already named its adapter rayfish.

fix(config): use reentrant user/group lookups (musl heap crash)

getgrnam and getpwnam return pointers into a process-wide buffer that
any concurrent lookup is allowed to move or free. Config saves run on
many threads at once, and on musl that race corrupted the heap: an
Alpine laptop's daemon crash-looped 136 times in a day with SIGSEGV,
and the concurrent-saves regression test segfaulted on unmodified
master. Both call sites now use the reentrant `_r` forms, which copy
into a caller-owned buffer.

Reproduced standalone on musl 1.2.6: 24 threads calling getgrnam
200k times each segfault inside the allocator; the same loop with
getgrnam_r completes cleanly. With the patch the full lib suite
(745 tests) passes on the machine where it previously crashed.

fix(dns): keep Magic DNS up when the router drops root-NS probes

Some consumer-router forwarders answer every dotted query but go
silent for root-zone ones, so the upstream liveness probe read a
healthy resolver as dead and the DNS takeover refused to run, leaving
the host without Magic DNS. The probe now falls back to an
`example.com A` question before giving up on an upstream, and a mock
resolver that drops root queries pins the behavior in tests.

Seen in the wild on 0.4.0: `.ray` names unresolvable for five days on
an Alpine host behind such a router while the mesh data plane stayed
healthy.

fix(ssh): offer no compression, so zlib clients keep their sessions

Russh's zlib is broken on the receive side: with `zlib@openssh.com`
negotiated, the second SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_DATA an OpenSSH client sends fails
to decompress and the connection dies with `SshEncoding: length invalid`.
The first message always works, so the session opens, prints the motd,
runs one command -- and then drops as soon as a second one is typed.

`Compression yes` in ssh_config is what selects that path, and it is
common enough that people hit it before anything else. Neither side says
why: the client reports "closed by remote host", the server logs only the
encoding error.

Offer "none" alone until russh's zlib is fixed. Traffic on a mesh link is
small and latency-bound; compressing it buys nothing worth a session that
cannot survive a second keystroke.

Russh's own client interoperates with russh's zlib, so a client/server
test here passes either way. The test reads the server's KEXINIT off the
wire instead and pins the advertisement.
